uc-ai-product-search.approach: Move from problem to production: first confirm that you genuinely need semantics (rather than a keyword fix), then prepare the catalog data, build embeddings and an index, add ranking and filters, measure quality on real queries, and only then roll out to the storefront under an A/B test. Every step produces a verifiable result so you don't build blind.
outcomes: You understand when semantics are truly needed versus just cleaning up keyword search
The catalog is prepared and turned into vectors, the index is built and re-indexes itself
Hybrid ranking works: keyword + semantic + availability and category filters
Search quality is measured with numbers (no-results rate, conversion, top clicks), not by feel
Search is rolled out to the storefront via an A/B test with a rollback path

applyIn.title: Large e-commerce catalog
applyIn.description: Catalog >5k SKUs where >15% of search sessions end in "no results" due to synonyms and phrasing.

applyIn.title: Multilingual storefront
applyIn.description: A site in several languages where keyword search fails to bridge queries and product descriptions across languages.

applyIn.title: Catalog with rich descriptions
applyIn.description: Products with detailed attributes and use cases that people search for "by meaning" rather than by exact name.

pitfalls: Replacing keyword search entirely: keyword wins on SKUs and exact codes — hybrid is mandatory
Not re-indexing the catalog: products change and sell out, and without index updates search shows out-of-stock items
Launching with no feedback loop: without click and purchase data, ranking never improves
Ignoring query analytics: AI searches well but doesn't explain why people search for "X" — that's a separate task
Rolling out with no A/B test: you can't prove the conversion lift and can't justify the embeddings cost

exercises.question: How do you use data to decide whether you need semantics or your keyword search quality is the problem?
exercises.hint: Look at the share of "no results" sessions and their queries: synonyms and phrasing mean you need semantics; typos and missing facets mean fix keyword.

exercises.question: Why is hybrid (keyword + semantic) better than pure semantics for a catalog?
exercises.hint: Semantics blurs exact matches on SKUs, codes and brands where keyword is more precise. Hybrid takes the best of both.

exercises.question: Which 3 metrics will you watch in the A/B test to call the launch a success?
exercises.hint: No-results rate, search conversion and time-to-first-click — all three should move the right way without a rise in complaints.

s1.title: Understand when semantics are needed and the target outcome
s1.why: Semantic search costs money on embeddings and infrastructure. Before building, you must prove the problem is genuinely about query meaning and not a broken keyword search. Otherwise you're solving the wrong problem.
instructions: Export search queries for 1-3 months and compute the share of sessions with "no results"
Label the failed queries: typos, missing facets are keyword; synonyms, meaning-based descriptions, other languages are semantic
Compare the scenario against neighboring cases in [[node:use-cases|use-cases]] so you don't rebuild a ready pattern
Fix the target outcome in numbers: no-results rate, search conversion, time-to-first-click
Decide the boundary: what stays with keyword (SKUs, codes) and what goes to semantics
s1.validate: You have a table of failed queries tagged "keyword/semantic" and the share of semantic failures is above the threshold that justifies the project.
s1.tip: If almost all failures are typos and missing filters, fix keyword first: it's cheaper and faster than semantics.

s2.title: Prepare the catalog and data
s2.why: Semantic search quality is never higher than the quality of the data you vectorize. Dirty, incomplete or inconsistent product records produce noisy embeddings and poor relevance.
instructions: Assemble a single text per SKU: name, key attributes, category, use cases
Clean the data: remove duplicates, empty descriptions, HTML junk, normalize units and categories
Add fields for filters: availability (in/out of stock), price, brand, record language
Fix the product document schema so re-indexing is reproducible
Set aside a small set of real queries with their "correct" products for later evaluation
s2.validate: You have a clean, consistent set of product records with fields for embedding and for filtering, plus a held-out query set for evaluation.
s2.tip: Build the embedding text deliberately: what's in it can be found, what's not in it will never be found.

s3.title: Build embeddings and a vector index
s3.why: This is the technical core: product records become vectors, and a vector index lets you find the products closest in meaning to a user's query in milliseconds.
instructions: Pick an embedding model per [[node:af-embeddings|af-embeddings]] (multilingual for a multilingual catalog)
Run the whole catalog through embeddings in batches and store vectors alongside product metadata
Stand up a vector store per [[node:af-vector-db|af-vector-db]] and load the index into it
Set up the re-indexing pipeline: new and changed products update their vectors automatically
Run sanity-check queries and confirm the nearest neighbors look meaningful
s3.validate: A test query returns a meaningful product list from the index in acceptable time, and a changed product is found correctly after re-indexing.
s3.tip: The same embedding model must be used for both the catalog and the queries — otherwise the vectors aren't comparable.

s4.title: Set up ranking and filters
s4.why: Raw vector proximity is not the final result list. You need to blend keyword and semantic into a hybrid, add reranking and mandatory filters (availability, category), otherwise users see irrelevant or sold-out products.
instructions: Assemble a hybrid result: keyword for exact matches + semantic for meaning, with weights
Add reranking of the top candidates by relevance to the query
Apply hard filters: don't show out-of-stock, respect the chosen category/price/language
Account for business rules: boost by margin, new arrivals or promos where appropriate
Test edge queries: exact SKU, broad meaning-based query, query in another language
s4.validate: On control queries keyword finds exact SKUs, semantic finds meaning-based ones, sold-out items don't appear, and the top results look relevant.
s4.tip: Start with simple hybrid weights and tune them based on evaluation results, not by guessing upfront.

s5.title: Evaluate search quality
s5.why: Without measurable evaluation you won't know whether it got better, and you can't justify the cost. Search quality is evaluated on real queries with numbers, not by feel.
instructions: Run the held-out query set and measure whether the "correct" product lands in the top results
Compare the new hybrid search against the old keyword search on the same queries
Measure no-results rate, the position of the relevant product, and the share of meaningful top results
Collect a blind rating from several people across a sample of queries to remove bias
Set up query analytics: which queries are frequent, which fail, what to search for next
s5.validate: You have a before/after table of key metrics, and hybrid search measurably beats the old keyword search on failed queries.
s5.tip: Analyze frequent failed queries separately — they directly tell you which products or synonyms to add to the catalog.

s6.title: Roll out to the storefront and launch checklist
s6.why: Search only drives revenue in production. Roll it out under an A/B test to prove the conversion lift on real money and keep a rollback path, then anchor it in the broader e-commerce loop.
instructions: Integrate hybrid search into the storefront per the [[node:ai-native-ecommerce|ai-native-ecommerce]] pattern
Launch an A/B test: part of traffic on the new search, part on the old one, for a meaningful period
Wire up the feedback loop: clicks and purchases flow back into ranking
Set up monitoring and alerts: latency, no-results rate, share of out-of-stock in results
Run the launch checklist: re-indexing works, filters are strict, rollback plan exists, metrics are up
s6.validate: The A/B test shows a statistically significant rise in search conversion and a drop in no-results rate, monitoring is green, and a rollback plan is ready.
s6.tip: Don't kill the A/B test the next day: let it accumulate enough sessions, or the lift turns out to be random noise.

uc-ai-conversion-optimization.title: Launch an AI-Augmented CRO Program
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.subtitle: From scattered tests to a structured, AI-augmented conversion-optimization program
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.whatItIs: A step-by-step scenario for launching a conversion-rate-optimization (CRO) program where Claude accelerates the team 5-10×: it generates hypotheses, helps read the data, and collapses post-mortems from days into hours. This isn't "AI does CRO" — it's "AI removes the bottlenecks at the front (ideas) and the back (synthesis)", while the A/B testing tool in between stays the same. Fits as one of the [[node:use-cases|use cases]] for [[node:ai-native-ecommerce|AI-native e-commerce]].
uc-ai-conversion-optimization.approach: We move from diagnosis to a loop. First we confirm CRO is even warranted (traffic, plateau, an existing function), then map the funnel and its bottlenecks. Claude then generates a stream of hypotheses, we disciplinedly select them into experiments, read the results correctly, and close the improvement loop with a checklist. AI expands throughput; the human keeps prioritization discipline and the final call.
outcomes: Hypothesis throughput grows from 2-3 to 10-15 per week — not via chaos, but via a structured backlog
An experiment post-mortem takes 2 hours instead of 2 days
Every hypothesis is prioritized by a clear framework (impact / confidence / effort), not by gut feel
Cumulative conversion uplift per quarter: +15-25% with the discipline of one variable per test
The team has a repeatable loop and launch checklist instead of one-off bursts of activity

applyIn.title: E-commerce funnel
applyIn.description: Product page, cart, checkout: Claude generates headline variants, benefit copy, and CTA microcopy while you test one variable at a time.

applyIn.title: SaaS onboarding and subscription
applyIn.description: Trial-to-paid, activation, pricing page: hypotheses about value framing and objection handling, validated on segments with enough traffic.

applyIn.title: Lead forms and landing pages
applyIn.description: Fewer fields, reworked value proposition, social proof: a fast ideation loop where conversion has plateaued and ideas have run dry.

pitfalls: Trusting AI variants without human review — Claude doesn't know your product and makes factual errors about features and prices
Testing everything: AI generates plenty, but a valid test = one variable over 2+ weeks. Discipline beats speed
Running tests on traffic where statistical significance is unreachable (<10k visitors/month per segment) — the findings are noise
Treating AI as a replacement for the CRO specialist: prioritization and the "ship to prod" decision stay with the human
Stopping a test the moment it "looks like a win" — peeking destroys the reliability of the result

exercises.question: Your site gets 4,000 visitors a month and conversion has been flat for 4 months. Should you launch a full AI CRO program right now?
exercises.hint: Look at the significance threshold in step 1: at that traffic an A/B test per segment accrues significance over months. Maybe start with qualitative methods (surveys, session replay) and growing traffic.

exercises.question: Claude proposed 12 hypotheses for the product page. What do you do next, before launching a single test?
exercises.hint: Recall steps 3 and 4: hypotheses go through human review for factual errors, then prioritization by impact/confidence/effort, and one variable goes into the experiment — not all 12 at once.

exercises.question: A test has run 5 days, variant B is already 8% ahead. The manager wants to "ship B". Your answer?
exercises.hint: Step 5: 5 days and no stated statistical significance is peeking. Wait for the pre-committed sample size and confidence interval, or you risk locking in randomness.

s1.title: Confirm you need a CRO program and lock in the target outcome
s1.why: An AI CRO program only makes sense with enough traffic and a real plateau. Launching "on 2,000 visits" yields noise instead of insight and erodes trust in the program from month one.
instructions: Check the entry conditions: traffic >10k visitors/month on the key segment, conversion plateaued for 3+ months, at least 1 person on the CRO function
Define one measurable program goal (e.g. +15% to checkout conversion this quarter)
Record the current baseline of the key metric — without it you can't prove growth
Decide what AI accelerates (ideation + synthesis) and what stays with the human (prioritization, the ship decision)
s1.validate: You have a written yes/no on launching and one measurable goal with a recorded baseline.
s1.tip: If you lack traffic, don't force A/B tests. Start with qualitative methods (surveys, session recordings) and traffic growth, then structured CRO.

s2.title: Gather funnel data and find the bottlenecks
s2.why: Hypotheses must come from data, not taste. Without a funnel map and drop-off points, AI will generate plausible but irrelevant ideas.
instructions: Build the funnel step by step (visit, then product, then cart, then checkout, then payment) and compute each transition's conversion
Find the 1-2 steps with the biggest drop-off — these are the priority zones for tests
Collect qualitative context: session recordings, surveys, frequent support complaints
Load anonymized data and a funnel description into Claude as context for analysis
Ask Claude to surface patterns and articulate exactly where users are lost
s2.validate: 1-2 funnel bottlenecks are identified with drop-off numbers and qualitative confirmation.
s2.tip: Don't hand AI a raw table without explaining the metrics — the model will guess column meanings wrong. Describe what each one is.

s3.title: Generate hypotheses with Claude
s3.why: Ideation is the main CRO bottleneck. This is where AI gives the biggest lift: 10-15 structured hypotheses a week instead of 2-3 improvised ones.
instructions: Give Claude context: the bottleneck from step 2, a product description, the audience, the baseline
Request hypotheses in one format: "If we change X, metric Y will rise, because Z"
Run human review on each hypothesis for factual errors about the product, prices and features
Filter out anything that can't be tested with a single variable or measured
Put the surviving hypotheses into one structured backlog
s3.validate: There is a backlog of 8-15 hypotheses in one format that have passed a factual-correctness check.
s3.tip: Make Claude state the reason (Z) in every hypothesis — it filters out "because it looks nicer" ideas and eases prioritization.

s4.title: Design A/B experiments and prioritize the backlog
s4.why: Without design discipline the program turns into test chaos. One test = one variable at a time; otherwise you can't tell what actually worked.
instructions: Prioritize the backlog by an impact / confidence / effort framework and take the top 2-3 hypotheses
For each, define one variable under test, plus control and treatment variants
Pre-commit the success metric, required sample size and test duration
Ask Claude to help compute duration from traffic and draft variant B
Schedule tests so they don't overlap on the same funnel zone
s4.validate: The top hypotheses have experiment cards: one variable, metric, sample size and duration locked before start.
s4.tip: Lock duration and sample size BEFORE launch. It's the only defense against the urge to stop a test on a random peak. Details in the [[node:ec-cro|CRO node]].

s5.title: Analyze results and collapse the post-mortem
s5.why: A post-mortem usually takes days and often never gets done. Claude collapses synthesis into hours — the second frontier where AI gives a breakthrough.
instructions: Wait for the pre-committed sample and duration — don't stop the test early
Check statistical significance and the confidence interval, not just the difference in means
Pass Claude the results and ask for a post-mortem draft: what was tested, what happened, why
Separate a reliable result from noise and inconclusive effects
Record the conclusion and decision: ship to prod, roll back, or retest
s5.validate: Each completed test has a post-mortem with a conclusion, a significance assessment and a decision.
s5.tip: AI drafts, the human rules. Never ship a variant to prod just because "the number is higher" — without significance it's a coincidence.

s6.title: Close the improvement loop and lock in a launch checklist
s6.why: CRO isn't a series of one-off tests but a repeatable loop. Without a checklist and a regular cadence the program fades after the first burst of enthusiasm.
instructions: Feed past-test insights back into ideation — wins spawn new hypotheses
Set a rhythm: e.g. 2-3 active tests in flight and a weekly review
Assemble a launch checklist: conditions, then data, then hypotheses, then design, then analysis, then decision
Document which steps Claude does and where human review is mandatory
Track cumulative uplift against the step 1 baseline, not individual wins
s6.validate: There is a written repeatable loop with a checklist and a set cadence; the first 2-3 pilot tests ran through it.
s6.tip: Discipline beats speed: 3 clean tests a quarter beat 30 dirty ones. Grow the program toward a broader [[node:ec-cro|experimentation system]].

ops-process-automation.title: AI Process Automation
ops-process-automation.subtitle: Turn recurring routine into a reliable pipeline of trigger, then AI, then result
ops-process-automation.whatItIs: A practical course on taking a recurring team process (onboarding, status updates, routine comms) and building it into an automation following the pattern input (trigger), then AI processing, then output (result + next action). The core stack is Skills, Hooks and RAG. This is part of [[node:ai-native-operations|AI-native operations]].
ops-process-automation.approach: Start from the process, not the technology. First pick a candidate by three criteria (frequency ≥5×/week, clear inputs/outputs, validatable result), describe it as-is, then break it into trigger and AI-processing steps, embed a quality gate, and only then scale. The golden rule: you can only automate a stabilized process.
outcomes: You can select candidate processes by frequency, clarity and validatability
You describe a process as-is: trigger, input data, steps, output, owner
You build an AI pipeline: trigger, then AI processing, then output with a next action
You embed a quality gate so a human reviews the result in minutes instead of redoing it for hours
You roll out the automation and scale it to similar processes using a readiness checklist

applyIn.title: Weekly status digest
applyIn.description: Trigger Monday 9am, then AI reads Linear/Jira for the week, then writes an executive summary in branded style, then human reviews for 15 min, then publishes to Slack. Was 2 hours, now 15 minutes.

applyIn.title: Onboarding and welcome comms
applyIn.description: A new client or hire is the trigger, then AI prepares a personalized email/checklist from a template and context, then the owner reviews and sends. Consistent quality instead of "depends who did it".

applyIn.title: Routine reports and digests
applyIn.description: A regular roll-up from several sources: AI gathers data, normalizes it, formats it into one consistent shape. Ideal for recurring tasks with clear inputs/outputs.

pitfalls: Automating a process that hasn't stabilized yet: if it changes weekly, the automation will constantly break. Stabilize manually first
Choosing a task with no clear inputs/outputs: AI can't produce a predictable result, and checking it takes longer than doing it by hand
Removing the human from the loop entirely: without a quality gate, errors ship and erode trust in the automation
Automating rare tasks (<5×/week): the payoff won't cover the setup and maintenance cost
Ignoring process drift: over time data sources and formats change — without monitoring the pipeline quietly degrades

exercises.question: Take your team and list 3 tasks done more than 5 times a week. For each, check: are there clear inputs/outputs and can the result be validated?
exercises.hint: Ideal candidates are weekly reports, welcome emails, internal digests. If a task has no stable output format, it isn't ready for automation yet.

exercises.question: For one chosen process, describe the pipeline: what is the trigger, what data does the AI read, what is the output, and what next action does it start?
exercises.hint: Use the pattern input (trigger), then AI processing, then output (result + next action). The trigger is a schedule or command; the next action is publishing, sending, or escalating.

exercises.question: Where in your pipeline should the quality gate sit, and how many minutes will the human review take?
exercises.hint: Compare how long the task took by hand versus the review. The goal is 70-90% savings while keeping quality.

s1.title: Why this and what result
s1.why: Without a clear goal, automation becomes a technical experiment with no payoff. Every team has 30-50% recurring tasks, and those deliver 70-90% time savings plus consistent quality instead of "depends who did it" variance.
instructions: State the pain the automation removes: lost time, uneven quality, forgotten steps
Fix the expected result in numbers: e.g. "was 2 hours a week — becomes 15 minutes of review"
Describe the principle: input (trigger), then AI processing, then output (result + next action)
Define what counts as success: both time savings and stable quality
s1.validate: You can name, in one sentence, the process, its current time cost, and the target saving.
s1.tip: Count not only minutes but consistency: a single uniform result is often worth more than the time saving itself.

s2.title: Where to start: process and data as-is
s2.why: You can only automate a stabilized process. If it changes weekly, the AI pipeline will constantly break. First you must see reality as it is.
instructions: Select a candidate by three criteria: done ≥5×/week, has clear inputs/outputs, the result can be validated
Describe the process as-is: trigger, input data and its sources, sequence of steps, output, owner
Check stability: has the output format changed over the last month
If the process isn't stabilized yet — stabilize it manually first and postpone automation
s2.validate: You have a written as-is description of the process with explicit inputs, outputs, and confirmation the format is stable.
s2.tip: Ideal first candidates: weekly reports, customer welcome emails, internal status digests.

s3.title: Key step 1: trigger and input collection
s3.why: The pipeline begins with the input. A reliable trigger and clean input data determine how predictable the whole result will be.
instructions: Choose the trigger type: schedule (Monday 9am) or command (/command)
Identify the data sources the AI reads: Linear, Jira, CRM, documents
Set up collection via the right stack mechanism: Hooks for triggers, RAG for pulling context
Make sure the input data is available the moment the trigger fires and in a stable format
s3.validate: The trigger fires at the right moment and the AI receives a complete, correct input set.
s3.tip: Start with a scheduled trigger — it's easier to debug than an event-based one and simpler to validate.

s4.title: Key step 2: AI processing and output
s4.why: This is the heart of the pipeline: the AI turns input data into a finished result and starts the next action. This is also where branded style and consistent quality are locked in.
instructions: Break processing into explicit AI steps: e.g. "read the week's data" and "write a summary in branded style"
Package repeating logic as a Skill so it's reused and not duplicated — see [[node:skills|Skills]]
Describe the output format precisely: structure, tone, length, required fields
Define the next action: publish to Slack, send an email, create a task
s4.validate: On a test input the AI produces a result in the right format and style, ready for human review.
s4.tip: The more precisely the output format is defined, the fewer edits at the quality gate — format saves more time than the model itself.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: Without review, errors ship and erode trust in the automation. The quality gate preserves the time saving without sacrificing quality.
instructions: Embed a quality gate: a human does the final review of the result before output
Measure review time and compare it to manual work — target 70-90% savings
List the risks: process drift, changing data sources, shifting output format
Set up monitoring and an escalation point for when the AI is unsure or data is incomplete
s5.validate: Every result passes a human review in minutes, and degradation risks are documented and tracked.
s5.tip: A 15-minute quality gate instead of 2 hours of writing is still a win; don't try to remove the human entirely at the start.

s6.title: Rollout and scale + checklist
s6.why: One working pipeline is a pilot. The value unlocks when you carry the approach to similar processes without breaking the system. This is the path to [[node:ai-native-operations|AI-native operations]].
instructions: Launch the automation in production mode and watch several cycles
Assemble a readiness checklist: stabilized process, clear inputs/outputs, working trigger, precise output format, quality gate, monitoring
Find 2-3 similar processes and apply the same template, reusing Skills
Document each pipeline so the team can maintain and evolve it without you
s6.validate: The automation runs stably for several cycles, the readiness checklist is passed, and there's a plan to carry it to neighboring processes.
s6.tip: Scale one process at a time — that way it's easier to catch drift and avoid an avalanche of broken pipelines.

ops-decision-intelligence.title: AI Decision Intelligence
ops-decision-intelligence.subtitle: AI as a "second opinion" for operational decisions: it structures the analysis, the human decides
ops-decision-intelligence.whatItIs: An approach where AI acts as a discipline tool for operational decisions: it analyzes data, context, and the history of past decisions, then produces a structured recommendation following a single template (context, then options, then pros/cons/cost/risk, then analysis, then human decision). AI does not replace the human — it forces the process to be consistent: consider alternatives, assess risks, tie the decision to metrics.
ops-decision-intelligence.approach: You introduce a single decision template for decisions worth >$10k impact or with a >2-week horizon. AI runs the situation through pattern-matching against past decisions and gives a recommendation with reasoning. The final decision and accountability stay with the human, but the reasoning and the outcome are logged — so that after a few months you see the patterns: where AI was right, where it erred, where intuition misled you.
outcomes: 50-70% reduction in reactive "gut-feel" decisions
Every significant decision passes through an explicit set of alternatives, risks, and metrics
Decision quality becomes measurable: you track outcomes and compare them to the forecast
A decision base with reasoning accumulates — personal and team patterns become visible
AI works as a "thoughtful junior": it offers perspective but carries no accountability

applyIn.title: Hiring and team
applyIn.description: Hire/no-hire decisions: AI structures the candidate against role requirements and past hires, surfacing risks and gaps before the offer.

applyIn.title: Resources and budget
applyIn.description: Resource allocation and vendor selection: comparing options by cost/risk/impact, checked against past spend and its actual payoff.

applyIn.title: Process changes
applyIn.description: Process change vs no-change: AI helps assess whether a workflow is worth changing, and the cost of inaction versus the cost of change.

pitfalls: Blindly following the AI recommendation — AI does not know your full context; the decision and accountability are yours
Applying the heavy template to minor decisions — it is for >$10k impact or >2-week horizons, otherwise you drown in bureaucracy
Not logging reasoning and outcome — without this you will never see patterns or be able to measure quality
Feeding AI incomplete or skewed context — bad input makes even good pattern-matching produce a bad recommendation
Using AI to offload accountability ("the AI advised it") instead of as a discipline tool

exercises.question: Take a real operational decision you recently made "by gut". Run it through the template retroactively: context, 3 options, pros/cons/cost/risk for each. Does your choice match what the structured analysis would suggest?
exercises.hint: If the structure surfaced an option you did not even consider, that is exactly the reactive gap this approach closes.

exercises.question: Define the threshold at which a decision goes through the template rather than "by gut". How exactly will you measure $10k impact or a 2-week horizon in your context?
exercises.hint: The threshold must be unambiguous so you do not argue each time. Tie it to money, time, or reversibility of the decision.

exercises.question: Pick 3 closed decisions and compare the forecast to the actual outcome. Where was AI right, where wrong, where was your intuition more accurate than the analysis?
exercises.hint: The goal is not to "prove" AI is good, but to find zones where its recommendations can be trusted and where your override is needed.

s1.title: Why this matters and what you get
s1.why: Operational decisions under pressure are often made "by gut" — without considering alternatives or risks. This produces reactive decisions whose quality you can neither assess nor improve. The aim of the approach is process discipline, not replacing the human.
instructions: Pin down the problem: which of your decisions are made reactively and what they cost when wrong
State the target outcome: 50-70% fewer reactive decisions and measurable decision quality
Adopt the core principle: AI is a "thoughtful junior" offering perspective, not the final arbiter
Write down 3-5 recent decisions you would want to run through the structure going forward
s1.validate: You have a list of real decision types and understand why the current process produces reactive outcomes.
s1.tip: Do not sell yourself "AI will decide for me". Sell "AI will not let me skip an alternative or a risk".

s2.title: Where to start: threshold and template
s2.why: The approach only works on decisions worth it. Without a clear threshold you will either apply the heavy template to trivia or forget to apply it at all. A single template is the contract that makes all decisions comparable.
instructions: Define the entry threshold: decisions with >$10k impact or a >2-week horizon (adapt to your scale)
Fix the 5-block template: context, then options, then pros/cons/cost/risk, then AI analysis, then human decision + log
Decide where the decision log lives: a doc, a sheet, or a note — what matters is that every decision lands there
Agree with yourself/the team: below the threshold, decide as before; above it, only through the template
s2.validate: The threshold is unambiguous, the template is written down, and there is a place where decisions and their reasoning are logged.
s2.tip: Start with one decision type (e.g. vendor selection) rather than all at once — the template gets battle-tested faster.

s3.title: Key step 1: context and options
s3.why: Recommendation quality depends entirely on the input. A concise, honest context and a set of real alternatives are what separate a structured decision from rationalizing one already made. AI cannot find an option you never showed it.
instructions: Describe the situation in 5 sentences: what is happening, what forces a decision now, what the constraints are
Formulate at least 3 options, including a "change nothing" variant where applicable
For each option write out pros, cons, cost, and risk — briefly, but without hiding known downsides
Give AI the full context: data, constraints, and the history of similar decisions if available
Check that you have not tailored the options to a pre-desired answer
s3.validate: AI has an honest context and 3+ real options with pros/cons/cost/risk — no hidden downsides.
s3.tip: If all options but one look clearly bad, you probably have not found the real alternatives. Dig further.

s4.title: Key step 2: AI analyzes, the human decides
s4.why: This is the heart of the approach: AI does pattern-matching against past decisions and gives a structured recommendation, but the decision and accountability stay with the human. AI knows patterns but does not know your full context — so an explicit human override is required.
instructions: Ask AI to match the situation against past decisions and produce a recommendation with reasoning
Read AI's reasoning critically: what assumptions it made, what context it lacks
Make the final decision yourself — matching AI, or an override if your context demands it
Log it: the chosen option, the reason, agreement/disagreement with AI and why
Record the expected outcome and the metric by which you will later check correctness
s4.validate: The decision was made by the human and recorded together with the reasoning, AI's position, and the expected measurable outcome.
s4.tip: An override is not an AI failure. A logged divergence "I decided otherwise because..." is the most valuable material for future patterns.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: Without quality control the approach degenerates into theater: a nice template with no impact on outcomes. And blind trust in AI is the main risk: it is strong at pattern analysis but carries no accountability and does not see your full context.
instructions: After 1-3 months, compare forecasts to actual outcomes on the logged decisions
Mark where AI was right, where it erred, and where your override turned out correct
Identify AI's systematic weak spots in your domain and log them as "mandatory override zones"
Check that the template has not become a formality — every decision genuinely considers alternatives
Track the share of reactive decisions: the target is a 50-70% reduction
s5.validate: There is a "forecast vs actual" table, the AI trust zones are clear, and the downward trend in reactive decisions is visible.
s5.tip: Trust in AI is calibrated by domain: in some it is reliably accurate, in others not. Do not trust "in general" — trust by zone.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: The approach only pays off as a sustained habit, not a one-off experiment. Rollout cements the threshold, the template, and the review ritual so decisions pass through the structure automatically.
instructions: Make the decision template easy to reach: a link, a snippet, or a pinned prompt
Build outcome review into a regular cadence (e.g. monthly) — without it there will be no patterns
Extend the approach to the next decision type only after the first one is battle-tested
Agree that no above-threshold decision ships without a logged reasoning
Once a quarter, revisit the threshold and the AI trust zones based on accumulated data
s6.validate: The template is at hand, the review ritual is scheduled, and you/the team follow the rule "above threshold — only through the structure".
s6.tip: Readiness checklist: threshold set ✓ template available ✓ log maintained ✓ outcome review in the calendar ✓ override zones known ✓

ops-reporting-automation.title: Operational Reporting Automation
ops-reporting-automation.subtitle: Turn 4 hours of manual reporting into 30 minutes of review
ops-reporting-automation.whatItIs: A course on building auto-generated recurring reports from structured data (CRM, analytics, project management). AI reads the data export, writes an insight-driven narrative and forms action items, while the human keeps review and executive judgment. The goal is not "pretty text" but a report structured as "what changed, then why, then what we do, then KPI".
ops-reporting-automation.approach: We move from pain to a working pipeline: first lock down why and the target result, then connect data sources, design the template/format, set up generation with number verification, close quality risks, and roll out with a checklist. Each step produces a verifiable artifact so the pipeline doesn't stay a demo.
outcomes: Cut time-to-report from 4 hours to ~30 minutes of review
One format, tone and structure for the whole team
Reports arrive on schedule, not "when I got around to it"
Every report ends with concrete action items, not just description
Numbers are reconciled with the source — data accuracy 100% (autopull)

applyIn.title: Sales / Revenue weekly
applyIn.description: Export deals and pipeline from CRM (HubSpot/Salesforce), then executive summary + 3 action items for the sales lead every week.

applyIn.title: Product / Analytics monthly
applyIn.description: Data from analytics (activation, retention, key metrics), then monthly report with trends and priorities for the next sprint.

applyIn.title: Project / Delivery status
applyIn.description: Export tasks from project management, then status report: what shipped, where the blockers are, what's at risk, what we do next.

pitfalls: A report without action items is trash: AI generates "pretty text" with no recommendations to act on
Not reconciling AI numbers with the source: the model may rephrase or round data incorrectly
Changing format week to week — consistency is lost, the audience can't compare
Automating a process where data can't be pulled via API/export — the pipeline collapses into manual entry
Removing the human from the loop entirely: executive judgment and final review stay with the human

exercises.question: You have a weekly sales report a manager assembles by hand in 4 hours. Which three conditions must you check before automating it with AI?
exercises.hint: Recall the "when to apply" block: regularity, data access via API/export, countable KPIs.

exercises.question: AI produced a report with a nice narrative but no "what we do" section. Why is such a report useless and how do you fix the prompt?
exercises.hint: Structure must be: what changed, then why, then what we do, then KPI. Action items are mandatory — write them into the format.

exercises.question: How do you make sure the numbers in the auto-report match the real data from the CRM?
exercises.hint: Autopull gives 100% accuracy only if AI doesn't recompute by hand. Add a step reconciling final figures with the export.

s1.title: Why and the target result
s1.why: Without a clear goal, automation becomes a text generator. Teams spend 4-8 hours a week on manual reporting — lock down that AI handles 80%, leaving the human with review and executive judgment.
instructions: Pick ONE recurring report (weekly/monthly) currently assembled by hand
Record current cost: how many hours and who spends them on assembly
Define the target: time-to-report from 4h to 30 min, one format for all
Identify the audience and what decision they make from the report
Lock down that 20% (review, executive judgment) stays with the human
s1.validate: You have a one-page brief: which report, who the audience is, how much time we save, what result we expect.
s1.tip: Pick the report that hurts most and repeats most often — automation ROI is then visible immediately.

s2.title: Data sources
s2.why: Reporting automation only works on structured data with API or export. If data can't be pulled programmatically, the pipeline collapses into manual entry and accuracy won't be 100%.
instructions: List every system the numbers come from: CRM, analytics, project management
Check each: is there an API or at least a regular CSV export
Describe the export format — which fields, units, period (per week/month)
Make sure the needed KPIs can be computed from this data
Run one test export and save a sample for the template
s2.validate: You have a real data file (e.g. CSV from CRM) for one period, from which all needed KPIs are computed.
s2.tip: If a field can't be exported automatically — either drop it from the report or set up the export first. Manual entry kills consistency.

s3.title: Report template and format
s3.why: One format, one tone — everywhere. The template locks the structure "what changed, then why, then what we do, then KPI" so the audience gets consistency and can compare reports across periods.
instructions: Describe a strict structure: executive summary, then key numbers and trends, then action items, then KPI
Create a Project with a system prompt: "you are a sales analyst, report format is XYZ"
Set the tone and length of each section (e.g. 3 action items, no more)
Add example phrasings for trends ("grew X% vs last week")
Lock the template separately — it must not change period to period
s3.validate: You have a ready Project with a system prompt where the report structure is written so two different runs produce the same format.
s3.tip: The system prompt in a Project is the place for role and format. Don't duplicate the format in every prompt — keep it in one source of truth.

s4.title: Generation and verification
s4.why: This is where the report is born: AI reads the period's data, writes an insight-driven narrative and forms action items. But numbers must be reconciled with the source — the model must not recompute by hand.
instructions: Pass the data export into the Project: "here is the week's data, write executive summary + 3 action items"
Get a draft: numbers, trends, recommendations in the template format
Reconcile every key number in the report with the original export
Check there's an action items section — what specifically we do
Run 2-3 periods of data to confirm format repeatability
s4.validate: A report is generated where all numbers match the source, action items are present, and the format is identical to the template across several runs.
s4.tip: Ask AI to cite the source of a number ("sales 120k — from the Total row in the CSV") so reconciliation takes seconds, not minutes.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: The main risk is "pretty text without action" and number mismatches. We close these failures with rules, otherwise the auto-report loses trust and people stop reading it.
instructions: Introduce a rule: a report without action items is not released
Add mandatory reconciliation of final figures with the export before sending
Lock down that the format doesn't change without an explicit decision — consistency over novelty
Describe what to do with empty/broken data (don't invent numbers)
Assign a human to final review and executive judgment
s5.validate: You have a list of 4-5 quality rules by which any report can be checked in a minute before sending.
s5.tip: The structure "what changed, then why, then what we do, then KPI" is itself the quality filter. Missing one block — the report isn't ready.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A pipeline is only valuable when it runs on schedule without you. Rollout turns one-off generation into a recurring process with an owner and a checklist.
instructions: Describe the schedule: when the export runs, when it's generated and who sends the report
Build a release checklist: data current, then numbers reconciled, then action items present, then format matches
Assign a process owner and a person for review
Run the first full cycle by the checklist from export to send
Measure the new time-to-report and compare with the original 4 hours
s6.validate: A report for a real period is released by the checklist, there's an owner and a schedule, time is cut to ~30 minutes of review.
s6.tip: Keep a human nearby for the first 2-3 cycles for control, then reduce their involvement to final review.

ops-resource-optimization.title: AI resource optimization for operations
ops-resource-optimization.subtitle: Spend audit, Claude model choice and the cost-to-quality balance in 6 steps
ops-resource-optimization.whatItIs: A systematic way to allocate team resources with AI: capacity planning, fitting tools to tasks, choosing the Claude model (Haiku vs Sonnet vs Opus) and managing API cost. The goal is to remove over-provisioning, model mismatch and idle resources while preserving quality.
ops-resource-optimization.approach: Instead of cutting costs blindly, you measure cost and quality in parallel. First gather data on real usage, then find tasks with a model mismatch, test alternatives on a limited volume, and roll changes out only once quality is confirmed. Every step produces a measurable artifact.
outcomes: A full map of AI spend: which tasks, which models, what they cost
A list of model-mismatch tasks with an estimate of potential savings
Quality metrics tied to every task you optimize
A 20-40% cut in operations spend with no drop in quality
A repeatable quarterly resource-review process instead of a one-off effort

applyIn.title: Quarterly resource review
applyIn.description: Run the spend audit each quarter and check whether task-to-model fit has drifted as load grew.

applyIn.title: Annual budget planning
applyIn.description: Before setting next year's budget, justify every AI spend line with real usage data.

applyIn.title: AI spend appears in the P&L
applyIn.description: When finance starts seeing AI spend in reporting, quickly show that costs are under control and optimized.

pitfalls: Optimizing only cost without measuring quality: a cheaper model may "save" $1000 but cut conversion by $5000
Pulling data over too short a window, so spikes and seasonality distort the estimate
Rolling a new model out to 100% of tasks at once, with no test window or rollback plan
Counting only API price while ignoring the cost of rework and the hours spent fixing bad answers
Doing the audit once and forgetting it: without a quarterly rhythm the savings erode within months

exercises.question: A ticket-classification task runs on Opus at $3k/month. How do you decide whether it can move to Haiku or Sonnet without harm?
exercises.hint: Define a quality metric for the task (classification accuracy), run a sample on each model, compare quality and cost, and only then calculate the savings.

exercises.question: An AI audit shows $4k/month in savings from moving to Sonnet. What should you check before reporting that number to leadership?
exercises.hint: That the quality drop is measured and acceptable, that the figure accounts for downstream effects (conversion, rework), and that there is a rollback plan if quality slips.

s1.title: Set the goal and the expected outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal the audit becomes "let's save something" and runs into the risk of cutting quality. You need to define success and the quality limits you must not cross up front.
instructions: State the goal in numbers, e.g. "cut operations spend by 25% this quarter with no quality drop"
Define guardrails: quality metrics that must not degrade (conversion, accuracy, SLA)
Record who decides on roll out and who owns the rollback
Write the baseline of current spend in one line ($/month) so you have a reference
s1.validate: There is a written goal with a number, a list of guardrail metrics, and the name of the decision owner.
s1.tip: "Save as much as possible" is a bad goal. "−25% with quality drop <5%" is a workable one.

s2.title: Gather data and constraints
s2.why: Optimization decisions are worth exactly as much as the data behind them. You need real usage logs over a representative window, not guesses.
instructions: Export all AI-API logs for 30 days (task, model, token volume, cost)
Group by task: what each costs per month and which model serves it
Mark constraints: tasks with a hard SLA, latency-critical, or regulatory ones
Check the window for spikes and seasonality and extend it if needed
s2.validate: There is a "task, then model, then volume, then $/month" table and a list of tasks with constraints.
s2.tip: 30 days is the minimum. If clear spikes show up, widen the window or your savings estimate will be inflated.

s3.title: Key step 1 — find the model mismatch
s3.why: The main source of over-spend is tasks run on Opus where Sonnet or Haiku would suffice. This is the fastest and largest savings lever.
instructions: Run the data through an AI analysis: "which tasks use Opus, can they move to Sonnet or Haiku?"
For each task, decide the minimum sufficient model tier based on the task's nature
Get the output: list of tasks + alternative model + estimated savings
Sort by potential savings and start with the most expensive tasks
s3.validate: A ranked list of candidate tasks with a proposed model and a savings estimate is ready.
s3.tip: Classification, extraction and simple answers rarely need Opus. Keep complex reasoning and long context on the higher tier.

s4.title: Key step 2 — test the new mix
s4.why: Estimated savings is a hypothesis. Before roll out you must confirm on real traffic that the cheaper model holds quality on the chosen tasks.
instructions: Take the candidate tasks from step 3 and run them on the new model at a limited volume (one week or a traffic share)
Measure the quality metrics from step 1 in parallel with cost — both axes, always
Compare against baseline: how much quality dropped and how much cost fell
Record a decision per task: move, keep, or needs prompt tuning
s4.validate: Each test task has a pair of numbers — quality drop and cost saving — plus a go/no-go decision.
s4.tip: Sometimes a cheaper model matches the higher tier after prompt tuning — try that before giving up the savings.

s5.title: Check quality and risks
s5.why: Savings that drop a downstream metric are a loss. Before a wide rollout, make sure guardrails are intact and there is a plan for a regression.
instructions: Reconcile test results against the guardrail metrics from step 1 — any breaches?
Recompute savings including downstream effects: rework, human hours, conversion
Describe the risks and rollback triggers: at what metric value you revert to the old model
Prepare a rollback mechanism that restores the old model in minutes, not days
s5.validate: All guardrails are green, net savings are calculated, and there is a documented rollback plan.
s5.tip: Count "net savings" after all hidden costs, not just "saved on API".

s6.title: Roll out and lock it in with a checklist
s6.why: Without roll out the savings stay on paper, and without a regular rhythm they erode. Rollout should become a repeatable quarterly process.
instructions: Move the tasks that passed the test to the new models (usually ~80% of candidates)
Turn on ongoing quality and cost monitoring with guardrail alerts
Schedule the next quarterly resource review in the calendar
Record the result: before/after $/month, quality drop, ROI
Capture the process as a checklist so the next audit runs faster
s6.validate: Tasks are moved, monitoring is live, the next review is scheduled, and the result is documented.
s6.tip: Use the real case as a reference: from $5k/month Opus to $1.2k/month Sonnet, quality drop <5%, ROI ≈ 4x.

ops-team-workflow.title: AI Operations Team Workflow
ops-team-workflow.subtitle: Turning individual AI usage into one shared team standard
ops-team-workflow.whatItIs: A course on the team operating model for working with AI: shared prompts, shared Projects, access, and knowledge management. It is not about how one person writes good prompts, but about how a team of several people gets predictable, consistent results without duplicating work or locking knowledge in someone's head.
ops-team-workflow.approach: We move from problem to system: first nail down why the team needs a unified process and what outcome is required, then split work between AI and people, build the two key artifacts (shared Project and CLAUDE.md), cover quality/risks/roles, and finish with rollout and a checklist. Every step produces a concrete artifact, not theory.
outcomes: A unified team standard for working with AI instead of a set of personal prompting styles
Shared Project and CLAUDE.md as the source of truth for rules, templates, and typical tasks
A clear split: what goes to AI, what stays with people, and who owns what
New hire onboarding in 2-3 days instead of 2 weeks
A measurable metric: % of tasks done through the shared workflow

applyIn.title: Operations team of 3-10 people
applyIn.description: When several people actively use AI and identical tasks yield different results — a shared process removes the drift.

applyIn.title: Fast onboarding
applyIn.description: A newcomer opens the shared Project and CLAUDE.md and immediately sees how the team works with AI, instead of learning over a colleague's shoulder.

applyIn.title: Recurring tasks
applyIn.description: Reports, decision analysis, routine emails — packaged as reusable Skills and templates used by the whole team.

pitfalls: Treating team workflow = "one person forces everyone to use their prompts". That is dictatorship, not a process — you need ownership and feedback loops.
Keeping knowledge "in Mary's head" instead of the shared Project and CLAUDE.md — when she leaves, the team loses everything.
Handing AI tasks that require human judgment and accountability (consequential decisions, sensitive communications).
Rolling out tools without assigning a standard owner — without one the process degrades within a month.
Launching without a metric — you can't tell whether the team actually moved to the shared workflow.

exercises.question: Five people on your team use AI in their own way. Where do you start the move to a unified process?
exercises.hint: First nail down the problem and the desired outcome, then create one shared source-of-truth artifact — don't try to unify everything at once.

exercises.question: Which operations-team tasks should go to AI and which should stay with people?
exercises.hint: AI — recurring, high-volume, templated (report drafts, first-pass analysis). People — consequential decisions, accountability, context, and judgment.

exercises.question: How do you know the team actually adopted the shared workflow rather than just sitting through a briefing?
exercises.hint: Introduce a measurable metric — e.g. % of tasks done through the shared workflow, and the newcomer's time to productivity.

s1.title: Why the team needs a unified process and what outcome is required
s1.why: Individual AI usage does not scale: a team of 10, each with their own style = different results and duplicated work. Without an explicit goal you can't tell whether the process helps.
instructions: Capture the symptoms: inconsistent results, duplicated work, newcomers who "don't know how we work with AI".
State the target outcome in numbers: team velocity (5 do what 8 used to), onboarding 2-3 days instead of 2 weeks.
Set the boundary: this is about the team operating model, not individual prompting skills.
Pick one success metric: % of tasks done through the shared workflow.
s1.validate: You have, in writing: the problem, the target outcome in numbers, and one metric.
s1.tip: Don't start with tools. First agree which pain you're removing — otherwise you'll roll out a process nobody needs.

s2.title: What to give AI and what to keep with people
s2.why: Without an explicit split the team either fears handing AI anything important, or delegates work that requires human accountability. Both break trust in the process.
instructions: List the team's typical tasks and tag them: recurring/high-volume, use AI; consequential decisions, use people.
AI: report drafts, first-pass data analysis, routine emails, summarization.
People: final decisions, accountability for outcomes, sensitive communications, context and judgment.
For mixed tasks set a format: AI drafts, then a human reviews and approves.
s2.validate: There is a task table marked AI / human / joint, clear to the whole team.
s2.tip: The boundary is not static: as trust grows, tasks migrate from "joint" to "AI". Revisit the tagging quarterly.

s3.title: Key step 1 — shared Project as the workspace
s3.why: A shared Claude Project with a team system prompt sets a single style and context for everyone. Without it each person re-explains to AI who we are and how we write.
instructions: Create a shared Claude Project "Operations Workspace".
Write the team system prompt: tone, response format, what counts as a finished result.
Load shared context into the Project: documents, terms, examples of reference tasks.
Give access to the whole team and assign an owner responsible for keeping it current.
s3.validate: Any member opening the Project gets a response in the team style without extra explanation.
s3.tip: The system prompt is a living document. Once a week collect where AI answered "not in our style" and refine the instructions.

s4.title: Key step 2 — CLAUDE.md and reusable Skills as the source of truth
s4.why: The Project sets the style, but rules, templates, and recurring tasks must be fixed in text available to everyone. That's how knowledge stops being locked in one person's head.
instructions: Create CLAUDE.md in the shared repo: working rules, templates, descriptions of typical tasks.
Package recurring tasks as reusable Skills (e.g. report-writer, decision-analyzer).
Link Skills and templates to the tasks from step 2 so everyone knows what solves what.
Make CLAUDE.md and Skills editable by the whole team — with review of changes.
s4.validate: A new recurring task is solved with a ready Skill or template rather than from scratch.
s4.tip: One rule — one source. If a template lives in both the Project and CLAUDE.md, they drift apart. Keep the truth in one place.

s5.title: Quality, risks, and roles
s5.why: A shared process without quality checks and owners degrades: rules go stale, AI errors reach production, no one owns the standard.
instructions: Assign a workflow owner: they keep the Project, CLAUDE.md, and Skills current.
Introduce a check on AI output wherever there are consequences — a human approves the final.
Set up a feedback loop: weekly "AI office hours" where the team shares discoveries and problems.
Describe the risks: data access, sensitive information, who can see and change what.
s5.validate: It's clear who owns the standard, how quality is checked, and where problems are discussed.
s5.tip: Office hours beat regulations: 30 minutes a week where people share findings delivers more than a long rulebook.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A process works only when it's actually used. Rollout is a separate stage with a measurable success signal, otherwise it all stays a pile of documents.
instructions: Run the process on one real task with the whole team, not in theory.
Run a newcomer through the onboarding checklist: Project, then CLAUDE.md, then Skills, then office hours.
Measure the metric from step 1: % of tasks through the shared workflow and time to productivity.
Readiness checklist: shared Project, team system prompt, CLAUDE.md, reusable Skills, owner, metric, office hours.
Quarterly, revisit the task tagging and update the standard.
s6.validate: A newcomer is productive in 2-3 days, not weeks — that's the Stage 3 sign the process has taken root.
s6.tip: Don't roll out everything to everyone at once. Pilot with one team, get it to Stage 3, then replicate.

mk-content-ops.title: AI Content Operations
mk-content-ops.subtitle: Build a content pipeline: brief, then AI draft, then human review, then publish
mk-content-ops.whatItIs: AI Content Operations is a content production pipeline where AI handles drafts (≈80% of the routine) while humans own strategy, facts, and tone. Input is a brief (topic, outline, audience); output is a finished piece that has passed a quality gate. It fits blog, email, social, and documentation at a volume of ≥10 pieces per month.
mk-content-ops.approach: We move from goal to rollout: first fix why the pipeline is needed and which result you measure; then assemble the foundation — brand voice and prompt templates; then build the two key transitions (brief to draft and review to edit); cover quality, tone, and risks; finish with rollout and a checklist. The core principle across all steps: human-in-the-loop — AI never publishes on its own.
outcomes: A described end-to-end pipeline: brief, then AI draft, then human review, then SEO, then publish
A brand voice document and a set of reusable prompt templates
Reduced time-to-publish from days to hours on a typical piece
A quality gate with factcheck, tone, and local context before every publish
Output and consistency metrics that make the pipeline's effect visible

applyIn.title: Blog and longreads
applyIn.description: Turn a brief (topic + outline + audience) into a 1000-1500 word draft and hand it to an editor for review and SEO polish instead of writing from scratch.

applyIn.title: Email and newsletter
applyIn.description: Generate email series in one tone from a single brand voice prompt; a human edits the offer and facts before sending.

applyIn.title: Social and documentation
applyIn.description: Repackage one long piece into posts for different channels and into tech docs, keeping a single tone across channels.

pitfalls: The "AI generates, then publish" pattern with no human gate — the reader spots generic text in seconds
Launching the pipeline without a documented brand voice — the output is an averaged tone with no recognizability
Briefs without audience and outline — AI fills the gaps, the draft misses the target, and review costs more
No factcheck — AI confidently outputs wrong numbers and facts, a reputational risk
No metrics (time-to-publish, output) — you cannot prove the effect or improve the pipeline

exercises.question: A team publishes 4 pieces per month and asks to roll out AI content ops. Should you launch the pipeline now?
exercises.hint: Compare against the entry threshold: the pipeline pays off at ≥10 pieces per month with an existing (or assemblable) brand voice.

exercises.question: An editor suggests dropping the review step to go faster: "AI already writes well." What argues against it?
exercises.hint: Think about what exactly the human gate catches: factcheck, tone, local context. What happens to text recognizability without it?

exercises.question: How do you measure that the pipeline actually works, not just "feels faster"?
exercises.hint: Fix a baseline before rollout and compare: time-to-publish, content output, single tone across channels.

s1.title: Why a pipeline and what result
s1.why: Without a clear goal and metric, the pipeline becomes "AI for AI's sake." The effect (time-to-publish from 2 days to 4 hours, output +200-300%) must be fixed as a baseline, otherwise there is nothing to prove the value.
instructions: Count current volume: how many pieces per month and how much time goes into drafts
Fix baseline metrics: time-to-publish, content output, an estimate of tone consistency
State the goal in numbers (e.g., time-to-publish down 5× with the same team)
Check the entry threshold: ≥10 pieces/month and an existing or assemblable brand voice
s1.validate: You have baseline numbers and target metrics on paper, and the team clears the entry threshold.
s1.tip: Plan the freed time for strategy, distribution, and performance analysis — where AI does not help.

s2.title: Brand voice and prompt templates
s2.why: Brand voice is the foundation of the pipeline: without it AI outputs an averaged tone indistinguishable from competitors. Prompt templates make the result repeatable rather than random from run to run.
instructions: Assemble a brand voice document: tone, vocabulary, prohibitions, 2-3 reference text samples
Set up the brand voice as a system prompt inside a Project "Blog" (or equivalent)
Create prompt templates per format: longread, email, social post
Parameterize templates with placeholders (topic, audience, outline) for reuse without editing
s2.validate: The same prompt on two different topics produces texts in one recognizable tone.
s2.tip: Reference samples in the prompt work better than abstract tone descriptions — AI copies an example more accurately than an instruction.

s3.title: Key step 1: brief, then draft
s3.why: Draft quality is set by brief quality. A brief with topic, outline, and audience yields an on-target draft; a "write about X" brief forces AI to guess and inflates the cost of review.
instructions: Assemble the brief from three mandatory parts: topic, outline (structure), audience
Add research input: SEO keywords and audience insights, if available
Run generation through the template with the brand voice prompt from step 2
Get a draft of the required length (e.g., 800-1500 words) and store it together with the brief
s3.validate: The draft structurally follows the brief's outline and is written in brand voice, with no obvious topic gaps.
s3.tip: If the draft misses, fix the brief, not the prompt: the problem is usually an underspecified outline or audience.

s4.title: Key step 2: review, then edit
s4.why: This is the mandatory human gate. Any AI text needs review: factcheck, tone, local context. Without human-in-the-loop the output is generic content the reader spots in 3 seconds.
instructions: Run the draft through the quality gate: editor review strictly before publishing
Check facts and numbers — AI confidently outputs plausible but wrong data
Match tone against brand voice and fix spots where AI drifted into averageness
Add local context and SEO optimization, finish the piece
s4.validate: The text passed factcheck, sounds in brand voice, and does not read as "AI-generated."
s4.tip: Keep a short review checklist (facts / tone / context / SEO) — it prevents skipping the step under deadline pressure.

s5.title: Quality, tone, and risks
s5.why: The pipeline accelerates not only good but also bad content. Without explicit quality rules and risk control, scaling replicates errors: factual, tonal, reputational.
instructions: Fix "ready to publish" criteria: facts confirmed, tone matches, context appropriate
Describe typical AI-text risks: fact hallucinations, generic tone, loss of local context
Make the human gate a non-overridable rule — no direct publishing from AI
Set up a feedback loop: feed review errors back into brand voice and templates
s5.validate: There are written quality criteria and a risk list, and the team cannot publish bypassing review.
s5.tip: Recurring editor edits are a signal to improve the prompt or brand voice, not to hand-fix each text.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: The pipeline survives only if it becomes a team process, not a one-off experiment by one person. A checklist and roles turn the pipeline into a reproducible operation.
instructions: Describe the pipeline as a process: brief, then AI draft, then review, then SEO, then publish, with an owner at each stage
Assemble a final publish checklist (brief complete / tone / facts / context / SEO)
Run 2-3 real pieces through the pipeline and compare metrics against the step 1 baseline
Lock in a rhythm: regularly update brand voice and templates from review feedback
s6.validate: The team shipped pieces through the pipeline, metrics improved against baseline, and the process is documented.
s6.tip: Start with one format (e.g., blog), tune it, and only then add email and social.

mk-campaign-intel.title: AI Campaign Intelligence
mk-campaign-intel.subtitle: Embed AI as a "second analyst" in planning and reviewing campaigns
mk-campaign-intel.whatItIs: A practice where AI helps at two points of the campaign lifecycle: pre-launch (analyzing past campaigns, generating angle/positioning variants, a rough performance forecast) and post-launch (reading metrics and comments, pattern-matching "what worked and why", documenting learnings into a shared knowledge base). The goal is to replace reactive decisions with structured analysis and accumulate an organized library of campaign learnings over a year.
mk-campaign-intel.approach: We follow the real campaign lifecycle. First we fix why and what result we expect, then we collect and normalize past-campaign data (without it pattern-matching fails). Next come the two key steps: pre-launch analysis with variant generation and a rough forecast, and a post-launch post-mortem with documentation. Then we build in quality checks and limits of applicability (AI = a colleague for brainstorming, not an oracle), and finish with rollout: a checklist and a rhythm of quarterly plus after every major campaign.
outcomes: You understand exactly where AI adds value in campaigns (pre-launch analysis and post-launch review) and where it does not
A normalized dataset of past campaigns is assembled and fit for pattern-matching
You have a working pre-launch workflow: similar-audience analysis, 5 angle variants, a rough forecast
You have a post-mortem workflow that turns metrics into documented learnings
Campaigns are planned on a rhythm (quarterly + a >$10k threshold), and decisions rely on an accumulated base rather than intuition

applyIn.title: Quarterly campaign planning
applyIn.description: Before the quarter you run the plan through AI: what was tried before on a similar audience, which angles are still unused, where there is a risk of repeating a past mistake.

applyIn.title: Launching a campaign with a >$10k budget
applyIn.description: For expensive launches you make pre-launch analysis mandatory: 5 positioning variants and a rough performance forecast, so you do not bet a large budget on an untested angle.

applyIn.title: Post-mortem after a major campaign
applyIn.description: Once finished, AI reads metrics and comments, surfaces what worked and why, and records learnings into the shared base so the next team does not start from scratch.

pitfalls: Using AI as an "ROI predictor" — it is strong at pattern-matching history, but new markets and channels are beyond its experience
Running pre-launch analysis without normalized past-campaign data — without history a forecast turns into hallucination
Doing the post-mortem "in your head" and not documenting it — learnings are lost and the library never accumulates
Treating a rough performance forecast as an exact number and baking it into a financial model
Planning campaigns reactively and attaching AI after the fact instead of embedding it into a quarterly + budget-threshold rhythm

exercises.question: You have an archive of 30 past campaigns in different formats (spreadsheets, decks, threads). What must you do BEFORE asking AI for a performance forecast on a new one?
exercises.hint: Pattern-matching only works on comparable data. Think about a single field schema: audience, channel, budget, angle, key metrics, outcome.

exercises.question: On pre-launch AI returned a forecast of "expected ROI +35%". How do you use this number correctly in a budget decision?
exercises.hint: Recall the main mistake: AI is not an oracle. The forecast is a prompt for brainstorming and hypothesis-checking, not a number for a financial model.

exercises.question: The campaign is over and metrics are collected. How do you structure the post-mortem so learnings actually fill the library rather than stay in a chat?
exercises.hint: Pattern-matching "what worked and why", then a document in the shared knowledge base with the same schema as the archive, so it feeds future pre-launch analyses.

s1.title: Why AI in campaigns and what result
s1.why: Campaigns are planned under pressure, hence reactive decisions and no learning loop. Before building a workflow, you must fix that AI adds structured analysis at two points — pre-launch and post-launch — and what effect you expect.
instructions: State the problem in your own words: where decisions are currently reactive and not grounded in past experience
Fix the two AI application points: pre-launch (what to try) and post-launch (what worked and why)
Write the target effect as a direction: better planning, faster learning, fewer reactive decisions
Agree on AI's role: a "thoughtful colleague for brainstorming", not an "ROI predictor"
s1.validate: You can explain in two sentences why AI belongs in pre-launch and post-launch and what result it gives the team.
s1.tip: Write target benchmarks (e.g. faster campaign review) as a direction, not as promised numbers — they depend on the quality of your data.

s2.title: Campaign data: collect and normalize
s2.why: AI pattern-matching only works on comparable historical data. If campaigns live in different formats with no single schema, every forecast and every review will be shallow.
instructions: Gather the archive of past campaigns in one place (spreadsheets, decks, reports, comments)
Define a single field schema: audience, channel, budget, angle/positioning, key metrics, outcome
Bring at least major campaigns to this schema, marking gaps explicitly
Tag comparability: which campaigns are similar by audience and channel — the basis for future comparisons
s2.validate: There is a table (or structured set) of past campaigns with unified fields, from which you can find "similar to the new one".
s2.tip: Do not chase completeness at once — start with 10-15 major campaigns on a single schema; add the rest as post-mortems happen.

s3.title: Key step 1 — pre-launch analysis and variants
s3.why: This is the first value point: before launch AI helps you see what was already tried on a similar audience and expands the idea space with angle/positioning variants plus a rough forecast.
instructions: Give AI a description of the new campaign and a slice of similar campaigns from the normalized archive
Ask it to analyze: what worked on a similar audience and what did not
Generate 5 angle/positioning variants with a short rationale for each
Request a rough performance forecast with an explicit uncertainty note
Pick 1-2 variants for A/B copy testing based on the analysis, not intuition
s3.validate: The output has 5 worked-out angle variants and a rough forecast grounded in specific similar campaigns from the archive.
s3.tip: If AI proposes an angle with no reference to past campaigns, it is likely a fantasy; send it back to the archive data.

s4.title: Key step 2 — post-launch post-mortem
s4.why: The second value point and the heart of the learning loop: after launch AI turns metrics and comments into structured learnings that feed the next pre-launch analyses.
instructions: Once the campaign ends, hand AI all metrics and audience comments
Ask for pattern-matching: what worked, what did not, and why (cause hypotheses)
Check AI's conclusions against the actual numbers — discard those not backed by data
Document learnings into the shared knowledge base using the same schema as the archive
Link the campaign to similar ones: extend the comparability tags for future comparisons
s4.validate: A campaign entry in the unified schema appears in the shared knowledge base, ready to be used in the next pre-launch analysis.
s4.tip: Document not only "what worked" but why — a cause hypothesis is more useful than a bare fact when you return to it a quarter later.

s5.title: Quality and limits of applicability
s5.why: The main risk is treating AI as an oracle. It is strong at pattern-matching history, but new markets and channels are outside its experience. You need explicit rules for where to trust conclusions and where not.
instructions: Introduce a rule: a rough forecast is a prompt for brainstorming, not a number for a financial model
Mark campaigns on new markets/channels as "outside history" — there AI conclusions are hypothetical
Check every post-mortem conclusion against confirmation by actual metrics
Record when AI was wrong in a forecast — that too is a learning for calibrating trust
s5.validate: The team has a clear rule on which AI conclusions are accepted as support and which require human checking or count as hypotheses.
s5.tip: Once a quarter, compare past rough forecasts with actuals — that reveals AI's real accuracy on your data.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Without a rhythm, AI gets attached after the fact and reactively again. You must wire pre-launch and post-launch into the campaign process and lock in launch triggers.
instructions: Tie pre-launch analysis to quarterly planning and to the >$10k budget threshold
Make the post-mortem a mandatory step after every major campaign
Assign an owner for keeping the shared knowledge base updated
Fix the checklist: data normalized, then pre-launch (5 variants + forecast), then launch, then post-mortem, then learnings in the base
After a quarter, assess whether the learnings library is growing and reactive decisions are fewer
s6.validate: Pre-launch and post-launch became mandatory process steps with clear triggers, and the learnings library grows after every major campaign.
s6.tip: Start with one major campaign as a full-cycle pilot — the team sees the value before the practice becomes mandatory for everyone.

mk-brand-voice.title: Tuning AI Brand Voice
mk-brand-voice.subtitle: From "we need to sound like us" to a reproducible voice guide the AI repeats in every piece
mk-brand-voice.whatItIs: A course on codifying brand voice so the AI generates text in your team's style instead of generic "like everyone". Voice becomes an explicit instruction: 3-5 attributes + Do/Don't + reference examples embedded in the system prompt and few-shot of every Project.
mk-brand-voice.approach: Voice cannot be described abstractly ("professional but friendly") — that does not help the AI. The course approach: collect real samples of your writing, break them into concrete attributes, describe them as an instruction with examples, test reproducibility across formats via blind review, and only then roll out. Specificity beats nice phrasing.
outcomes: A voice guide of 3-5 attributes with Do/Don't and reference paragraphs
System prompt and few-shot examples embedded in the right Projects
A reproducibility metric: blind review shows > 80% recognition
Reduced editor rewrite time and faster new-member onboarding
A review cadence so the voice does not drift from how the team actually writes

applyIn.title: Content team of ≥3 people
applyIn.description: When several authors write in parallel and styles diverge — the voice guide gives one reference that AI and people reproduce the same way.

applyIn.title: AI content operations roll-out
applyIn.description: Before scaling AI generation to the whole team, voice is fixed first; otherwise the output is generic and complaints "the AI tone isn't us" pour in.

applyIn.title: Brands with a meaningful vocabulary
applyIn.description: B2B, tech, lifestyle — where terminology and tone are recognizable. Explicit voice makes the AI invisible rather than noticeable in the output.

pitfalls: Describing voice abstractly ("professional but friendly") — the AI cannot reproduce it without examples
Collecting attributes without Do/Don't — without contrasting examples the model blurs the style's boundaries
Skipping reference paragraphs (few-shot) — attributes alone keep recognition below 80%
Testing voice on a single format only — it may fall apart in long reads or social posts
Fixing the voice guide once and never revisiting — the team's real writing changes and drift sets in

exercises.question: You have the line "we write professionally but in a friendly way". Why will the AI produce generic text from it, and what should you add?
exercises.hint: Think about what the model can copy literally from that phrase. Compare it with a Do/Don't pair and an actual paragraph.

exercises.question: How do you measure that the voice is truly reproducible and not just "the author likes it"?
