exercises.hint: Recall blind review: several people, the same brief, a blind choice between the AI version and generic.

exercises.question: The voice guide is built, but six months later the editor is rewriting a lot again. Where do you look for the cause?
exercises.hint: Drift: the references are stale, the team writes differently than six months ago. Check the review cadence.

s1.title: Why fix the voice and what the outcome is
s1.why: Without an explicit voice the AI outputs "like everyone" text, and it shows. Before collecting samples you need to understand the difference between "AI is noticeable" and "AI is invisible" and set a measurable outcome.
instructions: State the problem concretely: where the "AI tone isn't us" or authors write inconsistently
Fix target metrics: brand consistency, editor rewrite time, onboarding speed
Define scope: which formats and Projects the voice covers
Agree the course output is a voice guide + embedded system prompt and few-shot, not a document gathering dust
s1.validate: You have a written goal with a measurable metric (e.g. recognition > 80% in blind review) and a list of Projects where the voice must work.
s1.tip: The real setup investment is 2-3 days and it pays back in hours saved per piece. Treat it as an investment, not a one-off task.

s2.title: Collect voice samples
s2.why: Voice is reproducible only from real examples. Attributes and instructions invented from scratch yield abstraction — reference texts give the model a pattern to imitate.
instructions: Gather 10-15 texts the team considers exemplary in style
Pick fragments across formats: long read, post, email, product description
Mark what exactly sounds "like us" — specific turns of phrase, rhythm, vocabulary
Collect counter-examples: texts that sound generic or "not us"
s2.validate: You have a folder of references (sounds like us) and counter-examples (not us) across at least 2-3 formats.
s2.tip: Use recent texts from the last few months — old references may no longer reflect how the team writes now.

s3.title: Describe the voice as an instruction
s3.why: The AI works with an explicit instruction, not a feeling. The samples must be broken into 3-5 concrete attributes with Do/Don't — that is the codification of voice.
instructions: Extract 3-5 voice attributes (e.g. warm, expert, direct)
For each attribute give a Do/Don't pair with concrete phrases
Attach 10 reference paragraphs in your style as few-shot examples
Assemble everything into a "Voice Guide" document — attributes + Do/Don't + examples in one place
s3.validate: The voice guide holds 3-5 attributes, a Do/Don't pair for each, and around 10 reference paragraphs — with no abstract phrasing lacking examples.
s3.tip: The more concrete the attribute and the more contrasting the Do/Don't, the higher the reproducibility. Abstraction is the main enemy.

s4.title: Test across formats
s4.why: A voice that works in a post may fall apart in a long read or email. Reproducibility must be tested measurably and across several formats, not on the author's feeling.
instructions: Embed the voice guide into the system prompt and few-shot of a test Project
Give 5 different people the same brief across different formats
Generate the versions and run a blind review: AI version vs generic, blind
Note which formats drop recognition below 80% and refine the attributes/examples
s4.validate: In blind review > 80% pick the AI version as "sounds like us" across at least 2-3 formats.
s4.tip: Blind review removes bias: people judge the text without knowing which is generated — an honest voice metric.

s5.title: Quality and risks: drift
s5.why: The main long-term risk is drift: the team writes differently over time while the voice guide stays the same. Then the AI reproduces a stale voice and the editor rewrites a lot again.
instructions: Assign an owner for the voice guide and a review cadence (e.g. quarterly)
Set up an alert signal: rising editor rewrites or fresh "not our tone" complaints
Compare fresh samples with those in the guide and update examples on divergence
Version the voice guide so you can see when and why the voice changed
s5.validate: There is an owner, a review cadence, and an explicit signal that triggers a guide update.
s5.tip: Rising editor rewrite time is the earliest indicator of drift. Don't wait for complaints — watch the metric.

s6.title: Roll-out and checklist
s6.why: The voice guide is only useful when embedded in real Projects and used by the team by default, not sitting as a separate document.
instructions: Embed the system prompt with attributes and few-shot into all relevant Projects
Run a short team onboarding: where the guide lives and how to use it
Lock a publishing checklist: text matches the attributes, Do/Don't respected
Record before/after metrics (consistency, rewrite time) for the next review
s6.validate: The voice is embedded in the right Projects, the team knows the cadence, and a publishing checklist by attributes runs before each release.
s6.tip: A voice not embedded in Projects doesn't work: the author should receive it automatically, not have to remember a document.

mk-seo-optimization.title: AI SEO at Scale
mk-seo-optimization.subtitle: Every writer SEO-aware, with no separate SEO pass
mk-seo-optimization.whatItIs: A course on embedding AI into a content team's SEO process: keyword research, content briefs from SERPs, meta optimization, and internal linking. The goal is to move from "1 SEO specialist per 5 writers" to a team where every writer works SEO-aware, with AI acting as an advisor at each step.
mk-seo-optimization.approach: We go from strategy to execution: first the why and the target outcome, then theme and keyword clustering, two key working steps (brief generation and quality polish via E-E-A-T), then risks and final rollout with a checklist. AI does not replace keyword data from specialized tools — it amplifies writers.
outcomes: Know where AI truly speeds up SEO and where data must come from ahrefs/semrush
Build topical keyword clusters and map them to pages
Assemble a content brief from SERP gap analysis in minutes, not hours
Bring content to E-E-A-T standard without sliding into keyword spam
Roll out the SEO workflow to the team via a repeatable checklist

applyIn.title: B2B SaaS content
applyIn.description: 20+ pieces/month where organic is the main lead channel and SEO expertise does not scale to every writer.

applyIn.title: eCommerce catalog
applyIn.description: Hundreds of categories and product pages needing SEO coverage and internal linking at scale.

applyIn.title: Content-driven media
applyIn.description: An editorial team where publishing speed matters more than hiring a dedicated SEO specialist per stream.

pitfalls: Trusting AI keyword research fully: AI does not see fresh SERPs and does not know current trends (cutoff date)
Thin content: AI generates volume for keywords rather than value — a path straight to the Helpful Content filter
Keyword stuffing: cramming keywords on AI's suggestion instead of natural integration
Ignoring E-E-A-T: content without experience, expertise, and sources slips in rankings
Scaling the process before it is validated on 5-10 pieces

exercises.question: You have an article draft and the top-10 SERP for the topic. How do you phrase the prompt so AI returns the gap, not a summary?
exercises.hint: Ask it to compare subtopic coverage: what competitors have, what is missing in your draft, and which subtopics to add — a list, not prose.

exercises.question: AI suggested 12 keywords for a 1500-word article. How do you decide how many to actually integrate?
exercises.hint: One primary + 2-4 semantically related. The rest are candidates for separate cluster pages, not stuffing into one.

exercises.question: How do you tell E-E-A-T content from thin AI-generated text?
exercises.hint: Look for specifics: personal experience, data, sources, authorship. If the text could describe any product, it is thin.

s1.title: Why SEO at scale and the target outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal, teams adopt AI for AI's sake. SEO at scale is justified only at a certain output and organic role.
instructions: Fix the baseline: organic traffic, SEO coverage rate (% of pages targeting a keyword), monthly content volume
Check the entry threshold: output >20 pieces/month and SEO is critical to the business
Confirm there is budget for keyword research tools (ahrefs/semrush) — AI does not replace them
Define the target outcome: e.g., coverage from 30% to 80%, organic +30-60% in 6 months
s1.validate: You have a numeric baseline and a 6-month target metric.
s1.tip: If output is <20 pieces/month, manual SEO is cheaper — the AI process will not pay back its setup.

s2.title: Theme and keyword clusters
s2.why: SEO at scale works in clusters: a pillar page plus related subtopics, not scattered articles for random keywords.
instructions: Take keyword data from ahrefs/semrush — volume and difficulty come from there, not from AI
Use AI to group keywords into semantic clusters and find coverage gaps
Assign each cluster a pillar page and a set of supporting pieces
Map a primary keyword to a single page — avoid cannibalization
s2.validate: Each target keyword maps to exactly one page, and clusters have a pillar.
s2.tip: AI is good at grouping semantics, but final volume and difficulty always come from specialized tools.

s3.title: Key step 1 — generating the content brief
s3.why: A brief from SERP gap analysis is the main accelerator: the writer immediately sees what to cover and which keywords to integrate.
instructions: Give AI the top-10 SERP for the topic and ask it to highlight what competitors cover and what is missing
Feed in the writer's draft + gap analysis, then get a list of subtopics to add
Ask AI to suggest keywords to integrate from your cluster (not invent new ones)
Assemble the brief: subtopics, primary + related keywords, recommended structure
s3.validate: The brief contains concrete subtopics from the gap analysis and keywords from your cluster, not generic phrases.
s3.tip: AI does not see fresh SERPs — paste the current results into the prompt yourself.

s4.title: Key step 2 — quality and E-E-A-T
s4.why: AI easily produces volume, but value ranks. E-E-A-T (experience, expertise, authority, trust) separates content from thin text.
instructions: Add specifics AI cannot know: personal experience, data, cases, sources
Integrate keywords naturally: primary + 2-4 related, without stuffing
Add authorship and links to primary sources for trust signals
Run AI meta title + description optimization as the final step
Check that the text is useful in its own right, not written for the search engine
s4.validate: The content passes the "could this describe any product?" test — it can't, it is specific.
s4.tip: Meta optimization is the last step, not the first: value first, packaging second.

s5.title: Risks — thin content and penalties
s5.why: Scale without quality control leads to the Helpful Content filter and traffic loss — the opposite of the goal.
instructions: Introduce a QA threshold: no AI piece is published without a human E-E-A-T polish
Track thin content: pages with no unique value are candidates for rework
Do not scale volume for coverage's sake: 20 strong pieces beat 100 thin ones
Monitor traffic drops after algorithm updates as an early penalty signal
s5.validate: There is an explicit QA gate that no thin or spammy piece passes through.
s5.tip: A single thin-content penalty can undo months of work — slower but clean is better.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A workflow is only valuable if the team can reproduce it. A checklist turns a one-off win into a systematic process.
instructions: Describe the SEO workflow as 5 steps: draft, then SERP gap, then subtopics/keywords, then redraft, then meta
Validate the process on 5-10 pieces first, then scale to the team
Lock in the checklist: keyword from tools, brief from gap, E-E-A-T polish, QA gate, meta
Measure coverage and organic monthly against the baseline from step 1
s6.validate: Any writer on the team can run the workflow from the checklist without an SEO specialist alongside.
s6.tip: Connect this course to content operations practice (mk-content-ops) and the broader AI-native marketing model (ai-native-marketing).

mk-performance-analytics.title: AI Marketing Performance Analytics
mk-performance-analytics.subtitle: Turn dashboards into insight-driven reports with hypotheses and action items
mk-performance-analytics.whatItIs: A course on using AI to analyze marketing metrics (GA4, email, social, spend). Instead of "here are graphs, figure it out", AI builds a narrative layer: what grew/dropped, hypotheses why, 3 recommendations, and red flags. A human validates in 15 minutes and makes decisions.
mk-performance-analytics.approach: We go from goal to rollout: first nail down why analytics is needed and the target outcome, then gather data sources, then two key steps — analyzing metrics and turning insights into actions. We separately cover quality and risk (correlation ≠ causation, AI does not know the attribution model), and finish with rollout and a weekly-ritual checklist.
outcomes: Cut time-to-insight from days to hours: AI collects and interprets metrics instead of manual gathering
Get a structured weekly review with hypotheses and action items, not bare numbers
Clearly separate narrative and pattern matching (where AI is strong) from attribution and causation (where AI fails)
Have a reproducible prompt template for a report that works every week
Reduce the risk of false conclusions through an explicit "correlation or cause" check

applyIn.title: Weekly performance review
applyIn.description: The team spends >2 hours per week building the report. AI gathers deltas, explains anomalies, and suggests hypotheses — the human validates and decides.

applyIn.title: Investigating a metric drop
applyIn.description: When the reason for a traffic or conversion drop is non-obvious. AI looks for patterns in past data and formulates testable hypotheses.

applyIn.title: Monthly stakeholder report
applyIn.description: Turn a pile of dashboards into a coherent narrative with conclusions and recommendations that reads in 5 minutes instead of an hour.

pitfalls: Using AI as an attribution engine — it does not know the real attribution model (multi-touch, view-through) and will invent links
Mistaking correlation for cause: AI finds patterns, but coincidence in time does not prove causation
Feeding raw exports without context (seasonality, holidays, launches) — hypotheses will be detached from reality
Publishing the report without human validation — AI confidently gets numbers and conclusions wrong
Asking for "exact ROI" instead of narrative — leads into the zone where AI hallucinates precision

exercises.question: Traffic dropped 18% this week. How do you frame the AI request to get hypotheses rather than an invented cause?
exercises.hint: Give the AI historical context (past weeks, seasonality, known events) and explicitly ask for ranked hypotheses tagged as "needs verification", not one definitive conclusion.

exercises.question: AI writes: "The open-rate increase caused the conversion increase." What is wrong and how do you check it?
exercises.hint: This is correlation passed off as cause. Check: did the changes coincide in time, is there a third factor (new campaign, season), and ask the AI to tag cause-effect claims as hypotheses.

exercises.question: Assemble the minimal source set for your project's weekly report. What data is missing?
exercises.hint: Minimum: traffic/conversions (GA4), email (open/CTR), social engagement, spend. Check that each metric has a comparison period (delta) and event context.

s1.title: Why and what outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal, AI analytics becomes a pretty report nobody uses. First nail down which decision the report should speed up.
instructions: Write down which decision is made based on the report (budget, channel priority, what to fix next week)
Define the expected output format: deltas, hypotheses, 3 recommendations, red flags
Record how much time manual report-building takes now (baseline for measuring the effect)
Describe the report's audience: team, lead, stakeholders — this drives the level of detail
s1.validate: You have one sentence: "This report exists so we make decision X faster every week."
s1.tip: If people look at the report but make no decisions from it, that is a signal to reframe the goal, not to polish the visuals.

s2.title: Data and sources
s2.why: Insight quality is capped by input data quality. AI will not fix holes in your sources — it will mask them with confident text.
instructions: Gather the core sources: GA4 (traffic, conversions), email (open rate, CTR), social engagement, campaign spend
For each metric add a comparison period so the AI computes a delta, not an absolute
Attach event context: launches, holidays, budget changes, seasonality
Unify the export format (CSV/table) and check there are no gaps or duplicates
s2.validate: The AI receives metrics with clear periods, deltas, and a list of known events for the week.
s2.tip: One sheet with columns "metric / current / previous / delta / event note" works better than five separate dashboards.

s3.title: Key step 1 — analyze metrics
s3.why: This is the narrative layer: AI turns numbers into a coherent story of what grew, what dropped, and where the anomalies are. This is where AI is strong.
instructions: Give the AI the data and ask it to highlight what grew/dropped, with numbers and delta
Ask it to flag anomalies — sharp deviations from the past weeks' trend
Request ranked hypotheses "why", explicitly tagged as needing verification
Ask it to surface red flags — what needs deeper investigation
Constrain the output: no invented attribution and no exact ROI
s3.validate: The output is a structured breakdown: what changed (numbers + delta), anomalies, candidate hypotheses, and red flags.
s3.tip: Ask the AI to cite specific numbers from the input data in every claim — this sharply reduces hallucinations.

s4.title: Key step 2 — insights into actions
s4.why: Insight without action is useless. This step translates hypotheses into decomposed, doable tasks for next week.
instructions: Ask the AI for 3 recommendations for next week, tied to the hypotheses from step 3
For each recommendation request a concrete action, an owner, and a success metric
Mark which recommendations can be done immediately and which require testing the hypothesis
A human validates the list in ~15 minutes and keeps a realistic 3 actions
s4.validate: The report yields 3 decomposed action items with a clear "what we do and how we will know it worked".
s4.tip: Three executed actions beat ten on a list. Cut everything not tied to a testable hypothesis.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: The main analytics trap is taking correlation for cause and trusting AI as an attribution engine. This step guards against false conclusions.
instructions: For each cause-effect claim ask: is this correlation or a proven cause?
Remember: AI does not know the real attribution model (multi-touch, view-through) — do not delegate attribution to it
Test hypotheses for a third factor (season, parallel campaign) before acting
Cross-check any numeric conclusion against the source data — AI confidently gets numbers wrong
s5.validate: Every "X caused Y" in the report is tagged as a hypothesis, not a fact, and checked against alternative explanations.
s5.tip: Set a rule: AI owns narrative and pattern matching, the human owns causation and attribution. Do not mix them.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A one-off report does not change decision velocity. The value appears when it becomes a reproducible weekly ritual.
instructions: Lock in the report prompt template so you can run it every week without rewriting
Assign a day and an owner for the ritual: gather data, then run AI, then 15 min validation, then 3 actions
Compare the new time-to-insight against the baseline from step 1 and record the effect
Build a checklist: sources complete, deltas present, hypotheses tagged, correlation checked, 3 actions created
Once a month review the template: which hypotheses held up, which metrics are redundant
s6.validate: The report ships on schedule, takes a human ~15 minutes, and consistently yields 3 validated actions.
s6.tip: Connected to the ai-native-marketing approach: analytics is the feedback loop of the whole marketing cycle, not a standalone task.

mk-team-workflow.title: AI Marketing Team Workflow
mk-team-workflow.subtitle: From "everyone with their own Claude" to one collaborative system
mk-team-workflow.whatItIs: A practical course on turning scattered AI usage across a marketing team into one repeatable process: shared brand voice, a template library, reusable Skills, and a knowledge-sharing ritual. The goal is consistent quality and fast onboarding of new people.
mk-team-workflow.approach: We move from the business reason to rollout. First we fix why and what outcome is needed, then define what to hand to AI, build two key assets (a shared Project with a voice guide and reusable Skills), set up quality control and role ownership, and finally roll out the process with a checklist. Every step yields a verifiable artifact, not theory.
outcomes: A single brand voice and naming conventions the whole team follows
A shared Claude Project with a library of templates and playbooks
A set of reusable Skills (blog-post, email, social) with owners
An AI office hours ritual to share prompts and review failures
An adoption metric: share of content via shared workflow vs ad-hoc

applyIn.title: Content team
applyIn.description: Several writers produce blog, email and social — they need one brand voice and a shared template library instead of personal prompts for each person.

applyIn.title: Onboarding new marketers
applyIn.description: A new person becomes productive in 3-5 days instead of two weeks: the shared Project and voice guide show "how we work with AI".

applyIn.title: Scaling an agency
applyIn.description: An agency serves several clients — each gets its own voice guide and templates inside the shared workflow, without duplication or knowledge loss.

pitfalls: "Team workflow" = "one person dictates": without shared ownership the system dies once the author leaves
The voice guide is created but never updated — a month later the team writes inconsistently again
Skills and templates without an owner: nobody is accountable for freshness, so they go stale
Tools are adopted but the sharing ritual is not — learnings stay stuck in each person's head
No adoption metric — impossible to tell whether the team actually moved to the shared process

exercises.question: Write a short brand voice guide for your brand (tone, 3 rules, 3 don'ts) and check whether Claude generates consistent text from it on two different tasks.
exercises.hint: A good voice guide fits on one page: tone in 1-2 sentences, do/don't lists, 2-3 "before/after" examples.

exercises.question: Identify the 2-3 recurring tasks your team should turn into reusable Skills, and assign an owner to each.
exercises.hint: Candidates are things done the same way ≥1 a week: a blog post, an email campaign, a social snippet. The owner is whoever does it most often.

exercises.question: Design a 30-minute weekly AI office hours format: what you show, what you review, who runs it.
exercises.hint: A simple format: 1 winning prompt from each person, 1 failure of the week to review, voice guide updates based on the outcome.

s1.title: Why the team needs a shared process and what outcome
s1.why: Individual AI usage in marketing does not scale: voice is inconsistent, templates duplicate, learnings are lost. Without a clear goal, rollout becomes buying tools without changing how work is done.
instructions: Capture the problem in numbers: time to productivity for a new writer, how much results differ between people
State the target outcome: one voice, a shared library, onboarding in 3-5 days
Define a success metric: share of content done via shared workflow vs ad-hoc
Get the team's buy-in: shared ownership, not a top-down directive
s1.validate: You have a single "problem, then outcome, then metric" sentence the whole team agrees with.
s1.tip: If you cannot name an adoption metric, you do not yet understand what you are changing. Start there.

s2.title: What to hand to AI and what to keep with people
s2.why: Not everything in marketing is worth automating. A clear line "AI does the draft / people own strategy and the final decision" protects quality and removes the team's fear.
instructions: List the team's recurring tasks: blog, email, social, SEO descriptions, research
Mark what fits AI: first draft, variations, routine template-based formats
Mark what stays with people: strategy, the final brand voice, fact-checking, relationships
For each AI task, note the required input artifact (template, voice guide, brief)
s2.validate: You have a "task, then AI or human, then required input artifact" table for at least 5 key tasks.
s2.tip: AI is strong at drafts and variations, weak at strategy and fact-checking. The line is where the cost of error is high.

s3.title: Key asset 1 — shared Project and brand voice
s3.why: A shared Claude Project with a voice guide and templates is the foundation of consistency. It is where the team learns from shared rules and a new person immediately sees "how we work".
instructions: Create a shared Claude Project "Marketing Workspace"
Upload the files: brand voice guide, content templates, SEO playbook
Add a file with content rules and naming conventions for uniformity
Give the whole team access and verify that generation from the voice guide produces a consistent tone
s3.validate: Two different people, via the shared Project, get text in one recognizable brand voice.
s3.tip: A one-page voice guide works better than a 10-page document nobody reads to the end.

s4.title: Key asset 2 — reusable Skills with owners
s4.why: Skills turn winning prompts into repeatable team tools. Without an owner they go stale, so each part of the system gets someone accountable — that is shared ownership.
instructions: Turn 2-3 frequent tasks into Skills: blog-post-writer, email-drafter, social-snippet
Assign each Skill an owner — whoever uses it most often
Pin down who owns which part of the system: voice guide, templates, SEO
Agree that each contributor updates their part rather than waiting for a "lead"
s4.validate: Every Skill and every shared asset has a specific owner by name.
s4.tip: A Skill candidate is a task done the same way ≥1 a week. Do not turn one-offs into Skills.

s5.title: Quality, roles and risks
s5.why: A system without quality control degrades: AI drafts reach the client with errors, and blurred roles mean nobody is accountable for freshness. Here we close the risks.
instructions: Introduce mandatory human review and fact-check before publishing an AI draft
Lock in roles: who owns voice, who owns templates, who owns SEO, who runs office hours
Describe typical risks: voice drift, stale templates, a Skill without an owner
Agree on the cadence for updating the voice guide and templates (e.g., based on office hours)
s5.validate: There is a clear role split and a rule "no AI draft is published without human review".
s5.tip: The main risk is not bad AI but the absence of an owner for a shared asset. No owner — no freshness.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Tools without a sharing ritual do not change how the team works. Weekly AI office hours and a final checklist turn a one-time setup into a sustainable process.
instructions: Launch weekly 30-minute AI office hours: winning prompts, failure reviews, voice guide updates
Measure the adoption metric: share of content via shared workflow vs ad-hoc
Run the checklist: shared Project exists, voice guide exists, Skills have owners, review is in place, metric is tracked
After a month check the maturity sign: a new writer is productive in 3-5 days, everyone has consistent quality
s6.validate: Office hours ran at least once, the adoption metric is measured, the checklist is 100% closed.
s6.tip: If adoption does not grow week over week, the problem is not the tools but the ritual and ownership.

cs-tier1.title: AI Tier-1 Support Automation
cs-tier1.subtitle: A pipeline that closes simple tickets itself and escalates the hard ones cleanly
cs-tier1.whatItIs: Automating first-line support: AI reads an incoming ticket, classifies intent, finds the answer in the knowledge base via RAG, and either writes a personalized reply or escalates to a human. All of it is a pipeline with explicit quality gates and a confidence threshold — not a bot that answers everything.
cs-tier1.approach: We move from a business decision to a working pipeline. First we fix the why and the metric we measure, then prepare the knowledge base and the scope boundaries. Next we build the two key steps of the flow — generating the ticket reply and escalating to a human with ready context. We finish with quality control and a metrics-driven rollout. The throughline: AI answers only at high confidence; everything else escalates.
outcomes: You know which ~20 ticket patterns cover 40%+ of volume and why exactly those are worth automating
You can prepare a knowledge base and define boundaries: where AI answers vs where it must hand off
You built the reply-generation step with a confidence threshold and logging of every decision
You set up escalation that hands the human a ready AI summary, not a raw ticket
You roll the pipeline out with deflection and CSAT metrics and know how to hold quality in production

applyIn.title: SaaS support with FAQ flow
applyIn.description: Password reset, billing, account access — repeat questions at >100 tickets/week get closed automatically, freeing humans for the complex work.

applyIn.title: E-commerce and orders
applyIn.description: Order status, returns, delivery times — routine requests go to AI, while disputes and claims escalate with ready context.

applyIn.title: Internal IT/HR helpdesk
applyIn.description: Employee requests about access, settings, and policies are handled against a structured knowledge base, cutting Tier-2 load.

pitfalls: Trying to cover tier-1 at 80% content: edge cases accumulate and every AI failure becomes a bad customer experience
AI answering even at low confidence instead of escalating — better to hand off than to deliver a confidently wrong answer
Escalation handing the human a raw ticket with no AI summary or history — the agent wastes time re-investigating
No quality gate: without weekly review of a random sample, quality degradation goes unnoticed
Launching without deflection and CSAT metrics — you can't prove value or catch the moment AI starts hurting

exercises.question: You have 600 tickets/week, of which 250 are about password reset, order status, and billing. Should you launch Tier-1 automation, and where do you start?
exercises.hint: Volume >100/week and 40%+ in a few patterns signals yes. Start with the most frequent intents and check whether they have a structured knowledge base.

exercises.question: AI got a ticket, found a relevant article, but model confidence is 0.6 against a 0.8 threshold. What should happen?
exercises.hint: Below threshold — don't reply to the customer directly. Escalate to a human, attaching the found context and a draft reply so the agent resolves it faster.

exercises.question: After a month deflection is 55%, but CSAT on AI tickets dropped from 4.2 to 3.6. Where do you look for the cause?
exercises.hint: Check the quality-gate sample: likely AI is answering cases outside its scope or the confidence threshold is too low. Narrow scope or raise the threshold.

s1.title: Why, and what result we measure
s1.why: Without a clear goal and metric, automation turns into a bot-for-everything that piles up bad experiences. 30-50% of tickets are repeat questions; AI closes that mass with consistent quality, freeing humans for the complex.
instructions: Export 4-8 weeks of tickets and compute the share of repeat intents (password reset, billing, account access)
Check launch criteria: volume >100 tickets/week and 40%+ fitting into ~20 patterns
Fix target metrics: deflection rate (share of tickets closed by AI without a human) and CSAT on AI tickets
Get buy-in from the CS-lead and agree that Tier-2 (complex) stays with humans
s1.validate: You have a list of top patterns with their volume share and two numeric targets: expected deflection (40-60%) and minimum acceptable CSAT (e.g., 4.2).
s1.tip: Don't start with rare complex cases for a wow effect — the value comes from the mass flow of routine tickets.

s2.title: Knowledge base and scope boundaries
s2.why: AI doesn't answer from memory — it answers via RAG over the knowledge base. The base's quality and clear boundaries (where AI stays silent and escalates) directly determine accuracy and safety.
instructions: Build a structured knowledge base for the top patterns: atomic articles with unambiguous answers
For each pattern, describe the boundary: which sub-cases AI closes and which go straight to a human
Explicitly list forbidden zones (manual payments, legal questions, refunds/cancellations)
Set up RAG search and verify a relevant article is found for each intent
Create a test set of real tickets to run against base changes
s2.validate: For each top pattern, RAG finds the right article on the test set, and each pattern has an explicit 'AI answers / AI escalates' decision.
s2.tip: A narrow but polished base of 20 patterns beats a wide, contradictory one — contradictions in the base produce confidently wrong answers.

s3.title: Key step 1 — replying to the ticket
s3.why: This is the heart of the pipeline: intent classification, base lookup, generating a personalized reply, and the answer-or-not decision by confidence threshold. This is where deflection is born.
instructions: Add an intent classifier: FAQ or complex case (complex goes straight to the human queue)
For FAQ, run RAG search and generate a personalized reply in the customer's language
Introduce a confidence threshold (e.g., 0.8): above it AI replies, below it goes to escalation
Log every decision: intent, retrieved context, confidence, final reply
Run the test set and compare answers against the reference
s3.validate: On test tickets AI replies only above the threshold, answers are personalized and correct, and every decision is recorded in the log.
s3.tip: The confidence threshold is the main lever for the 'scope vs quality' balance. Start conservative (high threshold) and lower it as trust in the metrics grows.

s4.title: Key step 2 — escalating to a human
s4.why: Escalation isn't a failure — it's a normal path. The production rule: AI answers only at high confidence, otherwise it hands off. The value of escalation is that the agent gets ready context, not a raw ticket.
instructions: Define escalation triggers: low confidence, complex intent, forbidden zone from step 2
Build an AI ticket summary: the gist of the request, found articles, draft reply, escalation reason
Route to the correct human queue (Tier-2) with the attached context
Preserve history so the agent sees what AI already tried
Verify on test cases that escalation fires where it should and the context is complete
s4.validate: Tickets below threshold and from forbidden zones reliably go to a human with an AI summary and draft, instead of being lost or getting an auto-reply.
s4.tip: Measure whether the AI summary saves the agent time. If the human still starts from scratch, improve summary quality rather than escalation volume.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: The main risk is accumulating edge cases: every wrong auto-reply is a bad experience. A quality gate catches degradation before customers notice it.
instructions: Set up a quality gate: 10% of random AI replies per week go to human review
Create a review checklist: factual correctness, tone, staying within scope boundaries
Track edge cases and either extend the knowledge base or narrow scope on what you find
Tie CSAT drops to specific intents via the logs from step 3
Define a rollback procedure: on quality failure for an intent, temporarily route it back to humans
s5.validate: A weekly sample of replies is reviewed, found errors turn into base or threshold fixes, and a working rollback procedure exists for a problematic intent.
s5.tip: CSAT on AI tickets around 4.2/5 with good setup (vs 4.4 for humans) is a normal benchmark, not a reason to switch AI off.

s6.title: Rollout, metrics, and checklist
s6.why: Launching without metrics makes it impossible to prove value or catch harm. Deflection and CSAT are the two numbers behind every decision to widen or narrow scope.
instructions: Roll out in stages: shadow mode (AI drafts, human sends), then limited auto-reply, then full
Set up a weekly dashboard: deflection rate and CSAT on AI tickets, response-time trend
Compare response time: target is from a 4-hour median down to ~2 minutes on AI tickets
Expand scope to new patterns only after stable CSAT on the current ones
Fix a readiness checklist: base covers patterns, threshold tuned, escalation with context, quality gate live, metrics on dashboard
s6.validate: The pipeline runs in production, the dashboard shows 40-60% deflection and CSAT no lower than target, and the readiness checklist passes fully.
s6.tip: Shadow mode in the first weeks costs almost nothing but removes risk: you see AI reply quality before it ever reaches customers.

cs-agent-assist.title: AI Agent Assist for Support
cs-agent-assist.subtitle: An AI co-pilot that speeds up the agent while keeping the human in the driver seat
cs-agent-assist.whatItIs: A course on rolling out agent-assist: AI works as a co-pilot for tier-2/3 support agents — suggesting reply variants in real time, finding similar resolved tickets and relevant knowledge base articles, and generating drafts. The agent stays the decision-maker; AI only accelerates.
cs-agent-assist.approach: We start from value, not from a mandate. First we lock down the why and the metric we measure, then break down what exactly AI suggests and on what data, then two key launch steps (ticket context and reply generation), then quality control and risks with the human in the loop, and finally rollout with an adoption checklist driven by demonstrated time saved.
outcomes: Understand why agent-assist is less risky than tier-1 automation and delivers ROI faster
Know what AI suggests to the agent: reply variants, similar cases, KB articles
Be able to feed AI the ticket context and customer history so suggestions are accurate
Set up generation of 2-3 reply variants in different tones as an editable draft
Drive assist adoption through value (time saved per ticket), not coercion

applyIn.title: Tier-2/3 support team
applyIn.description: Agents write complex replies from scratch — assist gives a draft, response time drops from 8 to 3 minutes.

applyIn.title: New agent onboarding
applyIn.description: AI compensates the junior-agent gap: suggestions and similar cases cut ramp-up time by about 50%.

applyIn.title: Scaling without quality loss
applyIn.description: The team handles 50-70% more tickets per day while quality stays consistent — AI as draft, agent edits.

pitfalls: Forcing agents to use AI "mandatorily" — adoption is built on value, not on a mandate
Bad suggestions force writing from scratch and kill trust — fewer but more accurate is better
Not feeding AI ticket context and customer history — suggestions come out generic and useless
Treating assist as an agent replacement: the human always makes the final decision and edits
Not measuring time saved per ticket — without the metric you cannot prove value to the team

exercises.question: Why is agent-assist usually easier to roll out than tier-1 automation?
exercises.hint: Think about who stays in the loop and how the team perceives AI — helper or threat.

exercises.question: What three types of suggestions does AI give the agent when a ticket opens?
exercises.hint: Reply variants in different tones, similar resolved tickets, and one more knowledge source.

exercises.question: How do you raise assist adoption without forcing agents?
exercises.hint: Show a concrete savings metric per ticket.

s1.title: Why agent-assist and what result we measure
s1.why: Agent-assist is less risky than tier-1 automation: the human is always in the loop, so errors are caught before sending. ROI arrives fast — response time roughly halves immediately. The team sees AI as a helper, not a threat, and adoption is much higher.
instructions: Record the current response time per ticket (e.g. 8 minutes) as a baseline
Define the target metric: response time, tickets per agent per day, onboarding time
Pick a tier-2/3 team that writes complex replies from scratch
Frame the promise to the team: AI saves time, the human stays in charge
s1.validate: You have a baseline response time and one main metric to measure the effect against.
s1.tip: Don't promise "AI will replace the work" — promise "AI removes the chore of drafting".

s2.title: What exactly AI suggests to the agent
s2.why: The value of assist is in targeted suggestions at the moment of working on the ticket, not in a general chat. The agent should get ready material to resolve quickly without switching context.
instructions: List the three suggestion types: 2-3 reply variants, similar resolved tickets, relevant KB articles
Decide where they show: a browser plugin or an integration right inside the helpdesk
Describe the trigger: the agent opens a ticket — suggestions appear automatically
Agree that a suggestion is a draft: the agent selects, edits and sends
s2.validate: You can name the three suggestion types and where the agent sees them without switching context.
s2.tip: Three good reply variants beat ten mediocre ones — the agent shouldn't waste time choosing.

s3.title: Key step 1 — ticket context and customer history
s3.why: Suggestion quality depends directly on context. If AI reads only the current message, answers will be generic. With customer history and ticket context, suggestions become relevant.
instructions: Connect ticket data to AI: subject, messages, product, status
Add customer history: past contacts, plan, open issues
Connect a base of historical resolved tickets with good answers as an example source
Verify that sensitive data is handled per the privacy policy
s3.validate: On ticket open, AI sees the current context, the customer history, and the base of past resolutions.
s3.tip: Without a quality archive of resolved tickets, similar-case search won't work — it's the foundation.

s4.title: Key step 2 — reply variant generation
s4.why: The main accelerator is a ready draft. AI generates several variants in different tones, the agent picks the closest and refines it instead of writing from scratch. That's how response time drops from 8 to 3 minutes.
instructions: Set up generation of 2-3 reply variants in different tones: formal / friendly / technical
Show the variants next to the ticket so the agent selects and inserts in one click
Let the agent edit the inserted text before sending
Enable learning from edits: AI learns from how the agent refines drafts
s4.validate: The agent gets 2-3 editable reply variants and can send in minutes instead of writing from scratch.
s4.tip: Realistic target: ~70% of suggestions accepted with minor edits, 20% with significant edits, 10% unused.

s5.title: Quality and risks — the agent decides
s5.why: Assist is safe precisely because the human is in the loop. But bad suggestions destroy trust faster than good ones build it. Suggestion quality must be controlled, and the final decision always rests with the agent.
instructions: Lock the rule: AI gives a draft, the agent checks and sends — never the other way around
Track the share of accepted / significantly edited / discarded suggestions
If the discard share grows — improve context and examples, don't pressure agents
Protect sensitive customer data and check suggestions for factual accuracy
s5.validate: There's a suggestion-quality metric and a clear rule that the final decision always rests with the agent.
s5.tip: A high discard rate is a signal to improve the AI, not a reason to force agents.

s6.title: Rollout and adoption checklist
s6.why: Adoption is built on value, not a mandate. If you force "mandatory" AI use, bad suggestions will force writing from scratch and the team will turn away. Show the time saved — and agents will adopt assist on their own.
instructions: Run a pilot on part of the team, not everyone at once
Show each agent their time saved per ticket — concrete savings
Collect feedback on bad suggestions and improve context quickly
Don't enforce mandatory use — expand through voluntary adoption
Run the checklist: context connected, variants generated, quality metric visible, human in the loop
s6.validate: The pilot is running, each agent sees their own time savings, and expansion happens without coercion.
s6.tip: The best salesperson for assist is the agent who saved an hour in a day and told a colleague.

cs-knowledge-base.title: AI Knowledge Base Operations
cs-knowledge-base.subtitle: Turn your knowledge base from a "PDF dump" into a living source of truth for AI
cs-knowledge-base.whatItIs: A support knowledge base (KB) is not a folder of human-facing articles — it is the primary source your AI assistant draws answers from. AI Knowledge Base Operations is a set of recurring processes: structuring articles for vector search, auto-populating from resolved tickets, gap analysis (what is asked often but has no article), and keeping content current. The goal is for AI to find the right article instead of answering "I do not know".
cs-knowledge-base.approach: The course moves from diagnostics and structure to two key operations — populating from tickets and finding gaps — and ends with quality control and rollout. The core principle: KB quality is measured not by article count but by how reliably AI finds the correct answer. Structure (clear headers, atomic articles, metadata) matters specifically for AI retrieval, not just for human eyes.
outcomes: Understand why KB quality directly determines the success of all AI support
Can audit the base and rebuild taxonomy for vector search
Set up a weekly cycle that auto-populates articles from resolved tickets
Identify KB gaps from frequent unanswered questions and close them
Control currency, duplicates, and staleness risk through regular review

applyIn.title: Launching a tier-1 AI bot
applyIn.description: Before automating simple recurring questions, you need a KB optimized for AI search, or the bot will repeatedly answer "I do not know".

applyIn.title: Reducing agent load
applyIn.description: When agents waste time searching for articles and onboarding newcomers — a structured KB speeds up both.

applyIn.title: Ongoing content hygiene
applyIn.description: When the product changes faster than the base updates and stale, duplicate articles pile up.

pitfalls: Building the KB for humans only: modern optimization is for AI + humans, otherwise AI cannot find even an existing article
Measuring quality by article count: 500 unstructured articles are worse than 100 atomic ones with metadata
Not tracking currency: the product changed but the article did not — AI starts serving wrong answers as fact
Ignoring gaps: if AI answers "I do not know" to >20% of questions, the problem is coverage, not the model
Running population without human review: auto-drafts from tickets must be checked before publishing

exercises.question: Why are atomic articles with clear headers and metadata more important for AI than large overview documents?
exercises.hint: Think about how vector search works: it retrieves relevant fragments, not the whole file. The tighter the article boundaries, the more precise the match.

exercises.question: You have 400 articles but a low AI deflection rate. Where do you start diagnosing?
exercises.hint: Article count does not equal quality. Look at findability via vector search and the share of questions with no match.

exercises.question: How do you turn a stream of resolved tickets into KB articles without creating duplicates?
exercises.hint: First cluster the frequent questions, check them against existing articles, and only then draft new ones.

s1.title: Why and the outcome
s1.why: Without understanding that the KB is the single source of truth for AI, teams invest in article count instead of findability. KB quality sets the ceiling for all AI support.
instructions: State the thesis: AI cannot be better than the base it draws answers from
Record current metrics: findability, AI deflection rate, agent onboarding time
Define targets (e.g., findability from 50% to 90%, deflection +15-20%)
Agree with the team that the success metric is the share of tickets with a KB match, not base volume
s1.validate: You have 3 baseline "as-is" metrics and their target values written down
s1.tip: Separate the two KB audiences upfront — AI and humans. From here, optimize for both at once.

s2.title: Audit and base structure
s2.why: AI retrieval depends directly on structure: atomic articles, clear headers, and metadata give precise matches. A PDF dump cannot be found even with vector search.
instructions: Run an inventory: how many articles, when last updated, any duplicates
Build a structured taxonomy — categories and subcategories with no overlap
Break overview documents into atomic articles (one article — one question)
Add metadata: tags, product/section, update date, article owner
Enable vector search instead of keyword search
s2.validate: Every article is atomic, has a header and metadata, and fits exactly one taxonomy category
s2.tip: Check findability empirically: ask 20 real questions and see whether AI finds the right article.

s3.title: Populating and updating with AI
s3.why: Resolved tickets are the prime source of fresh, validated content. A weekly cycle turns them into articles and keeps the base from going stale.
instructions: Set up a weekly run: AI reads the week's resolved tickets
AI clusters frequent questions and checks them against existing articles
AI drafts new articles from ticket solutions in atomic KB format
A KB editor reviews drafts, edits, and publishes
Tag the article source (which ticket) for traceability
s3.validate: A repeatable weekly cycle is running, and at least one batch of auto-drafts has passed review and been published
s3.tip: Never publish auto-drafts directly — mandatory human review guards against errors and duplicates.

s4.title: Finding gaps from tickets
s4.why: If AI answers "I do not know" to >20% of questions, the problem is coverage. Gap analysis shows what is asked often but has no article.
instructions: Collect questions where AI found no match or answered "I do not know"
Group them by frequency — high-frequency gaps get closed first
Map gaps to agent complaints of "cannot find the article"
Feed the prioritized list into the population cycle (step 3)
Track the trend: the share of questions with no KB match should fall
s4.validate: A prioritized gap list exists, and top gaps are queued for article creation
s4.tip: Gaps are the cheapest way to grow deflection rate: you close exactly what is actually being asked.

s5.title: Quality, currency, risks
s5.why: A stale article is more dangerous than a missing one: AI serves a wrong answer as fact. Regular review keeps the base current and duplicate-free.
instructions: Set up a monthly analysis: which articles are cited and which are dead
AI flags outdated content (product changed — article did not)
AI suggests merging duplicate articles
Assign owners and a review date for critical articles
Keep a risk log: wrong answers, duplicates, loss of source-of-truth on manual edits
s5.validate: A monthly review is running, outdated articles are flagged, duplicates merged or queued
s5.tip: Tie the staleness signal to product releases — when functionality changes, check the related articles.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A one-off audit does not keep a KB alive. You need locked-in cycles (weekly and monthly) with owners and metrics, or the base degrades again.
instructions: Lock in roles: KB editor, article owners, metrics owner
Fix the cadence: population — weekly, quality review — monthly
Surface a metrics dashboard: findability, deflection rate, share of unmatched questions
Run the checklist: taxonomy, atomicity, metadata, vector search, population cycle, gap analysis, currency review
Schedule a quarterly check of metrics against the targets from step 1
s6.validate: Cycles are scheduled, roles assigned, the metrics dashboard works, the checklist is fully passed
s6.tip: Make deflection rate a metric visible to the whole team — it turns KB ops from a chore into a source of real impact.

cs-escalation.title: Smart Support Escalation
cs-escalation.subtitle: AI decides when to hand off to a human and exactly to whom — with ready context
cs-escalation.whatItIs: Smart escalation is a layer between first-line AI support (tier-1) and humans (tier-2). The AI decides when it can't cope, routes the ticket to the right specialist (by topic, load, severity), and hands it over not empty but with a ready summary: what the customer wants, what the AI already tried and why it failed, and the recommended next step.
cs-escalation.approach: Escalation is not "the AI gave up" but a managed handoff that preserves context. We build it in three blocks: triggers (when to escalate), routing (to whom), and context handoff (with what). The key risk is threshold calibration: escalating too aggressively kills deflection (the AI's ability to close tickets itself), while escalating too little drops quality. So every step is tied to measurable metrics.
outcomes: An escalated ticket reaches the agent with ready context — reading takes 30 seconds instead of 5 minutes
Routing accuracy grows from 80% to 95%: the right specialist on the first try, with no bouncing between queues
Time-to-resolution for escalated tickets drops by roughly 40%
The escalation threshold is calibrated: deflection is preserved and quality does not fall
Agents complain less about "why was this passed to me" — escalations are relevant and contextual

applyIn.title: B2B SaaS with separate teams
applyIn.description: Billing, technical, and account questions go to different queues. The AI classifies the domain and routes the ticket to the right team rather than a shared pool.

applyIn.title: High volume of routine requests
applyIn.description: Tier-1 AI closes simple things itself and escalates the complex ones with a summary. Humans handle only what truly needs a human.

applyIn.title: Support with severity-based SLAs
applyIn.description: Critical incidents are escalated immediately with a severity tag and history, bypassing the general queue so the SLA is not breached.

pitfalls: Escalating "just in case" at low confidence: if the AI errs in 10% of cases but escalates 50%, that's degradation, not insurance
Handing off a ticket without context: the agent spends time reading the history and the whole point of smart escalation is lost
Routing to a shared pool instead of a specific team — the routing-accuracy gain is lost
Not calibrating the threshold against metrics: too high kills deflection, too low drops quality
Not collecting agent feedback on escalation quality — without it you can't tell whether handoffs are relevant

exercises.question: The AI escalates 50% of tickets but errs in only 10% of cases where it could have answered itself. What's wrong and which way should the threshold move?
exercises.hint: Compare the share of escalations with the share of real AI errors. If escalations are many times higher, the confidence threshold is too low and is killing deflection.

exercises.question: Define the minimal set of escalation-summary fields so an agent understands the ticket in 30 seconds.
exercises.hint: Lean on the node's example: customer info + history, what the customer wants, what the AI tried and why it failed, recommended next step.

exercises.question: Which metric should be the main signal of escalation quality (not speed)?
exercises.hint: Speed is measured via time-to-resolution. Handoff quality is best captured by agent feedback on relevance and completeness of context.

s1.title: Why smart escalation and what result
s1.why: Dumb escalation is a ticket without context: the agent spends 5 minutes reading the history. Smart escalation shows the agent a summary, what was already tried, and the recommended step. Velocity grows without quality loss. First fix the goal and metrics, otherwise there's nothing to calibrate the threshold against later.
instructions: Describe the current pain: how long an agent spends getting up to speed on an escalated ticket and how often escalations are irrelevant
Fix target metrics: time-to-resolution for escalated tickets, routing accuracy, agent feedback on escalation quality
Identify where escalation is the bottleneck today: bouncing between queues, lost context, breached SLAs
Agree that escalation is a managed handoff, not "the AI gave up": deflection stays a goal
s1.validate: There is a list of 3 metrics with current values (baseline) and targets, and the main process pain is clear.
s1.tip: Without a baseline you can't prove the effect. Capture current numbers before rollout, even rough ones.

s2.title: Escalation triggers and threshold calibration
s2.why: The trigger decides WHEN the AI hands a ticket to a human. This is also the biggest risk of the whole process: the confidence threshold. Too high kills deflection (the AI is afraid to answer itself), too low drops quality. Calibration matters more than it seems.
instructions: List explicit triggers: low AI confidence, an explicit human request from the customer, high severity, sensitive topic (money, security)
Set the confidence threshold and fix it as a parameter you'll move based on metrics
Tie the share of escalations to the share of real AI errors: if escalations are many times higher than errors, the threshold is too low
Describe edge cases: what to do at borderline confidence (e.g., an AI attempt plus a quick agent check)
s2.validate: The trigger list is ready, the confidence threshold is set as a tunable parameter, and there's a rule linking "share of escalations vs share of errors".
s2.tip: Calibrate the threshold iteratively from data, not by gut. Start conservative and lower it while watching deflection and quality.

s3.title: Key step 1 — routing to the right team
s3.why: Routing accuracy is hitting the right specialist on the first try (goal from 80% to 95%). A ticket in a shared pool means bounces and lost time. The AI must classify the problem domain and pick a queue.
instructions: Define domains and queues: billing, then billing_team; technical, then tech_support; account, then account_specialists
Set up AI problem classification before queue selection — the domain is determined by the substance of the request, not by keywords
Add a second routing factor beyond topic: queue load and severity, so critical items don't get stuck
Describe a fallback: where to route the ticket if the domain isn't confidently determined (e.g., a general triage with a tag)
s3.validate: Each domain maps to a specific queue, classification runs before queue selection, and there's a fallback for an undetermined domain.
s3.tip: Measure routing accuracy as the share of tickets with no bouncing between queues. That's fairer than "the AI named a category".

s4.title: Key step 2 — context handoff
s4.why: The main value of smart escalation: the agent gets ready context, not just "here is a ticket". The goal is to understand the ticket in 30 seconds instead of 5 minutes. Without a summary, all the routing is pointless.
instructions: Fix the mandatory summary fields: customer info + history, what the customer wants, what the AI tried and why it failed, recommended next step
Make the AI generate the summary automatically at the moment of escalation, not the agent assembling it by hand
Include the escalation reason (which trigger fired) in the handoff — the agent instantly grasps the decision context
Check that the summary is short and reads in ~30 seconds: no raw logs, only what's relevant
s4.validate: An escalated ticket arrives with a full summary per the schema, and the agent grasps the gist in 30 seconds without reading the whole history.
s4.tip: The field "what the AI tried and why it failed" is the most valuable: it saves the agent from repeating steps already taken.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: Escalation can degrade quietly: the AI starts over-insuring, routing drifts, summaries become formal. You need quality metrics and feedback, otherwise the process rots unnoticed.
instructions: Collect agent feedback on escalation quality: was the handoff relevant and was the context complete
Track deflection and quality together: a rise in escalations at the same AI quality is a sign of over-insuring
Monitor routing accuracy over time: a drop means domains or classification are outdated
Set a rule to revisit the confidence threshold based on metrics, not on one-off complaints
s5.validate: There is a regular quality signal (agent feedback) and three metrics monitored: deflection, routing accuracy, time-to-resolution.
s5.tip: The main handoff-quality metric is agent feedback, not speed. Speed without relevance is deceptive.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Launching without staging and a checklist risks dropping either deflection or quality at once. We roll out gradually, starting with one domain, and expand by confirmed metrics.
instructions: Launch on one domain (e.g., billing): triggers + routing to a single queue + summary
Capture metrics over a period and compare against the baseline from step 1 before expanding
Expand to the remaining domains only after confirming routing accuracy and positive agent feedback
Run the checklist: triggers set, threshold being calibrated, queues mapped to domains, summary auto-generated, metrics monitored
Make the threshold and domain review a regular process, not a one-off
s6.validate: The single-domain pilot shows improvement against baseline, the 5-point checklist is passed, and there's a metric-driven expansion plan.
s6.tip: Don't roll out to all domains at once. One domain, then metrics, then expansion protects both deflection and quality.

cs-quality-monitoring.title: AI Support Quality Monitoring
cs-quality-monitoring.subtitle: How to catch AI degradation before customers notice it
cs-quality-monitoring.whatItIs: A continuous process for controlling AI response quality in support: a weekly random sample of conversations, then human review, then extraction of failure patterns, then adjustments to prompts and the knowledge base (KB). Without monitoring, AI degrades silently: errors accumulate and customer satisfaction (CSAT, a 1-5 scale) drops only after the fact.
cs-quality-monitoring.approach: The course moves from understanding why monitoring is needed to a working weekly cycle. First we fix the quality criteria (accuracy, tone, completeness), then we set up two review tiers: cheap auto-evaluation of all conversations and expensive human review on a sample. We separately address the risk of bias in the evaluation itself, and close with an implementation checklist anchored on an action loop, without which monitoring becomes theater.
outcomes: You understand why AI quality degrades silently and how drift precedes a CSAT drop
You formulate measurable quality criteria: accuracy, tone, completeness with a >4/5 threshold
You set up auto-evaluation of conversations as a first filter over 100% of traffic
You organize a 10% sample for human review with extraction of failure patterns
You embed an action loop: every error found leads to a prompt or KB fix

applyIn.title: AI tier-1 launch
applyIn.description: From day 1 of automating simple, typical questions, monitoring is turned on immediately, not 'when a problem appears'.

applyIn.title: Seasonal product changes
applyIn.description: A release of new plans or features changes customer questions — monitoring catches the slip of an AI trained on the old KB.

applyIn.title: Scaling volume
applyIn.description: As conversation volume grows, auto-evaluation keeps control over 100% of traffic while humans review only a representative sample.

pitfalls: Monitoring without an action loop: found errors do not lead to changes — that is theater, not quality control
Reviewing only on complaints: drift accumulates for weeks, and by the time complaints arrive CSAT has already dropped
Trusting auto-evaluation alone: the LLM judge inherits the same blind spots as the AI it evaluates
Taking a non-representative sample: reviewing only escalations skews the picture toward the worst cases
A single combined score with no breakdown: 'quality 4/5' hides that tone is great while accuracy failed

exercises.question: AI support worked great all quarter with no complaints. Why spend resources on weekly review?
exercises.hint: Think about silent degradation: the KB and product change, and the absence of complaints does not equal quality — it may just mean drift has not yet crossed the customer's irritation threshold.

exercises.question: Auto-evaluation shows 95% of responses >4/5, but customers complain. Where is the gap?
exercises.hint: An LLM judge can share the evaluated AI's misconceptions. Cross-check auto-evaluation against human review on the same sample — the divergence is the judge's blind spot.

exercises.question: Quality dropped below 4/5 for two weeks in a row. What action does the process call for?
exercises.hint: Escalation: pause AI tier-1 and investigate, not 'let's watch one more week'.

s1.title: Why monitor and what is the outcome
s1.why: AI is not static: the KB changes, the product changes, customer questions change. AI that worked in Q1 slips in Q3. Monitoring catches drift before customers notice and CSAT drops. Without it, errors accumulate silently.
instructions: Fix the thesis: no complaints ≠ quality, degradation happens silently
Define the goal of monitoring — drift detection before a CSAT drop, not reporting
Decide that monitoring runs from day 1 of the AI tier-1 launch, not 'when there is a problem'
Write down the expected outcome: every week prompts and the KB get better
s1.validate: The team agrees that monitoring is continuous and mandatory, not reactive
s1.tip: Frame monitoring as insurance against silent degradation, not as control over the AI — it is easier to get resources for review that way.

s2.title: Quality criteria and metrics
s2.why: Without measurable criteria, 'quality' is subjective and reviewers rate differently. A breakdown into accuracy, tone, completeness shows WHAT exactly is slipping, not just 'it got worse'.
instructions: Define three dimensions: accuracy (factual correctness), tone (fit with brand voice), completeness (fullness of the answer)
Set the threshold: share of AI responses rated >4/5 is the main metric
Add a trend metric: better/worse week over week
Fix tracking of the top-3 failure categories
Set the escalation threshold: quality <4/5 for two weeks in a row, then pause AI tier-1
s2.validate: Any reviewer using the same criteria gives close scores to the same conversation
s2.tip: Do not reduce everything to one score: a combined '4/5' hides that tone is perfect while accuracy failed.

s3.title: Key step 1 — auto-evaluation of conversations
s3.why: A human physically cannot check 100% of conversations. Auto-evaluation (an LLM judge using the same criteria) gives a cheap first filter over all traffic and flags suspicious conversations for a human.
instructions: Describe the accuracy/tone/completeness criteria as a rubric for the LLM judge
Run 100% of AI responses through auto-evaluation, scoring each dimension
Set up automatic routing of conversations scored <4/5 into the review queue
Store the scores to compute the weekly trend and the top-3 failure categories
s3.validate: Auto-evaluation runs all traffic and flags low scores without manual involvement
s3.tip: Do not trust auto-evaluation blindly — it is a first filter, not a final verdict; calibrate the judge against human review.

s4.title: Key step 2 — sample for human review
s4.why: Auto-evaluation inherits the AI's blind spots. A human catches what the judge misses and formulates concrete failure patterns that lead to prompt and KB fixes.
instructions: Take a random sample of at least 10% of AI responses weekly (not only escalations)
The quality team rates each conversation on accuracy, tone, completeness
Extract patterns: 'AI confuses billing X with Y', 'loses context Z'
For each pattern, define an action: KB fix / system prompt fix / new edge case
Cross-check human scores against auto-evaluation on the same sample to calibrate the judge
s4.validate: Over the week the top-3 failure categories are extracted and each has a concrete action assigned
s4.tip: The sample must be random and representative: reviewing only complaints skews the picture toward the worst cases.

s5.title: Evaluation quality and bias risk
s5.why: The evaluation system itself can be biased: the LLM judge shares the AI's misconceptions, a non-representative sample skews metrics, and a combined score masks problems. If the evaluation is not controlled, monitoring gives false comfort.
instructions: Regularly cross-check auto-evaluation against human evaluation — divergence points to the judge's blind spot
Check sample representativeness: distribution across topics and channels close to real traffic
Control inter-rater agreement of reviewers on shared conversations
Avoid averaging into one score — track each dimension separately
Periodically revisit the rubric: outdated criteria are also a source of bias
s5.validate: The auto-vs-human divergence is known, the sample is representative, and reviewers are aligned
s5.tip: Treat the evaluation system as one more AI component that can itself drift and needs calibration.

s6.title: Implementation and checklist
s6.why: Monitoring without a built-in action loop is theater. Found errors must turn into prompt and KB fixes every week, otherwise the process does not improve quality.
instructions: Embed monitoring into the weekly product rhythm: Mon — review, Tue — fix, Wed — validate
Assign an owner for each action from the failure patterns
Check the checklist: criteria set, auto-evaluation over 100% of traffic, 10% sample for review, bias control, escalation at <4/5 for two weeks
Track the weekly trend and top-3 categories as an ongoing metric
Confirm that every error found leads to a change, not just to a log entry
s6.validate: A full review, then fix, then validate cycle has run for at least one week with real fixes
s6.tip: If no fix surfaced in a week — check the representativeness of the sample and the strictness of the criteria, not the AI's perfection.

cs-support-analytics.title: AI Support Analytics
cs-support-analytics.subtitle: Turning tickets and chats into product insights and the voice of the customer
cs-support-analytics.whatItIs: A system where AI reads support metrics and ticket content and writes insight reports: trending issues, customer sentiment, agent performance patterns, product feedback. Support stops being a stream of scattered tickets and becomes a source of product decisions.
cs-support-analytics.approach: Support is free user research: thousands of conversations with real customers. But the team drowns in dashboards and never reads tickets by hand. The idea of this course is to build a repeatable weekly cycle: gather ticket and CSAT data, then let AI extract themes and trends, then turn insights into concrete product actions, then close the feedback loop (ticket, then insight, then product change, then fewer tickets). AI builds the narrative layer on top of the numbers; a human validates and decides.
outcomes: A weekly Support Analytics Report ships automatically: top trending issues with ticket counts and deltas
Time-to-insight drops from days to hours
The product team gets the voice of the customer and trending issues without manually digging through tickets
Every insight is tied to a concrete action: a product task, a knowledge base update, or a fix
The feedback loop is closed: delivery channels for insights into product and marketing are set up

applyIn.title: Weekly support review
applyIn.description: Instead of manually scanning dashboards, the team gets a ready narrative report with top issues, sentiment, and recommendations for the past week.

applyIn.title: Product request for the voice of the customer
applyIn.description: When the product team wants to understand what really hurts customers, support analytics provides ranked themes with quotes and ticket counts.

applyIn.title: Systematic pattern detection
applyIn.description: When there is a hunch of "many complaints about feature X", AI finds correlations (feature release, then spike in tickets about it) instead of eyeballing it.

pitfalls: Doing support analytics in isolation: if insights never reach product and engineering, they are useless
Trusting AI numbers without verification: the model can invent a trend or a correlation, so a human validator is required
Dumping everything into one report without prioritization — the team drowns in insights just as it drowned in dashboards
Ignoring privacy: tickets contain customer personal data and must not be fed carelessly to external models
Stopping at the report and not closing the loop — without action and result verification the cycle does not work

exercises.question: Which data sources will you collect for the first weekly report, and where do they physically live?
exercises.hint: At minimum: all tickets for the week (closed + open), customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores with comments, product release notes. Check whether you can access them via export or API.

exercises.question: Take one trending insight from the report and turn it into a concrete action with an owner. Who does what?
exercises.hint: An insight without an owner and an action is just an observation. Frame it: problem, then proposed action (product task / KB update), then who owns it, then how we verify it worked.

exercises.question: How will you make sure a correlation found by AI is real and not a coincidence?
exercises.hint: Cross-check against release dates and look at absolute ticket counts, not just percentages. A small sample produces large percentages from a tiny signal.

s1.title: Why and what outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal, analytics turns into pretty dashboards nobody uses. First, pin down which decision the report should drive.
instructions: State the report's core question: "what hurts customers this week and what should product do about it"
Define the recipients: product, engineering, marketing — who makes which decision
Fix the success metric: reduced time-to-insight and share of insights that reach action
Describe the output format: top issues with numbers and deltas, sentiment, recommendations
s1.validate: You have one sentence describing which decision, and by whom, will be made based on the report.
s1.tip: If you cannot name a concrete decision the report will change, the goal is not ready yet.

s2.title: Gather ticket and chat data
s2.why: Insight quality depends entirely on the completeness of the input. AI cannot see a trend in data it was never given.
instructions: Collect all tickets for the period: both closed and open — open ones reveal fresh trends
Add customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores with text comments — the source of sentiment
Attach product release notes for the period for later correlations
Make sure data is anonymized or access to personal data is restricted and approved
s2.validate: You have a single dataset: tickets + CSAT + release notes for the same period in an AI-readable format.
s2.tip: Open tickets often carry the freshest signal — do not discard them for the "cleanliness" of closed-only data.

s3.title: Key step 1: themes and trends
s3.why: Raw tickets are useless without grouping. AI's first value is collapsing thousands of contacts into a few trending themes with dynamics.
instructions: Ask AI to cluster tickets by theme and name each one in plain language
For each theme, get the ticket count and the delta vs. the previous period (up/down)
Add sentiment analysis: where customers are especially frustrated
Sort themes into a top 5 by a mix of volume and negativity, with 1-2 quotes per theme
s3.validate: You have a list of top trending issues with ticket counts, dynamics, and example quotes.
s3.tip: Demand absolute numbers next to percentages: +200% on three tickets is noise, not a trend.

s4.title: Key step 2: insights into product actions
s4.why: Trends alone change nothing. Value appears when each insight becomes a concrete action with an owner.
instructions: For each top theme, ask AI to find correlations with releases (e.g., "feature X shipped, then tickets about X +40%")
Formulate recommendations for the product team: what to fix or change
Formulate knowledge base update recommendations for recurring questions
Attach an owner and a result-verification method to each insight
s4.validate: Every top insight has a proposed action, an owner, and a way to verify the effect.
s4.tip: The "insight, then action, then owner" chain matters more than the number of insights. Three followed through beat twenty observations.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: AI can fabricate a trend, invent a correlation, or expose personal data. Without quality control the report erodes the team's trust.
instructions: Introduce a manual check: a human confirms the top insights before distribution
Test correlations for causation: timing coincidence is not a cause
Watch privacy: customer personal data must not leak into the model or the report
Log "AI said / what actually happened" gaps to improve the prompt and trust
s5.validate: There is a manual validation process for top insights and a rule for handling personal data.
s5.tip: One public false insight costs more than ten correct ones: the team will stop reading the report.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Analytics works only when it becomes a regular ritual with a closed feedback loop, not a one-off experiment.
instructions: Set up delivery channels: a weekly "Support Insights" post in the product channel, a monthly review session
Lock in a schedule and an owner for shipping the report
Close the loop: track how product changes reduce the volume of the related tickets
Quarterly, revisit the themes, metrics, and prompt quality
s6.validate: The report ships on schedule, reaches product, and there is at least one example of "insight, then change, then fewer tickets".
s6.tip: A closed loop is the main sign of maturity: ticket, then insight, then product change, then fewer tickets about the same problem.

cs-team-workflow.title: AI Customer Support Team Workflow
cs-team-workflow.subtitle: How to build a CS team process where AI is part of the operating model, not an individual hack
cs-team-workflow.whatItIs: A practical breakdown of how to turn scattered AI use by individual agents into a shared team process. You will define what to hand to AI (Tier-1 and agent-assist), what to keep with humans, build the two key steps of the operating model — a shared workspace and quality calibration — and lock in roles, risks, and a rollout plan. The result: the team operates as a single AI-augmented unit, and customers get the same quality answer no matter who is on shift.
cs-team-workflow.approach: From "AI = a tool" to "AI = part of how we operate".
