We follow the logic of an operating model: first the why and the outcome, then the human/AI division of labor, then the two core steps (shared setup and calibration), then quality and roles, and finally rollout with a checklist. Each step gives concrete actions, a validation, and a tip drawn from real CS team practice.
outcomes: You understand why a team needs a shared AI workflow and what measurable result it delivers (velocity, onboarding, quality consistency)
You clearly split the work: what AI closes on Tier-1, where AI assists the operator, and what stays with the human
You can deploy a shared team workspace: knowledge base, brand voice, scenario templates, response rules
You introduce regular quality calibration — the team reviews AI-handled tickets and holds a single standard
You lock in roles, an AI-aware growth path, and risk controls before launching across the whole team

applyIn.title: Growing support team
applyIn.description: A team of 5+ agents where everyone uses AI differently and customers get varying quality depending on the shift.

applyIn.title: New agent onboarding
applyIn.description: Newcomers arrive and "don't know how" — you need a repeatable process that cuts time-to-productivity from weeks to days.

applyIn.title: Multiple shifts / time zones
applyIn.description: Distributed support where keeping a single standard of tone and quality across shift teams matters, without manually checking every answer.

pitfalls: Treating AI as an agent's "individual perk" — without a team workflow, customers get an inconsistent experience
Deploying a shared workspace without brand voice and escalation rules — AI produces answers off the company tone
Handing AI tasks that need human judgment (conflicts, exceptions, emotions) instead of Tier-1 and assist
Launching the process without regular calibration — quality drifts and no one notices the degradation
Rewarding only "more tickets", ignoring those who improve the team's AI workflow itself

exercises.question: Take your team's last 10 tickets and tag each one: pure Tier-1 for AI, agent-assist (AI draft + human edits), human-only. What share falls into each category?
exercises.hint: Tier-1 — repeatable questions answerable from the knowledge base. Assist — non-standard but template-solvable. Human — conflicts, exceptions, strong emotions, legal/money.

exercises.question: Describe what must live in the shared team workspace so a new agent answers in the company tone on day one without personal mentoring.
exercises.hint: Minimum: indexed knowledge base, brand voice guide, templates for common scenarios, and response rules with escalation criteria.

exercises.question: Design the weekly calibration format: how many tickets to review, what questions to ask the team, how to capture decisions.
exercises.hint: 5 AI-handled tickets per meeting. Questions: what worked, what you'd change, whether rules/templates need updating. Decisions flow back into the shared workspace.

s1.title: Why a team needs a shared AI workflow and the outcome
s1.why: Without a shared operating model, AI stays a personal habit of individual agents. The customer gets varying quality depending on who picked up the ticket. A team workflow delivers consistency — support's core asset.
instructions: Capture the problem in numbers: how much quality and speed differ between agents and shifts today
State the target outcome: higher velocity (agents handle 50%+ more tickets), shorter onboarding (from 4 weeks to 2), quality consistency across shifts (+60%)
Frame the paradigm shift for the team: moving from "AI = a tool" to "AI = part of how we operate"
Define the launch trigger: team of 5+ agents, new people who "don't know how", quality fluctuating between shifts
s1.validate: You have a 1-page rationale with current and target metrics — understandable by both the manager and a frontline agent.
s1.tip: Don't sell "AI is faster" — sell "the customer gets an equally good answer from any agent". Consistency convinces faster than speed.

s2.title: What to hand to AI and what to keep with humans
s2.why: The main mistake is handing AI everything or, conversely, only drafts. A clear division of labor defines where AI closes the ticket itself (Tier-1), where it assists the operator (assist), and where a human is mandatory.
instructions: AI on Tier-1: repeatable questions answerable from the knowledge base — AI prepares the full answer, the human confirms or it auto-sends per rules
AI in assist mode: non-standard but solvable tickets — AI gives a draft and context, the operator edits and decides
Human-only: conflicts, policy exceptions, strong emotions, money/legal questions — AI may summarize but not answer
Write the split criteria as rules so it is a team decision, not each agent's separate call
s2.validate: Any agent can sort a ticket into Tier-1 / assist / human in seconds using shared criteria, not intuition.
s2.tip: The boundary isn't static: what's "human-only" today often moves to assist after calibration. Revisit the split in weekly meetings.

s3.title: Key step 1 — the shared team workspace
s3.why: Consistency is impossible while every agent has their own set of prompts. A shared workspace — one source of knowledge, tone, and templates — makes AI answer the same way for any operator.
instructions: Create a shared Claude Project "Support Workspace" with an indexed knowledge base
Add a brand voice guide — the tone for talking to customers, so answers sound like the company, not like different people
Add templates for common scenarios and a shared CLAUDE.md with response rules, escalation criteria, and tone rules
Connect the team's shared skills: e.g. response-drafter (answer draft), ticket-summarizer (ticket summary), escalation-formatter (escalation formatting)
s3.validate: A new agent on day one, using only the shared workspace, answers in the company tone without personal mentoring.
s3.tip: The brand voice guide matters more than it seems: without it AI is technically correct but sounds alien. Build it from 10-15 real good answers from your team.

s4.title: Key step 2 — quality calibration
s4.why: A shared setup without regular review degrades: rules go stale, templates drift from reality. Calibration is the process that holds a single standard and trains the team on live examples.
instructions: Set up a weekly calibration meeting: the team jointly reviews 5 AI-handled tickets
For each ticket discuss two questions: what worked and what you'd change
Capture conclusions as edits to the shared workspace — update CLAUDE.md, templates, brand voice guide
Move tickets between categories (human, then assist, then Tier-1) as trust in AI grows
s4.validate: After calibration, concrete edits are in the shared workspace and the team leaves with a shared understanding of the standard for the next week.
s4.tip: Don't turn calibration into a review of individual agents' mistakes — focus on the process and rules, or people will stop bringing honest examples.

s5.title: Quality, roles, and risks
s5.why: Without explicit roles and risk controls, the AI workflow rests on enthusiasts and breaks during turnover. You must lock in who owns what and pre-empt the typical quality risks.
instructions: Assign an owner of the shared workspace — who updates the knowledge base, brand voice, and rules after calibrations
Introduce an AI-aware growth path: agents who improve the team workflow move to the senior track, not just "answer more tickets"
Mitigate key risks: tone control (brand voice), guarding against off-policy answers (escalation rules), banning AI answers in sensitive categories
Agree that personal prompts don't replace the shared workspace — changes go into the shared setup, not personal copies
s5.validate: Every workflow element has an owner, and the team has a clear answer to "what happens if AI answers incorrectly".
s5.tip: Tie an agent's growth to improving the shared workflow — it's the only reliable way for the system to evolve without constant top-down pressure.

s6.title: Rollout and launch checklist
s6.why: A workflow designed on paper doesn't work without a managed rollout. The checklist turns the model into action and guards against launching team-wide with gaps in setup or rules.
instructions: Launch with a pilot group (2-3 agents) for 1-2 weeks before rolling out to the whole team

Check the readiness checklist: shared workspace assembled (KB + brand voice + templates), CLAUDE.md with rules and escalation ready, Tier-1/assist/human split fixed, skills connected, calibration on the calendar, owner assigned
Collect pilot feedback and apply edits to the shared workspace before full launch
Roll out to the whole team and lock in the rhythm: weekly calibration + updating the setup as an ongoing process
s6.validate: The team operates as a single AI-augmented unit: a new agent ramps in days, quality holds across shifts, and the workflow updates itself through calibration.
s6.tip: Don't launch team-wide without a pilot — with 2-3 agents you'll find rule gaps in a week that would cost weeks of chaos at 20 agents.

pd-discovery-research.title: AI Discovery Research
pd-discovery-research.subtitle: Turn interview synthesis and competitive analysis from a week of manual work into a one-hour AI pass with PM validation
pd-discovery-research.whatItIs: An AI-native approach to discovery research: instead of manually reading dozens of interviews, the PM builds a workflow where AI extracts themes, clusters quotes, and finds gaps in an hour, while the human validates and interprets. It does not replace research; it rebuilds the process: time-to-insight drops from days to hours, and coverage grows from 10 interviews to 50.
pd-discovery-research.approach: The course moves from setting the goal to a working research pipeline. First we fix why and what outcome is needed. Then we gather sources and index them in a Project with RAG. The key steps are theme extraction with frequency and sentiment, and quote clustering with gap detection. Then we embed human validation as a mandatory quality control against false insights. Finally, we put the workflow into a quarterly rhythm with a checklist.
outcomes: You build a repeatable research workflow: sources, then Project with RAG, then AI extraction, then PM validation, then structured report
You cut time-to-insight from days to hours and process 50 interviews instead of 10 without losing structure
You get themes with frequency and sentiment plus a hypothesis matrix instead of scattered notes
You embed mandatory validation of a 10-20% sample that catches false insights before they reach decisions
You run discovery as a repeatable quarterly process rather than a one-off heroic sprint

applyIn.title: Quarterly customer research
applyIn.description: You collect 30-50 interviews and support tickets per quarter, AI extracts shifts in themes and sentiment, the PM decides what is actionable.

applyIn.title: Competitive monitoring
applyIn.description: You index competitor reviews from G2/Trustpilot, AI finds what people praise and criticize, and you track landscape changes without manual reading.

applyIn.title: Pre-discovery before a feature
applyIn.description: Before launching a direction, you run accumulated customer calls through the workflow to surface gaps — what people often ask for but we do not do.

pitfalls: Relying on AI without human validation — AI misses irony, edge cases, and cultural context, and false insights leak into decisions
Not validating a sample: skipping the 10-20% quote check leaves you with no confidence in the other 80%
Mixing extraction and interpretation — AI extracts themes, but the call on what is actionable stays with the PM
Running the workflow on 3-5 interviews: AI synthesis pays off from >10 sources per topic, otherwise manual reading is faster
Ignoring raw data retention — without access to original quotes, the report cannot be rechecked or defended

exercises.question: You have 25 interviews and a month of support tickets on one topic. How do you organize the sources so AI can synthesize them?
exercises.hint: Think of a Project with a RAG index: all transcripts and tickets in one place so AI searches the full corpus, not a single file.

exercises.question: AI produced 12 themes with frequency and sentiment. Which ones do you validate manually and why those?
exercises.hint: Validate a 10-20% sample; prioritize high-frequency themes or those feeding a decision, where the cost of a false insight is highest.

exercises.question: AI found a 'gap': a feature is often mentioned but is missing from the product. What do you do before putting it on the roadmap?
exercises.hint: Check the original quotes in raw data — mention frequency does not equal actionable; make sure it is real pain, not a few isolated voices.

s1.title: Why and what outcome: the goal of the discovery pipeline
s1.why: Discovery is the most time-intensive part of PM work: 50 interviews = a week of manual synthesis. Without a clear goal, an AI workflow becomes a pretty but useless report. We fix that time-to-insight must drop from days to hours and coverage must grow from 10 to 50 sources.
instructions: State the research question in one sentence: exactly what you want to learn from the data
Fix the target metric: time-to-insight and theme coverage (how many sources you will actually process)
Define the output format: a structured research report plus accessible raw data for rechecking
Separate the AI task (extraction, clustering, gaps) from the PM task (validation, interpretation, decision)
s1.validate: You have one research question, a target metric, and an explicit split of 'what AI does / what the human does'.
s1.tip: If a topic has fewer than 10 sources, AI synthesis does not pay off — read manually. The workflow earns its value at scale.

s2.title: Where to start: gather and index the sources
s2.why: AI synthesizes only what it sees. Scattered files give scattered conclusions. By gathering transcripts, tickets, and competitor reviews into a single Project with a RAG index, you give AI a unified corpus — the basis for frequency and sentiment analysis across all data at once.
instructions: Gather inputs: interview transcripts, support tickets for a period, competitor reviews from G2/Trustpilot
Create a Project 'Research' and load all sources into its RAG index
Normalize transcripts to a single format (speaker, date, topic) so AI can tell apart utterances
Keep raw data separately — it must stay accessible for rechecking quotes
s2.validate: All sources sit in one Project with RAG, and AI answers a test question with references to specific quotes.
s2.tip: Tag the source of each fragment (interview #, ticket, review) — later this is critical for tracing an insight back to data.

s3.title: Key step 1: theme extraction with frequency and sentiment
s3.why: This is the first AI pass the whole pipeline is built for: in an hour instead of a week, AI extracts themes and computes their frequency and sentiment. This turns scattered notes into structured themes — the basis for every downstream decision.
instructions: Ask AI to extract themes across the whole corpus with mention frequency
Add sentiment to each theme: positive/negative/neutral and in what context
Require each theme to be backed by references to specific original quotes
Sort themes by frequency — this is the primary, not final, priority
s3.validate: You have a list of themes with frequency and sentiment, and for each you can open the original quotes in raw data.
s3.tip: Do not trust frequency blindly: a rare but sharp pain can matter more than a frequent minor wish. The PM decides this in step 5.

s4.title: Key step 2: quote clustering and gap detection
s4.why: Themes without structure are still noise. Clustering similar quotes and detecting gaps turn data into a map: what people often mention but we do not do. This is where the hypothesis matrix is born — the actionable output of discovery.
instructions: Ask AI to group similar quotes into clusters within each theme
Request gaps: what is often mentioned in the data but absent from the product
Generate a hypothesis matrix: theme, then hypothesis, then which data supports it
Link clusters to competitive context from reviews where relevant
s4.validate: You have quote clusters, a gap list, and a hypothesis matrix where each row references data.
s4.tip: A gap is a signal, not a verdict. Before putting it on the roadmap, check whether it is pain or a few isolated voices.

s5.title: Quality and risks: human validation against false insights
s5.why: The main mistake is relying on AI without validation. AI misses irony, edge cases, and cultural context, and then false insights flow into decisions. Sample validation is the mandatory quality control that turns an AI draft into a reliable result.
instructions: Take a 10-20% sample of quotes and check them against the real meaning of the source
Prioritize validation of high-frequency themes and those feeding a decision
Check edge cases and irony: where AI might have read sarcasm as positive
Mark themes as actionable / needs follow-up / rejected
s5.validate: You validated a 10-20% sample, marked the status of each theme, and recorded where AI was wrong.
s5.tip: Validation on a small sample raises confidence in the whole corpus: checking 15% calibrates the reliability of the other 85%.

s6.title: Rollout: workflow into a quarterly rhythm + checklist
s6.why: A one-off synthesis is a sprint, but value comes from repeatability. By embedding the workflow into quarterly customer research, you get systematic visibility into shifts in themes, sentiment, and the competitive landscape — the foundation of AI-native product transformation.
instructions: Formalize the pipeline as repeatable: inputs, then Project with RAG, then AI extraction, then PM validation, then report
Set a cadence: quarterly customer research and regular competitive monitoring
Compare reports quarter over quarter — track shifts in themes and sentiment
Run the final checklist before drawing conclusions
s6.validate: The workflow is documented and on a cadence, the checklist is passed, and the report references raw data.
s6.tip: Checklist: >10 sources per topic; raw data accessible; themes with frequency+sentiment; gaps checked; 10-20% sample validated; actionable statuses set.

pd-spec-generation.title: AI Spec Generation
pd-spec-generation.subtitle: From a rough idea to a ship-ready PRD in hours, not days
pd-spec-generation.whatItIs: AI writes PRDs, user stories, and technical specs from a rough idea and research input. The PM stops spending days formatting what they already know in their head and focuses on content quality. Time-to-PRD drops from 2 days to 4 hours including iterations.
pd-spec-generation.approach: The course walks through adopting spec generation as a repeatable workflow: first the why and the target outcome, then gathering quality input (template + examples + research), then generating the draft and iterating with the PM, then quality and risk control, and finally embedding it into the team's process with a checklist. The core principle: quality output requires quality input.
outcomes: A reproducible workflow that turns a rough idea and research into a PRD in 4 hours instead of 2 days
A single spec format across the team based on a fixed template
AI catches missing sections: success metrics, edge cases, open questions, technical considerations
The PM iterates on a draft for 3-5 rounds instead of writing from scratch
A measurable time-to-spec metric and dev-team feedback on PRD quality

applyIn.title: New feature from idea to PRD
applyIn.description: The PM jots down 3-5 sentences of rough idea, attaches research and a template, and AI produces a structured draft with a problem statement, user stories, and metrics to refine.

applyIn.title: Standardizing specs across the team
applyIn.description: When the team has inconsistent PRD formats, one template and 2-3 reference examples get locked in, and every new spec is generated in a single shape.

applyIn.title: Clearing the bottleneck before a sprint
applyIn.description: When the team loses momentum between "have an idea" and "PRD written", AI handles the writing part and the spec backlog stops piling up.

pitfalls: Generating a PRD without research input — "write a PRD for feature X" yields a generic shell useless to the team
Treating the AI draft as final — without 3-5 rounds of edits the PM's content quality stays low
No fixed template — AI produces a different structure each time and consistency is lost
Feeding a rough idea with no constraints or product context — AI fills gaps and steers the spec off course
Ignoring sections AI flagged as open questions — those often hide the real risks

exercises.question: Why does "write a PRD for feature X" almost always produce a useless result?
exercises.hint: Recall garbage in = garbage out: AI lacks the product context, research, and constraints, so it outputs generic content.

exercises.question: What must go into the AI input for the PRD draft to be high quality?
exercises.hint: Three components: the PM's rough idea, the research output, and an existing template plus 2-3 reference examples.

exercises.question: Which part of the work does AI take off the PM, and which does the PM keep?
exercises.hint: AI handles the writing/structuring part; the PM focuses on content quality through iterations.

s1.title: Why it matters and the target outcome
s1.why: PRD writing is a shipping bottleneck. The PM spends days formatting what they already know, and the team loses momentum between idea and written spec. Understanding the goal sets the right success metric — time-to-spec, not "a pretty document".
instructions: Record the team's current time-to-PRD in days — this is the baseline for comparison
Define the goal: draft in hours, iterations with the PM, a ship-ready PRD as output
Agree that AI handles the writing part while the PM owns content quality
Choose measurable metrics: time-to-spec and dev-team feedback on PRD quality
s1.validate: You can state the current time-to-PRD in days and the target in hours
s1.tip: Don't sell this as "AI writes our PRDs" — sell it as "the PM stops spending days on formatting".

s2.title: Where to start: gather the input
s2.why: Quality output requires quality input. The most common mistake is generating without research, which produces a generic shell. Preparing the input is 80% of the result.
instructions: Assemble a documented PRD template — without it AI produces a different structure each time
Pick 2-3 high-quality finished PRDs as a reference for format and depth
Prepare the research output (e.g. from the discovery phase) on the feature topic
Phrase the rough idea: 3-5 sentences from the PM with the core and product context
s2.validate: You have a template, 2-3 examples, research, and a rough idea — all four components
s2.tip: If there's no research, get it first; a PRD without research input will be generic by definition.

s3.title: Key step 1: generate the draft
s3.why: This is the moment the input was gathered for: AI turns the rough idea and research into a structured draft in minutes, lifting the writing and formatting load off the PM.
instructions: Hand AI the rough idea, research output, template, and examples as one package
Ask it to generate a problem statement and user stories with acceptance criteria
Request success-metrics proposals and an open-questions block
Add technical considerations for engineering if the PRD goes into development
Make sure the draft strictly follows your template structure
s3.validate: You have a structured draft with all template sections, not free-form text
s3.tip: The more precisely constraints and context are set in the input, the less AI drifts off the product.

s4.title: Key step 2: iterate with the PM
s4.why: The draft is not the final. The PM's value is content quality, and iterations are what turn a generic draft into a ship-ready PRD. 3-5 rounds of edits is the norm, not a flaw.
instructions: Read the draft and mark where AI guessed or drifted from the point
Refine problem sections with targeted edits rather than rewriting from scratch
Bring success metrics and acceptance criteria to specifics for your product
Resolve each open question — these are often hidden risks and gaps
Iterate 3-5 rounds until it's ship-ready
s4.validate: The PRD reads as ready for development, with open questions closed or clearly flagged
s4.tip: Edit content, not wording for its own sake — the format is already set by the template.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: Without quality control an AI-PRD slides into generic, and hidden risks lurk in missing sections. Checking before handoff to development protects the team from rework.
instructions: Compare the PRD against reference examples for section depth and completeness
Verify that success metrics, edge cases, and open questions are present and meaningful
Collect dev-team feedback on PRD quality as a control metric
Watch for garbage in = garbage out: weak spots usually stem from weak input
s5.validate: The PRD has been checked against examples and received dev-team feedback
s5.tip: If quality is consistently low, fix the input (research, examples, constraints), not the edits.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: One-off generation doesn't change the process. The value comes when spec generation becomes a repeatable team workflow with a single format and a measurable metric.
instructions: Lock the workflow: input, then generation, then 3-5 iterations, then ship-ready PRD
Store the template and reference examples in a place accessible to the whole team
Introduce a time-to-spec metric and regular dev-team feedback collection
Run a checklist on every PRD: research present, template followed, sections complete, open questions closed
s6.validate: The team generates specs via a single workflow and time-to-spec is measured
s6.tip: Compare the new time-to-spec with the baseline from step 1 — that's the proof of value.

pd-roadmap-intelligence.title: AI Roadmap Prioritization
pd-roadmap-intelligence.subtitle: Turn roadmap decisions from "gut feel" into a structured framework with explicit weights and documented reasoning
pd-roadmap-intelligence.whatItIs: AI as a "second analyst" in roadmap discussions. It analyzes feedback patterns, competitor moves, customer requests, and internal data, then outputs ranked priorities with explicit reasoning for each opportunity. It is not a replacement for the PM's decision but a structured input into it: explicit criteria (impact, effort, strategic fit, risk), data-based scoring, and playing out alternative orderings.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.approach: The course walks through implementing AI prioritization end-to-end: first you fix why you need it and what outcome you expect, then you gather the data for scoring, run the two key steps (AI scoring and the human override decided by the PM), check quality and risks, and embed the process into a quarterly rhythm. The final decision always rests with a human — AI adds discipline, it does not remove judgment.
outcomes: Understand where AI prioritization delivers real value and where the human stays in charge
Gather the full set of inputs for scoring: backlog, feedback themes, competitor analysis, metrics, strategic objectives
Run AI scoring with explicit criteria and weights — get a ranked list with reasoning for each opportunity
Make the final decision as a PM, deliberately overriding the AI where it lacks context (politics, executive priorities, launches)
Embed the process into quarterly planning so next quarter you can explain "why we chose this"

applyIn.title: Quarterly planning
applyIn.description: Before the quarter starts, run the whole backlog + new ideas through AI scoring to enter planning with a ranked list instead of a blank page and opinions.

applyIn.title: Roadmap review with executives
applyIn.description: Prepare documented reasoning for each priority in advance — at the review you answer "why this, not that" with data, not intuition.

applyIn.title: The "everyone has their own opinion" debate
applyIn.description: When stakeholders pull the roadmap in different directions, explicit criteria and weights give a shared frame for the conversation and reduce roadmap thrashing.

pitfalls: Accepting the AI roadmap as final — AI does not know board politics, executive priorities, or upcoming launches; it is an input, not the decision
Feeding AI incomplete data: without feedback themes and metrics the scoring rests on guesses, not reality
Hiding the criteria weights — if impact/effort/strategic fit/risk are not explicit, scoring is not reproducible and not convincing at review
Not preserving reasoning: without documented rationale, a quarter later no one remembers why this was chosen, and the roadmap drifts again
Changing priorities under stakeholder pressure while ignoring your own criteria — the whole point of a structured framework is lost

exercises.question: Take 8–10 real opportunities from your backlog. Which 5 inputs do you need for the AI to score them meaningfully, and which of that data do you actually have right now?
exercises.hint: Lean on the workflow list: opportunities, feedback themes, competitor analysis, internal metrics, strategic objectives. Mark the gaps — that is your work in the data-gathering step.

exercises.question: Run 3 opportunities through the impact / effort / strategic fit / risk criteria and capture the reasoning. Where would your PM judgment diverge from a purely numeric ranking?
exercises.hint: Look for factors absent from the data: an upcoming launch, a customer promise, an executive priority. That is exactly where a deliberate override belongs.

exercises.question: Articulate how you will explain at the next roadmap review why one priority beat another. Is the documented reasoning enough to hold up without "gut feel"?
exercises.hint: A good answer cites specific weights and data, not authority. If you have to say "I just feel it", the reasoning is incomplete.

s1.title: Why and the expected outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal, AI prioritization becomes another report no one uses. Roadmap prioritization is usually done "by gut" under stakeholder pressure — this step fixes that AI brings a structured framework and what measurable outcome you expect.
instructions: Describe the current pain: how roadmap decisions are made today and where this causes reactive prioritization and thrashing
State the AI's role in one sentence: a "second analyst" giving ranked priorities with reasoning, not the final decision
Fix the expected effect in measurable terms: fewer reactive decisions, faster stakeholder alignment, less frequent roadmap flipping
Define the moment of use: quarterly planning, before a roadmap review with executives, the "everyone has their own opinion" debate
s1.validate: You have a one-sentence "why" and 2–3 measurable expected outcomes that are clear to the team and leadership.
s1.tip: Write the goal so it can be checked a quarter later. "Improve the roadmap" is not a goal; "answer at review with data, not intuition" is.

s2.title: Data for prioritization
s2.why: AI scoring is only as good as the inputs. Feeding it incomplete data means the ranking rests on guesses. The full data set is the foundation of the whole workflow.
instructions: Gather all product opportunities: current backlog + new ideas in one place
Add customer feedback themes (e.g., from feedback-synthesis) — what users actually ask for
Connect competitor analysis and internal metrics: revenue impact, retention
Fix the strategic objectives of the current quarter — the frame everything is judged against
Note data gaps: what is missing now and whether it can be gathered before scoring
s2.validate: All five input categories are gathered in one document; explicit gaps are either closed or marked as known limitations.
s2.tip: Quality of feedback themes and metrics matters more than volume. Ten well-described opportunities with data beat a hundred lines of raw backlog.

s3.title: Key step 1 — AI scoring
s3.why: This is the heart of the process: AI rates each opportunity against explicit criteria and makes the reasoning explicit. Without fixed weights the scoring is not reproducible and not convincing at review.
instructions: Set criteria and weights explicitly: impact, effort, strategic fit, risk
Run each opportunity through scoring, requiring reasoning per criterion for every opportunity
Ask the AI to play out alternative orderings, not a single "correct" list
Preserve the ranking together with the reasoning — this is the future documented rationale for review
s3.validate: There is a ranked list of opportunities where each shows scoring across the four criteria and a text reasoning, and the criteria weights are fixed.
s3.tip: If the AI returns a rank with no explanation, it is not a finished result. Per-item reasoning is mandatory, or step 4 (override) is impossible.

s4.title: Key step 2 — the human decides
s4.why: AI scoring is based only on the data you gave. It does not know board politics, executive priorities, or upcoming launches. The PM and leadership make the final decision, deliberately overriding the ranking where there is context beyond the data.
instructions: Walk the AI ranking top to bottom with leadership and mark items where intuition diverges from the numbers
For each divergence, name the factor outside the data: a launch, a customer promise, an executive priority, politics
Make the override explicit — record what you raised/lowered relative to the AI ranking and why
Fix the final order as a joint PM + leadership decision
s4.validate: There is a final priority order where every override from the AI ranking is accompanied by a recorded reason from real context.
s4.tip: An override is the norm, not an AI failure. The dangerous opposite is accepting the AI roadmap as final without applying human judgment.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: A structured framework works only if scoring is reproducible and reasoning is preserved. This step catches the typical risks: incomplete data, hidden weights, lost rationale, caving to stakeholders.
instructions: Check that reasoning is preserved for every priority — a quarter later you will need it to explain
Re-check input completeness: is any scoring still resting on guesses due to data gaps
Make sure criteria weights are fixed and the decision is reproducible, not based on authority
Test resilience to pressure: do priorities change only when data/criteria change, not under stakeholder pushing
s5.validate: Any priority can be explained by reference to data and weights; no position stands only on "gut feel" or pressure.
s5.tip: Quality test: in 3 months, can you answer "why we chose this" from the records? If not, the documented reasoning is incomplete.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A one-off run does not change the decision culture. To get a durable effect (less reactive prioritization, faster alignment), the process is embedded into a quarterly rhythm with a fixed checklist.
instructions: Tie the process to quarterly planning and to preparing the roadmap review with executives
Lock in the entry checklist: inputs gathered, then weights set, then AI scoring with reasoning, then human override recorded, then reasoning preserved
Assign an owner for refreshing the data (feedback themes, metrics) before each cycle
After the cycle, compare predictions with reality — what AI underrated, which criteria to reweight
Keep the documented reasoning as the source of truth for the next quarter
s6.validate: The process is tied to the quarterly rhythm, there is a data owner and a checklist by which any next cycle is reproducible without you.
s6.tip: Start with one quarter as a pilot. The pilot's goal is not a perfect roadmap but proof that decisions are now explainable with data.

pd-experimentation.title: AI Feature Experimentation
pd-experimentation.subtitle: Turn chaotic A/B tests into a structured experimentation engine with AI
pd-experimentation.whatItIs: A system where AI supports the full experiment cycle: it sharpens hypotheses, generates variant ideas, helps interpret statistics, and synthesizes learnings into a knowledge library. A shift from "ran A/B, forgot results" to an engine where every experiment becomes product knowledge.
pd-experimentation.approach: We follow the real experiment lifecycle: first fix why the team needs this engine and what outcome we want, then learn to write strong hypotheses, design with power analysis, read results, check statistical significance and risks, and finally roll out with a checklist. AI participates in sharpening hypotheses, generating variants, and post-analysis — but it does not predict the outcome.
outcomes: Every experiment starts with a measurable hypothesis (metric, effect size, timeframe, required sample)
AI generates 3-5 concrete variants with pros/cons instead of one obvious option
Results are interpreted with confidence level, caveats, and follow-up
Share of experiments with clear learnings grows from ~50% to ~90%
A searchable library of outcomes accumulates: "did we try this before?"

applyIn.title: Team with a flow of experiments
applyIn.description: When a product team runs 3+ experiments per quarter and loses results between sprints.

applyIn.title: Scaling across multiple teams
applyIn.description: When you need a uniform quality of hypotheses and analysis across teams, not a personal style per PM.

applyIn.title: Onboarding and activation
applyIn.description: When funnel changes are tested (e.g. cutting onboarding steps) and you must not confuse noise with a real effect.

pitfalls: Asking AI to "predict the A/B outcome before launch" — AI is not predictive; if it could predict, you wouldn't need an A/B
Running an experiment without power analysis and the required sample — conclusions will be noise
Stopping the test when the metric "looks good" (peeking) — inflates false positives
Not recording learnings into the library — knowledge evaporates by next quarter
Testing many changes in one variant — you can't tell what worked

exercises.question: Take the weak hypothesis "the new onboarding is better" and rewrite it as measurable with metric, magnitude, timeframe, and sample.
exercises.hint: Use AI as a critic: ask which of the four parameters are missing and to suggest values by analogy with past tests.

exercises.question: For one hypothesis, ask AI to generate 3 variant approaches and write down one risk for each.
exercises.hint: A good set covers different mechanics (visual, copy, step order), not three shades of one idea.

exercises.question: Given results: variant B +3% activation, p=0.18, n=400. What do you decide and why?
exercises.hint: Compare the p-value to the threshold and check whether the sample met the power analysis — the test may simply be underpowered.

s1.title: Why and what outcome
s1.why: Without an explicit goal the experimentation engine becomes a ritual. First fix the pain you solve: weak hypotheses, forgotten results, no scaling.
instructions: Describe the current pain: how many experiments per quarter and how many yield clear learnings
State the target outcome in numbers (e.g. learnings from 50% to 90%, velocity +50%)
Decide which cycle stages AI takes on: hypothesis sharpening, variant generation, post-analysis
Fix what AI does not do — predicting the outcome before launch
s1.validate: You have a one-pager: current state, target metrics, and AI's role in the cycle.
s1.tip: If the team runs <3 experiments per quarter — grow the flow first; the engine is premature.

s2.title: Hypotheses
s2.why: A strong hypothesis is the foundation. A weak one ("the new onboarding is better") is untestable: no metric, magnitude, timeframe, or sample.
instructions: Write the hypothesis as "if [change], then [metric] changes by [magnitude] over [timeframe]"
Run it through an AI critic: which of the four parameters are missing
Add the required sample size (n) as part of the hypothesis
Drop hypotheses you cannot measure with existing metrics
s2.validate: The hypothesis contains a metric, expected effect size, timeframe, and minimum sample.
s2.tip: Example of a strong wording: "cutting onboarding from 5 to 2 steps lifts activation by +15% over 4 weeks (n>1000)".

s3.title: Experiment design
s3.why: Design decides whether the result can be trusted at all. Here you settle variants, sample, and stopping conditions.
instructions: Ask AI to generate 3-5 concrete variants and discuss the pros/cons of each
Run a power analysis: what n is needed to catch the stated effect size
Fix the timeframe and stopping rule in advance (no peeking)
Make sure one variant changes one thing — otherwise attribution is impossible
Define the control group and success metric unambiguously
s3.validate: Variants, required n, timeframe, stopping rule, and control are fixed — before launch.
s3.tip: If the power analysis shows an unreachable n for your traffic — simplify the hypothesis or raise the expected effect.

s4.title: Analyzing results
s4.why: Raw numbers without interpretation are useless. AI helps turn data into a conclusion with a confidence level.
instructions: Feed AI the results: metric per variant, sample size, p-value/confidence interval
Ask it to state "winner with X confidence" or "no effect detected"
Request caveats: segments, anomalies, external factors of the period
Get a recommended follow-up — what to check next
s4.validate: You have a conclusion with a confidence level, a list of caveats, and a next step.
s4.tip: If AI gives a confident conclusion with no caveats — ask about segments and seasonality; they often change the picture.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: This is where false conclusions get cut. Statistical significance and data cleanliness decide whether the result becomes a decision.
instructions: Compare the p-value to the predefined threshold and check the sample met the plan
Verify there was no peeking — the test wasn't stopped early on a "nice" metric
Assess the multiple-comparisons risk if many metrics were viewed at once
Separate statistical from practical significance: does the effect size matter for the business
Mark the result as reliable / inconclusive / needs a rerun
s5.validate: The result passed significance, peeking, and practical-importance checks — a status is assigned.
s5.tip: +3% at p=0.18 and n=400 is not a win but a signal of an undersampled test; usually a rerun, not a rollout.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: An experiment is useless if its conclusions reach neither the product nor the knowledge library. Here we close the loop.
instructions: Make the call: roll out the winner, roll back, or rerun the experiment
Record the outcome in a searchable library: hypothesis, design, result, learning
Tag the entry so you can answer "did we try X before?"
Run the final checklist: hypothesis measurable, power analysis done, peeking excluded, significance checked, learning recorded
s6.validate: Decision made, outcome in the library, checklist closed on all points.
s6.tip: The library is worth more than any single test: a year later it saves the team months of repeated experiments.

pd-feedback-synthesis.title: AI Feedback Synthesis
pd-feedback-synthesis.subtitle: From "PM read 50 comments" to "AI processed 5000 and found the patterns"
pd-feedback-synthesis.whatItIs: A pipeline where AI aggregates feedback from all sources (NPS comments, support tickets, reviews, sales call notes, social), cleans and dedupes it, categorizes it, scores sentiment and extracts themes — turning a raw stream into structured insights with week-over-week trends.
pd-feedback-synthesis.approach: We move from goal to working loop: first fix why and what outcome, then connect the sources, then teach AI to extract themes and prioritize them into actions, then check representativeness and risks, and finally close the loop with the roadmap. Synthesis with no feedback into planning is polite theater, so rollout and a checklist are mandatory.
outcomes: Feedback coverage grows from ~5% (what a PM can physically read) to 100% of the volume processed
Time-to-trend drops from ~2 months to ~2 weeks: sentiment shifts are visible before they show up in churn
Roadmap decisions rest on data with magnitude and delta, not on "I remember someone complained"
Every theme is backed by real quotes and routed to the right team (product / engineering / marketing)
A closed loop: synthesis, then product review, then roadmap update, then measure impact

applyIn.title: Weekly voice-of-customer
applyIn.description: A regular report with top-5 themes, magnitude and delta instead of quarterly manual reading of a comment sample.

applyIn.title: Early churn detection
applyIn.description: Tracking week-over-week sentiment shifts to catch dissatisfaction before it turns into churn.

applyIn.title: Roadmap prioritization
applyIn.description: Themes with measurable weight and trend feed directly into product review as decision input, not a read-only reference.

pitfalls: Doing synthesis in a vacuum: the report goes nowhere. Output must feed roadmap planning, otherwise it's polite theater
Ignoring representativeness: loud social channels outweigh the quiet majority, and a trend becomes an artifact of one source
Reading magnitude without delta: what matters is not only a theme's size but its week-over-week change
Trusting AI categorization without spot checks — category drift and theme hallucinations distort priorities
Losing the quote-to-theme link: without supporting examples teams won't trust the findings or act on them

exercises.question: You have 5 feedback sources but 80% of the volume comes from support tickets. How does this skew the top-5 themes and what do you do?
exercises.hint: Think about weighting by source and segment rather than raw mention counts — tickets are biased toward problems, not satisfied silent users.

exercises.question: AI surfaces a "pricing" theme with magnitude 120 mentions, delta +5%. Engineering wants proof. What do you show?
exercises.hint: Representative quotes broken down by segment plus a multi-week trend to separate noise from a real signal.

exercises.question: The report ships 3 weeks straight but the roadmap doesn't change. Where is the break and how do you fix the loop?
exercises.hint: Check whether there's an explicit product review step with a decision owner and a feedback write-back of impact — synthesis without action is dead.

s1.title: Why and what outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal, synthesis becomes a pretty report no one reads. First fix the problem: feedback is fragmented across 5-10 sources, the PM physically can't read it all, and trends surface too late.
instructions: State the problem in one phrase: "voice of customer is anecdotal today, we need it systematic"
Fix target metrics: feedback coverage (from 5% to 100%) and time-to-trend (from 2 months to 2 weeks)
Define the consumers of the output: product (decisions), engineering (bugs), marketing (positioning)
Agree that output flows into roadmap planning, not into a read-only report
s1.validate: You have one sentence on the problem, 2 numeric metrics, and a list of 3 consumer teams.
s1.tip: If you can't name the decision the report will change, you're building theater, not a tool.

s2.title: Collect the sources
s2.why: Synthesis makes sense with ≥3 sources. Each source is biased differently (tickets toward problems, NPS toward loyalty), so they must be gathered together and normalized to one format.
instructions: List available sources: NPS comments, tickets with CSAT, App Store / G2 reviews, sales call notes, social
Set up regular collection (weekly) noting the volume of each source
Normalize records to one schema: text, date, source, customer segment
Run cleaning and deduplication — remove duplicates and empty/noise records
s2.validate: There are ≥3 sources in one format, with date and source on every record, no duplicates.
s2.tip: Keep the "source" field all the way through — you'll need it for the representativeness check in step 5.

s3.title: Extract themes (key step 1)
s3.why: This is the heart of synthesis: AI categorizes records, scores sentiment and extracts recurring themes. Here the raw stream becomes a structure you can rely on.
instructions: Set a fixed category set (feature, UX, pricing, performance, ...) to avoid drift
Run AI: categorization + sentiment analysis + theme extraction
For each theme collect magnitude (mention count) and representative quotes
Do a spot check of 20-30 records against the AI's findings
s3.validate: You have a list of themes, each with magnitude, sentiment and 2-3 real quotes; the spot check confirms categories.
s3.tip: Freeze the category list between weeks — otherwise delta becomes incomparable due to renamings.

s4.title: Prioritize into actions (key step 2)
s4.why: Themes without priority are just a list. You need to rank them by magnitude and delta (week-over-week change) and turn the top ones into concrete actions for teams.
instructions: Compute each theme's delta versus last week
Select the top-5 themes by a combination of magnitude and delta
Flag critical issues that need separate investigation
Attach each theme to an owning team: product / engineering / marketing
s4.validate: You have top-5 themes with magnitude and delta, a list of critical issues, and an owner per theme.
s4.tip: A sharp delta on a small magnitude is an early signal; don't discard it just because of a small absolute count.

s5.title: Quality and representativeness
s5.why: The main risk of synthesis is mistaking the artifact of one noisy source for a trend. Loud social easily outweighs the quiet majority, and AI hallucinations distort priorities.
instructions: Check source balance: is one source dominating the top themes
Weight themes by segment/source rather than counting raw mentions only
Separate noise from trend: confirm delta with a multi-week trajectory
Re-check questionable themes against quotes — any fabricated or AI-merged conclusions
s5.validate: For each top theme you can see the source distribution, and trends are confirmed by at least 2-3 weeks of data.
s5.tip: If a theme rests on a single source — mark it "needs confirmation", not as a trend.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Synthesis with no feedback into planning is polite theater. The loop closes only when findings reach the roadmap and impact is measured.
instructions: Assemble the weekly report: top-5 themes (magnitude + delta), quotes, critical issues
Run the cycle: synthesis, then product review, then roadmap update, then measure impact
Assign a product review owner who turns themes into decisions
Track metrics: feedback coverage and time-to-action on trending issues
s6.validate: At least one full cycle has run: report, then review, then roadmap change, then recorded impact.
s6.tip: A per-week checklist: sources collected, themes verified, representativeness accounted for, decision made and recorded.

pd-product-analytics.title: AI Product Analytics: From Data to Hypotheses
pd-product-analytics.subtitle: Turn "here is a dashboard" into "here is what happened and why" — AI writes hypotheses, the human verifies causation
pd-product-analytics.whatItIs: A workflow where AI reads product usage data (Amplitude, Mixpanel, GA) and, instead of a dry dashboard, produces an insight report: what changed, ranked hypotheses for "why did this happen?", and a list of investigations to run. Analysts and PMs stop spending hours formulating hypotheses by hand — AI does the first pass, the human validates.
pd-product-analytics.approach: We don't replace the analyst — we speed up the most expensive step: moving from numbers to explanations. AI handles detecting changes, correlations, and anomalies, generates ranked hypotheses, and suggests which queries and segments to check. Critically: AI outputs correlations and guesses, while causation ("release X caused metric Y to grow") is always confirmed by a human via cohort/A-B/before-after analysis.
outcomes: Cut time-to-hypothesis from days to hours in weekly product reviews
Get a structured insight report after every major release instead of a raw dashboard
Raise the share of analytics-backed decisions from ~30% to 70%+ of the team
Every notable metric change gets a documented explanation
Clearly separate correlation from causation, never treating an AI hypothesis as proven fact

applyIn.title: Weekly product review
applyIn.description: AI prepares the report in advance: what changed in DAU/MAU, retention, activation, feature usage — the team arrives to discuss hypotheses rather than build them from scratch.

applyIn.title: Post-release analysis
applyIn.description: After every major release, AI maps the release timeline against metric movements and proposes impact hypotheses — the human validates them via cohort analysis.

applyIn.title: Anomaly investigation
applyIn.description: When a metric unexpectedly grows or drops and the team "doesn't understand why", AI surfaces anomalous segments and ranks possible causes to check.

pitfalls: Trusting AI causal claims: "release X caused +5%" is correlation, not causation; human validation is mandatory
Accepting the first hypothesis as truth without testing it via cohort, A/B, or before-after analysis
Ignoring statistical significance — reacting to noise and seasonal swings as if they were real signal
Feeding AI dirty or incomplete data (broken tracking, duplicate events) — hypotheses will be confident but false
Failing to capture learnings: hypotheses get re-checked every week and knowledge never accumulates

exercises.question: AI writes: "The new onboarding launch raised 7-day retention by 8%." What must you do before treating this as a fact?
exercises.hint: It's correlation. Validate via cohort analysis (users before and after the release), rule out other changes and seasonality, and assess significance.

exercises.question: DAU grew 12% this week. What inputs should you give AI so it produces meaningful hypotheses rather than guesses?
exercises.hint: Top-line metrics with deltas, segment breakdowns, feature usage, and a list of recent releases and external events (marketing, holidays).

exercises.question: How do you set up the process so the share of "explained" metric changes grows week over week?
exercises.hint: Document confirmed hypotheses in a knowledge base, reuse them as context for AI, and close every notable change with an explanation.

s1.title: Lock in the why and the expected outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal, AI analytics turns into a pretty report nobody uses. The goal is to shorten the path from numbers to testable hypotheses and raise the share of data-backed decisions.
instructions: State the problem: the team sees "what happened" but spends hours on "why".
Define the trigger moments: weekly review, after a major release, on an unexpected metric move.
Set measurable goals: time-to-hypothesis (from days to hours) and share of analytics-aware decisions (from 30% to 70%+).
Agree on the core principle: AI generates hypotheses, the human confirms causation.
s1.validate: You have on paper: the problem, the launch triggers, 2 success metrics, and an explicit AI/human role split.
s1.tip: The anchor metric for the whole process is "% of metric changes with a documented explanation." Start measuring it from week one.

s2.title: Collect data on user behavior
s2.why: Hypothesis quality never exceeds input data quality. AI needs a structured slice of behavior, not one aggregate chart.
instructions: Connect usage data sources: Amplitude, Mixpanel, or GA.
Gather top-line metrics: DAU, MAU, retention, activation — with deltas vs. the previous period.
Add feature usage (new and existing features) and behavior across key segments.
Attach context: a list of recent releases and external events (marketing, holidays).
Check data hygiene: no broken tracking, duplicate events, or gaps.
s2.validate: A single input is ready: metrics with deltas + segments + feature usage + release timeline, with no obvious tracking gaps.
s2.tip: Dirty data produces confident false hypotheses — invest in verifying tracking once; it pays off in every review.

s3.title: Key step 1 — analysis: what changed and where anomalies are
s3.why: Before asking "why", you must know exactly "what". This is the foundation hypotheses are built on.
instructions: Have AI capture what changed: numbers, delta, and statistical significance.
Surface correlations like "release X, then metric Y +Z%" — as observations, not causes.
Run anomaly detection: unusual behavior in specific segments.
Separate real signal from noise and seasonality, noting the confidence level.
s3.validate: You have a list of changes with delta and significance, a list of correlations, and anomalous segments — with no causal conclusions.
s3.tip: Require AI to flag the significance of each change; otherwise the team starts reacting to noise.

s4.title: Key step 2 — hypotheses and suggested investigations
s4.why: This is the most expensive step for the human and AI's core value: turning observations into ranked, testable hypotheses.
instructions: Have AI formulate "why did this happen?" hypotheses and rank them by likelihood.
For each hypothesis, require suggested investigations: which queries to run, which segments and cohorts to examine.
Drop hypotheses that can't be tested with available data.
Phrase each hypothesis as a falsifiable statement, not a conclusion.
s4.validate: You have a ranked list of hypotheses, each tied to a concrete way to test it.
s4.tip: A good hypothesis sounds like "if true, in cohort A we should see X" — that immediately defines how to disprove it.

s5.title: Quality and risks: causation, not correlation
s5.why: The process's main failure is treating AI correlation as causation. Here the human protects the team from false conclusions.
instructions: Take the top hypotheses and validate them via proper analysis: cohort, A/B, before-after.
Rule out competing explanations: other releases, seasonality, external events.
Downgrade unconfirmed hypotheses to "needs further validation".
Explicitly mark where only correlation remains, and don't present it as a cause.
s5.validate: Every hypothesis acted upon is confirmed by an analysis method; unconfirmed ones are honestly flagged.
s5.tip: The phrasing "release X caused Y to grow" is allowed only after cohort/A-B validation — until then, write "correlates with".

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: The process delivers value only when it runs regularly and accumulates knowledge, instead of rebuilding hypotheses from scratch each week.
instructions: Establish the rhythm: weekly review + analysis after every major release.
Document confirmed hypotheses and decisions in a knowledge base.
Reuse past learnings as context for the next AI analysis.
Track the metrics: time-to-hypothesis and % of changes with an explanation.
Run the final checklist before each review (see tip).
s6.validate: The process runs on schedule, learnings accumulate, and both success metrics grow week over week.
s6.tip: Per-review checklist: data is clean, then changes are significant, then hypotheses are ranked, then causation is human-verified, then learnings are recorded.

pd-team-workflow.title: AI Product Team Workflow
pd-team-workflow.subtitle: From "every PM with their own Claude" to a collaborative AI-powered team with shared institutional memory
pd-team-workflow.whatItIs: A product team operating model with AI: a shared research workspace, common spec templates, a feedback synthesis pipeline, and regular AI office hours. The goal is to turn scattered individual use of Claude into a single process with shared institutional memory.
pd-team-workflow.approach: First fix why the team process is needed and what outcome you expect, then decide what to delegate to AI, then build the two key elements — the shared workspace and common conventions in CLAUDE.md. After that close quality, roles (especially the librarian) and risks, and finally roll the process out with a readiness checklist.
outcomes: A shared research workspace where one PM's findings are available to the whole team and survive after launch
Common PRD and spec templates — output no longer depends on the author
Institutional memory grows over time: decision quality improves instead of repeating old mistakes
New PM onboarding shrinks from ~6 to ~3 weeks through shared knowledge
A librarian is assigned to keep the workspace from turning into a junk drawer

applyIn.title: Growing product team
applyIn.description: ≥3 PMs actively use AI, but everyone has their own approach to specs and their own set of prompts

applyIn.title: Knowledge lost after launches
applyIn.description: Research findings and experiment learnings sit in personal chats and vanish once a feature is in production

applyIn.title: Onboarding new PMs
applyIn.description: A newcomer does not know "how we work" and spends weeks reconstructing context the team already has

pitfalls: Running the team workflow without a librarian role — without upkeep the shared workspace becomes a junk drawer within six months
Templates and conventions exist but are not captured in CLAUDE.md, so everyone interprets them differently
The workspace fills up but no one does a quarterly cleanup — outdated content confuses the team
AI office hours become a formality with no review of actual successful and failed prompts
Metrics (velocity, onboarding time, decision quality) are not tracked — there is no way to prove the process works

exercises.question: In your team one PM's research findings are lost to everyone else. Which first element of the team workflow fixes this, and why?
exercises.hint: Think about a shared, indexable store rather than personal chats — what exactly should land there right after research.

exercises.question: Why does a shared workspace degrade without a dedicated person, and which two recurring operations save it?
exercises.hint: Recall the librarian role: one operation is weekly, the other is about outdated content.

exercises.question: How do you prove to leadership that the team AI process actually works rather than just being trendy?
exercises.hint: Lean on measurable signals: team velocity, onboarding time, and the Stage 3 sign — a shipping-ready PRD in the first month.

s1.title: Why a team process and what outcome
s1.why: Individual AI use in product does not scale: findings are lost between PMs, specs are inconsistent, knowledge is not shared. Before building a process you must fix a measurable goal — otherwise there is nothing to validate success against.
instructions: State the problem with the current state: where exactly research findings are lost and why specs differ
Fix target metrics: team velocity, new PM onboarding time (benchmark from 6 to 3 weeks), decision quality
Describe the readiness sign (Stage 3): a new PM writes a shipping-ready PRD by the end of the first month
Align the goals with the team so the process is not seen as imposed bureaucracy
s1.validate: There is a written problem statement and 3 measurable goals the team has signed off on.
s1.tip: Pick metrics you already measure today — otherwise there will be nothing to compare a quarter from now.

s2.title: What to delegate to AI
s2.why: The team process starts with a split: what a human does and what Claude takes on. A clear boundary stops you from expecting AI to make decisions that belong to the PM, and from forcing people to do routine AI handles faster.
instructions: List the team's recurring tasks: research synthesis, PRD drafts, feedback categorization, experiment design
Mark what is delegated to AI as a skill: research-synthesizer, prd-drafter, feedback-categorizer, experiment-designer
Fix what stays with the human: prioritization, final decisions, trade-offs, ownership of the launch
Agree that AI prepares a draft, while the decision and validation are always done by the PM
s2.validate: A list of 4 team skills is compiled and the human's zone of responsibility is explicitly separated.
s2.tip: Start with the one or two skills that hurt most rather than trying to automate everything at once.

s3.title: Key step 1 — the shared research workspace
s3.why: A shared Claude Project "Product Workspace" is the team's institutional memory. Without it findings sit in personal chats and are lost after launch. With it any PM builds on accumulated context.
instructions: Create a shared Claude Project "Product Workspace" with access for the whole team
Set up indexable sections: research transcripts, a library of past PRDs, experiment learnings, categorized customer feedback
Agree on the rule: any research result goes into the workspace immediately, not into a personal chat
Verify that searching the workspace returns relevant past context for a typical query
s3.validate: The workspace is created, filled with real material, and at least one PM has found someone else's finding via search.
s3.tip: Structure sections by content type, not by person — the team's memory must not depend on who contributed it.

s4.title: Key step 2 — common conventions in CLAUDE.md
s4.why: A shared workspace without common rules still produces inconsistent specs. CLAUDE.md fixes writing conventions, a PRD template, and decision frameworks so output does not depend on the author.
instructions: Describe writing conventions in CLAUDE.md: tone, structure, required sections
Fix a single PRD template used by the whole team
Add decision frameworks — how the team makes and justifies decisions
Link CLAUDE.md to the workspace and skills so PRD drafts follow the conventions from the start
s4.validate: PRDs from two different PMs, written from the CLAUDE.md template, match structurally.
s4.tip: The related node on CLAUDE.md is the entry point: a single conventions file matters more than any individual style.

s5.title: Quality, roles and risks
s5.why: The main risk of a team workflow is degradation. A shared workspace without maintainership turns into a junk drawer in six months. That is why you need an explicit librarian role and recurring rituals that hold quality.
instructions: Assign a librarian responsible for keeping the workspace clean
Introduce a weekly review of new content: what to add, what to reword
Introduce a monthly/quarterly cleanup of outdated content so memory does not confuse the team
Run weekly AI office hours (30 min): best prompts, failed experiments, cross-team learning
Tie the rituals to the metrics from step 1 to see the quality trend
s5.validate: A librarian is assigned, and the calendar has a weekly review, cleanup, and AI office hours with owners.
s5.tip: Office hours are valuable for reviewing what does NOT work — failed prompts save the team more time than successful ones.

s6.title: Rollout and readiness checklist
s6.why: A process only works when it is actually used. The final step is to embed the workflow into daily work and check readiness against an objective checklist, not a feeling.
instructions: Run a short kickoff for the team: where the workspace is, where CLAUDE.md is, which skills and rituals exist
Assign an owner to each element (workspace, librarian, office hours)
After a month, check against the metrics from step 1 and the Stage 3 sign
Go through the readiness checklist: workspace is filling up, specs are consistent, the librarian is active, metrics are tracked
Record what is outdated and schedule the next quarterly review
s6.validate: The readiness checklist passes: a new PM writes a shipping-ready PRD by the end of the first month (the Stage 3 sign).
s6.tip: Do not consider the process embedded until it has survived at least one cleanup cycle — that is when you see whether quality holds.

en-transformation-strategy.title: AI Transformation Strategy
en-transformation-strategy.subtitle: How to assemble a working enterprise-grade AI strategy: from vision to a plan with checkpoints
en-transformation-strategy.whatItIs: AI Transformation Strategy is a document-based strategy for 12-24 months that answers not "let us use AI" but "here is HOW we win from AI": vision, north-star metrics, sequencing of initiatives, investment thesis, and success criteria. This course walks you through assembling such a document (8-12 pages) step by step — from justifying why it is needed to a finished plan with quarterly checkpoints.
en-transformation-strategy.approach: Strategy is not assembled in a vacuum but on top of real pilots already running across several departments. We move from diagnosis (readiness, vision) to choosing priorities (a portfolio of strategic bets), then to execution (pilots, then scale), risk management, and a final plan. The key principle: every element of the strategy is tied to a measurable outcome, and the document itself refreshes quarterly, because the AI landscape changes every 6 months.
outcomes: A finished AI Transformation Strategy document of 8-12 pages with vision, metrics, bets, and sequencing
A set of 3-5 north-star metrics tied to business results (cost, revenue, NPS, retention)
A prioritized portfolio of 3-7 strategic bets with explicit quarterly sequencing
A governance and risk-management mechanism built into the strategy, not bolted on the side
A plan with checkpoints and a quarterly-review cadence to keep the strategy alive

applyIn.title: Annual planning
applyIn.description: Before annual planning, the strategy gives leadership a single base of AI priorities and investments, instead of scattered departmental initiatives.

applyIn.title: Board conversation about ROI
applyIn.description: When the board asks about AI returns, a document with metrics and success criteria turns abstract promises into verifiable commitments.

applyIn.title: Hiring an AI lead and scaling
applyIn.description: The strategy sets the mandate and priorities for the AI lead you hire and determines which pilots to scale and which to wind down.

pitfalls: Making a strategy doc "once and forgotten" — the AI landscape changes every 6 months, and without a quarterly refresh the document goes stale
Vision without metrics: a strategy without measurable outcomes becomes a wish list that cannot be verified
Writing the strategy before pilots — without 6-12 months of real departmental experience, bets are built on guesswork
Bloating the portfolio to 15+ bets: spreading resources thin kills leverage, keep 3-7 strategic bets
Governance as a separate "later" document: risks and principles must be part of the strategy from day one

exercises.question: Take one of your current AI initiatives and formulate a north-star metric for it. Is it tied to a business result (cost/revenue/NPS/retention), or is it a process metric like "number of requests"?
exercises.hint: A good north-star metric measures business value, not activity. "20% reduction in cost-to-serve" beats "1,000 tickets processed".

exercises.question: List all AI initiatives currently running across different departments. How many of them are coordinated with each other? Where do you see redundancy or conflicting priorities?
exercises.hint: This fragmentation is exactly what the strategy doc solves as an alignment tool. If there are more than 7 initiatives and they are unrelated, that signals you need a portfolio of bets.

exercises.question: Imagine a quarter has passed. By which 2-3 checkpoints will you know the strategy is working rather than sitting as a dead document?
exercises.hint: One working indicator from the node: % of strategic decisions referencing the doc (target >80% within 6 months).

s1.title: Why a strategy and what outcome
s1.why: Without an explicit strategy, AI initiatives sprawl: different departments do different things, with no leverage and no priorities. The strategy is an alignment tool for leadership, delivering decision velocity (3× faster on AI decisions) and a shared understanding of priorities in days, not months.
instructions: Fix the trigger: why the strategy is needed right now (board asking about ROI, annual planning, hiring an AI lead)
Check the precondition: are there 6-12 months of successful pilots across several departments — without them the strategy will be guesswork
Define the target output of the document: 8-12 pages with vision, metrics, bets, sequencing, investment thesis, governance, success criteria
Determine the document owner and authors: executives + tactical leads, a 2-3 week process
s1.validate: You have a single sentence explaining which specific alignment problem the document solves, and confirmation that pilots already exist.
s1.tip: If there are no pilots yet, that is not a reason to write a strategy "for the future". Run 1-2 pilots first, otherwise the bets will be detached from reality.

s2.title: Readiness audit and vision
s2.why: Vision sets the 2-year direction, and the readiness audit shows the real starting point: where the company is already strong in AI, where the data and skills are, and where the gaps are. Without honest diagnosis, vision turns into fantasy.
instructions: Gather facts from the pilots: what worked, what data/infrastructure/skills exist, where the bottlenecks are
Write a 1-page vision: where the company is in 2 years with AI — concretely, not as a slogan
Assess readiness along axes: data, talent, infrastructure, culture of AI adoption
Connect vision to readiness: which gaps must be closed for the vision to become achievable
s2.validate: You have a vision page and an honest readiness map with explicit gaps between "where we are" and "where we want to be".
s2.tip: The vision must be verifiable through the next step's metrics. If it cannot be measured, it is a slogan, not a vision.

s3.title: Priorities and the initiative portfolio
s3.why: This is the core of the strategy: north-star metrics and a portfolio of strategic bets turn vision into choices. 3-7 bets create leverage; more means spreading resources thin. Metrics make every bet verifiable.
instructions: Choose 3-5 business-tied north-star metrics: cost reduction, revenue growth, NPS, talent retention
Formulate 3-7 strategic bets (e.g. "Stage-by-stage AI in customer support", "AI-augmented product development")
For each bet, specify which north-star metric it drives and the expected effect
Write the investment thesis: where we spend, where we save — linking costs and returns across the portfolio
s3.validate: A portfolio of 3-7 bets, each tied to a north-star metric, plus an investment thesis balancing spend and savings.
s3.tip: If there are more than 7 bets, merge or defer the weakest. Leverage comes from focus, not from the number of initiatives.

s4.title: Pilots and scale (sequencing)
s4.why: Sequencing answers "what do we do in Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4". Without an explicit sequence the portfolio stays a wish list. The "pilot, then validate, then scale" logic reduces the risk of expensive mistakes during rollout.
instructions: Lay strategic bets across Q1-Q4 quarters, accounting for dependencies and closing the readiness gaps from step 2
For each bet, set a gate: which pilot result earns the right to scale
Decide what to scale from current pilots and what to wind down based on the audit
Fix resources and owners per quarter so sequencing is executable
s4.validate: You have a Q1-Q4 quarterly map with explicit "pilot, then scale" gate criteria and assigned owners.
s4.tip: Do not scale a pilot without passing the gate. Premature scaling is the most common way to burn budget and trust in AI.

s5.title: Governance and risks
s5.why: Governance and risk principles built into the strategy protect against failures at scale: data privacy, model quality, accountability for decisions. Bolted-on governance does not work — it must be part of the document.
instructions: Formulate risk & governance principles: data, security, accountability, quality control of AI output
Tie risks to specific bets: which of the 3-7 bets carry the highest risk and how it is mitigated
Describe who makes AI decisions and under what rules (decision rights)
Set red lines: what the company fundamentally does not do with AI
s5.validate: The governance section explicitly links risk principles to the bet portfolio and records decision rights and red lines.
s5.tip: The best governance is short and applicable. A few clear principles people actually reference beat a 20-page regulation no one reads.

s6.title: Plan and checklist
s6.why: The final step turns the strategy into a living tool: success criteria, checkpoints, and a quarterly-review cadence. The main mistake is making the document "once and forgotten"; the AI landscape changes every 6 months, so a refresh is mandatory.
instructions: Describe success criteria + checkpoints for each north-star metric and bet
Set the cadence: a quarterly review of the whole strategy with updates to sequencing and metrics
Add a liveness indicator: % of strategic decisions referencing the document (target >80% within 6 months)
Assemble the final readiness checklist: vision, metrics, bets, sequencing, investment thesis, governance, success criteria — all 7 blocks present
Schedule the date of the first quarterly review in the calendar
s6.validate: The 8-12 page document contains all 7 blocks, with success criteria, checkpoints, and a first quarterly-review date set.
s6.tip: Track the share of decisions referencing the document: if it has not reached 80% within 6 months, the strategy has not become an alignment tool — make it more concrete and applicable.

en-change-management.title: AI Change Management
en-change-management.subtitle: How to lead a team through the shift to AI-native work: from fear to a lasting habit
en-change-management.whatItIs: A structured approach to changing team behavior during the shift to AI-native operations. It is a distinct discipline: tech adoption delivers the tools, while change management changes how people actually behave. The course moves from articulating the "why" through resistance and stakeholder work, communication and training, champion pilot teams, and risk control — to making the new behavior the norm.
en-change-management.approach: We progress in phases, like a real change framework: first awareness and the "why", then resistance diagnosis and a stakeholder map, then communication and training, launching champion pilots, managing quality and the fear of replacement, and finally reinforcement through metrics and a checklist. Each step produces a concrete artifact you can show the team tomorrow. The core principle: training ≠ change management — training delivers a skill, change management changes a habit.
outcomes: A clear "why" for the change and a measurable target result (adoption rate, time-to-value)
A stakeholder map and resistance diagnosis split into champions, skeptics, and neutrals
A communication and training plan that explicitly answers "will I lose my job?"
Launched champion pilot teams and a mechanism to spread their wins
Reinforcement metrics and a checklist that shows the change became the norm, not a one-off campaign

applyIn.title: Rolling out a tactical direction to the full team
applyIn.description: The first pilots worked, but the move to the full team stalls. Change management closes the gap between "works for enthusiasts" and "works for everyone".

applyIn.title: Team split into champions and skeptics
applyIn.description: Some people rush ahead, others quietly ignore or sabotage. You need stakeholder work and targeted communication, not a blanket "everyone use AI" call.

applyIn.title: Adoption stalled after training
applyIn.description: You ran workshops and delivered the skill — but people do not use AI in real work. This is the classic training vs behavioral shift gap; the course shows how to close it.

pitfalls: Believing training is change management. Training transfers a skill; change management shifts behavior. Without the second, the first is wasted.
