Not answering "will I lose my job?". Silence does not remove fear — it amplifies it, and doubt grows.
Rolling out to the full team at once, without champion pilots. Without visible local wins, the change feels imposed from above.
Expecting resistance to disappear entirely. The goal is to reduce it and make it manageable, not to "defeat" it.
Not embedding AI usage into metrics and growth criteria. Without reinforcement, adoption reverts to old habits within a couple of months.

exercises.question: Your team of 12: 3 active champions, 6 neutrals, 3 open skeptics. Who do you start the rollout with, and why?
exercises.hint: Champions produce the first visible wins and lower risk. Neutrals join by watching the wins. Skeptics are not convinced first — they are won over by pilot results, not arguments.

exercises.question: An employee asks directly: "Will this AI replace my job?" What do you say?
exercises.hint: You cannot dodge it — that grows doubt. Be honest: which tasks AI removes, which it augments, and what the career path looks like for an AI-augmented role. Evasion is worse than an uncomfortable truth.

exercises.question: Adoption rate is stuck at 35% a month after training. Where do you look for the cause?
exercises.hint: The problem is likely not the skill (training is done) but behavior: no embedding into processes, no visible wins, fear not addressed. This is change management, not repeating training.

s1.title: Articulate the "why" and the target result
s1.why: The most common cause of failed AI initiatives is not tech but adoption. People do not move without a clear "why". Without a measurable goal, the change cannot be tracked or reinforced.
instructions: Describe the change in one sentence: what exactly changes in the team's work and why now.
Capture the starting point: current adoption rate (% of the team using AI weekly) and current time-to-value.
Set a measurable goal: e.g., adoption from 30% to 80%, time-to-Stage 3 −50%.
State the benefit for the employee, not just the business — what they personally gain.
s1.validate: You have a one-sentence "why", a baseline metric, and a measurable goal you can show the team.
s1.tip: The goal must be about behavior ("% actively using weekly"), not the fact of training ("everyone attended the workshop").

s2.title: Map stakeholders and diagnose resistance
s2.why: Teams fear (job loss), do not believe (saw hype before), do not know (skills gap). These three causes need different answers. Without a stakeholder map, communication misses the target.
instructions: Split the team into three groups: champions, neutrals, skeptics.
For each group, identify the root cause of resistance: fear / disbelief / lack of knowledge.
Mark influential people whose opinion pulls others along.
Record champions by name — this is your future pilot.
s2.validate: You have a list split into three groups with a stated resistance cause for each.
s2.tip: Resistance is not removed by head-on arguments. Understand the source first — fear is cured by honesty, disbelief by results, lack of knowledge by training.

s3.title: Build communication and training
s3.why: These are the Awareness and Education phases. Communication removes fear and disbelief; training closes the skills gap. But training without an honest answer to "will I lose my job?" will not work.
instructions: Run an all-hands: "here is what we are doing + why", with an open Q&A session.
Answer "will I lose my job?" directly and honestly — which tasks AI removes, which it augments.
Launch hands-on workshops for everyone (target ~10 hours of structured learning).
Train champions deeper than the rest — they become the pilot's backbone and mentors.
s3.validate: You ran an all-hands with open Q&A, have a training program, and the fear of replacement was spoken aloud, not bypassed.
s3.tip: Training transfers a skill. Change management shifts a habit. A workshop without a follow-on behavior change is wasted time.

s4.title: Launch champion pilot teams
s4.why: This is the Adoption phase. Champion wins lower risk and convince neutrals and skeptics better than any argument. A "to everyone at once" rollout usually fails.
instructions: Pick a pilot team of champions using AI in real work daily.
Set up office hours for quick help and to clear small blockers.
Collect concrete wins: time, quality, removed routine — with numbers.
Spread wins widely: show neutrals and skeptics real results from colleagues.
s4.validate: The pilot team uses AI daily, and there are at least a few documented wins with numbers.
s4.tip: A win from a colleague on the next team convinces a skeptic more than a management presentation. Make wins visible.

s5.title: Manage quality, risk, and the fear of replacement
s5.why: Speed without quality control breeds distrust, and an unaddressed fear of replacement quietly grows resistance. Both risks roll adoption back, even if the pilot succeeds.
instructions: Introduce quality control for AI outputs: checks, review, clear limits of applicability.
Define where AI helps and where the decision stays with a human — this reduces fear.
Openly show the career path for AI-augmented roles: how work changes rather than disappears.
Track early rollback signals: quiet sabotage, dropping usage, rising complaints.
s5.validate: There is a quality control mechanism and an explicitly stated career path; early resistance signals are being tracked.
s5.tip: Resistance is reduced, not "defeated". Manageable skepticism is healthier than performative enthusiasm — it catches real problems.

s6.title: Reinforce the change and run the checklist
s6.why: This is the Reinforcement phase. Without reinforcement, adoption reverts to old habits within a couple of months. The change must become the norm, embedded in processes and growth criteria.
instructions: Include AI usage in growth and evaluation criteria — what gets measured gets reinforced.
Create and sustain a career path for AI-augmented roles and a continuous-learning culture.
Measure the key metric: % of the team actively using AI weekly.
Run the reinforcement checklist: you have a "why", stakeholder map, training, a pilot with wins, quality control, and the metric in processes.
s6.validate: The adoption metric hit its target and holds; AI usage is embedded in growth criteria; the reinforcement checklist is fully complete.
s6.tip: If the change holds only through your manual control, it is not yet reinforced. The norm is when it works without reminders.

en-governance.title: AI Governance: how to build it
en-governance.subtitle: From "can we or can't we?" to a structured framework for responsible AI use
en-governance.whatItIs: AI Governance is a set of rules and processes governing how AI is used in the organization: data classification, model selection, output validation, vendor management, and compliance. It is not "security forbids everything" but a structured framework for responsible use that speeds up decisions and reduces regulatory risk (GDPR, EU AI Act).
en-governance.approach: We move from goal to rollout: first state why governance is needed and what outcome we measure, then build usage policies, data classification and privacy, assign roles, set up audit and compliance, and finish with a rollout plan and checklist. Each step produces an artifact, not theory. Governance is framed as an enabler ("here is how to do this responsibly"), not a list of prohibitions — otherwise shadow AI appears.
outcomes: You understand why governance matters and can measure its outcome (incidents per quarter, target 0 high-severity)
There is an AI usage policy with data classification: what can/cannot go into AI flows
Data, privacy and security are covered: consent, data residency, PII encryption, vendor DPAs
Roles and responsibility are assigned: who decides, who validates outputs, who responds to incidents
Audit and compliance are set up: audit logs, regular reviews, incident response playbook

applyIn.title: Production AI before launch
applyIn.description: You implement governance before production use cases, not after — once customer data, financial data, or PII enters the flow.

applyIn.title: Multiple departments and tools
applyIn.description: When teams use different AI tools, a single approved list and data classification remove shadow AI and chaos.

applyIn.title: Regulatory pressure
applyIn.description: GDPR, EU AI Act and industry rules: governance provides an audit trail and provable risk reduction for auditors and customers.

pitfalls: Doing governance as a "list of prohibitions" — it breeds shadow AI: teams move to unauthorized tools
Implementing governance after an incident rather than before production — compliance gaps have already accumulated
Not classifying data: without splitting public/internal/customer/PII, any rule is meaningless
No audit trail — nothing to show an auditor and no way to investigate an incident
Assigning governance without role owners — rules exist but nobody is accountable for decisions and validation

exercises.question: Name the 4 data classes and, for each, which AI tool is allowed.
exercises.hint: Public, then any tool; Internal, then approved enterprise only; Customer, then with consent + data residency; PII, then encryption + DPA.

exercises.question: Why does governance as a "list of prohibitions" lose to the enabler form?
exercises.hint: Prohibitions offer no alternative, so teams find workarounds, causing shadow AI usage with unauthorized tools.

exercises.question: Which governance metric will you track quarterly and what is the target?
exercises.hint: Incidents per quarter; target — 0 high-severity. Reviewed every quarter + after any incident.

s1.title: Why governance and what outcome we measure
s1.why: Without a clearly stated goal, governance turns into bureaucracy. The goal is not "control for its own sake" but prevented incidents, customer trust, and decision speed (no "can we or can't we" debates).
instructions: Frame the problem in risk terms: data leaks via AI inputs, customer data in third-party models, missing audit trail
Fix the outcome as a measurable metric: incidents per quarter, target 0 high-severity
Describe governance as an enabler: "here is how to do this responsibly", not "here is what's forbidden"
Define rollout triggers: customer/financial data, PII in flows, multiple departments with different tools
s1.validate: You have a one-page document with the goal, metric, and enablement framing, understandable to both an engineer and an executive.
s1.tip: Tie the goal to the regulatory context (GDPR, EU AI Act) — this resolves arguments about governance priority with the business.

s2.title: AI usage policies
s2.why: Policy is the operationalization of the goal. It answers "what exactly can we do with AI" so teams don't waste time on approvals and don't drift into shadow AI.
instructions: Compile an approved AI tools list with an owner and update date (at least quarterly)
Describe usage rules for each tool: for which tasks, with which data
Set a process for adding a new tool to the list (who requests, who approves)
Frame the policy as an enablement guide, not a prohibitive regulation
s2.validate: Any employee finds the answer to "can I use tool X for task Y" in a minute without contacting security.
s2.tip: Update the approved list on schedule (quarterly): a stale list is the main reason teams return to shadow AI.

s3.title: Data, privacy and security
s3.why: Most AI incidents are data leaks: PII or customer data ends up in third-party models. Data classification is the foundation without which the other rules don't work.
instructions: Build a data classification: Public, Internal, Customer, PII
Bind allowed tools to each class: Public — any; Internal — approved enterprise only; Customer — with consent + data residency check; PII — encryption + DPA
Verify a DPA (data processing agreement) is in place with every vendor processing data
Describe data residency and consent requirements for customer data
s3.validate: For any data type in your AI flows it is unambiguous which tool is allowed and which protections are mandatory.
s3.tip: PII always requires both encryption and a DPA — not one of the two. A missing vendor DPA = a blocker for any customer/PII flow.

s4.title: Roles and responsibility
s4.why: Rules without owners don't get executed. You must explicitly assign who decides, who validates AI outputs, and who responds to incidents — otherwise accountability dissolves.
instructions: Assign an owner of the governance framework (responsible for policies and reviews)
Define who validates customer-facing AI outputs (human review)
Assign owners for quality monitoring and bias testing
Describe incident response roles: who receives the report, who escalates, who decides
s4.validate: Every governance process (policies, validation, monitoring, incidents) has a named owner, not "the team in general".
s4.tip: Output validation for customer-facing outputs is a mandatory human-in-the-loop; statistical quality monitoring complements but does not replace it.

s5.title: Audit and compliance
s5.why: The audit trail is what separates governance from declarations. Without logs you can neither prove compliance to an auditor nor investigate an incident. Regulators (GDPR, EU AI Act) require provability.
instructions: Enable audit logs across all vendors and tools where possible
Set up quality monitoring (statistical) and regular bias testing of outputs
Create an AI-specific incident response playbook with reporting channels
Set the review cadence: quarterly + after any incident
s5.validate: On an auditor's request you can show logs, quality metrics, and review history; a ready playbook exists for an incident.
s5.tip: Tie reviews to the calendar and to the trigger "after any incident" — otherwise governance goes stale between scheduled checks.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A document without rollout is dead. The final step turns the framework into a working process with a verifiable production-readiness checklist.
instructions: Assemble all artifacts into one governance document: goal+metric, policies, classification, roles, audit
Run the pre-production checklist: data classification applied, tool in approved list, DPA in place, validation owner assigned, logs enabled
Communicate the framework to teams as an enablement guide, not a prohibition
Schedule the first quarterly review and a checkpoint for the incidents-per-quarter metric
s6.validate: A new production AI use case clears the entire checklist in one pass, with no hanging "can we or can't we" questions.
s6.tip: The best success indicator is reduced shadow AI: if teams use approved tools voluntarily, the enabler framing worked.

en-coe.title: Building an AI Center of Excellence
en-coe.subtitle: A central team that doesn't build everything itself but accelerates AI initiatives across the company
en-coe.whatItIs: An AI Center of Excellence (CoE) is a central team of 3-10 people (AI lead, ML engineers, AI product manager, ethics & governance lead) that supports tactical teams with best practices, shared infrastructure, training, and a governance liaison. The CoE doesn't run every AI project itself — it enables other teams so each new initiative launches several times faster.
en-coe.approach: This course moves from justifying the CoE to a working operating model. First we articulate why the CoE exists and what outcome it delivers, then we lock down its mandate and team. Next comes the key decision: what to centralize versus what to federate to teams. Then we stand up the CoE's services (training, templates, review, office hours), set value metrics, and launch the CoE against a checklist. The guiding principle throughout: CoE = enablement, not execution.
outcomes: Understand the difference between a CoE as an enablement function and a CoE as an "AI department" that builds everything itself and becomes a bottleneck
Articulate the CoE mandate and assemble a core team of 3-5 roles tied to real functions, not staffed "for growth"
Clearly split what to centralize (infrastructure, governance, tooling) from what to federate (building specific solutions)
Stand up the CoE's services: a template library, three-level training, office hours, and lightweight architecture review
Measure the CoE's value via time-to-launch, reuse, and the number of CoE-enabled launches

applyIn.title: Launching a CoE after early wins
applyIn.description: The company has 2-3 successful tactical AI directions and "where do I find an AI expert?" has become a regular question — time to assemble a central team so knowledge and infrastructure aren't reinvented by every team.

applyIn.title: Scaling AI across dozens of teams
applyIn.description: When AI initiatives multiply, the CoE turns one-off experience into reusable templates, LLM API contracts, and monitoring, cutting new-project time-to-launch from months to weeks.

applyIn.title: Coordinating governance and tooling
applyIn.description: The CoE becomes the single point for "which AI tools company-wide" decisions and the liaison with security/legal, so each team doesn't run approvals from scratch.

pitfalls: Turning the CoE into an "AI department" that builds every solution itself — this makes the CoE a bottleneck instead of an accelerator
Staffing a large team "for growth" before real functions and demand from tactical teams exist
Centralizing everything, including building specific products — teams need execution autonomy while the CoE owns the shared layer
Launching the CoE without value metrics — a quarter later you can't prove it accelerated anything
Ignoring governance and security until an incident — coordination must be built into CoE services from the start

exercises.question: A team asks the CoE to "just build" them a full RAG service. Is this a request for enablement or execution, and how do you respond correctly?
exercises.hint: CoE = enablement. Think about what the CoE can provide as reusable (a template, infrastructure, review, pairing hours), leaving the build to the team itself.

exercises.question: List 3 functions worth centralizing in the CoE and 3 things best left to tactical teams.
exercises.hint: Centralize what's shared and expensive to duplicate (infra, governance, tooling decisions). Federate what's specific to a team's domain (concrete features and products).

exercises.question: Which single metric would you put forward as the CoE's headline metric, and why that one?
exercises.hint: From the node: "CoE-enabled launches per quarter." It directly reflects the enablement mission rather than the volume the CoE builds itself.

s1.title: Why a CoE and what outcome
s1.why: Without an explicit goal, a CoE easily slides into an "AI department" that builds everything itself. First we fix the problem (every team reinvents the wheel: discovering RAG, prompt engineering, vector DBs) and the expected outcome (time-to-launch from 6 months to 2 months, cheaper shared infra, spread of best practices).
instructions: Gather proof of need: 2-3 successful tactical AI directions and the recurring question "how and where do I find an AI expert?".
Describe the duplication problem: what exactly each team currently does from scratch (infrastructure, prompt practices, tool selection).
Articulate 3-4 expected outcomes in measurable terms: time-to-launch, infrastructure cost, quality, career path for talent.
Lock in the boundary: the CoE enables others, it does not run every project.
s1.validate: You have a one-page document: the duplication problem + 3-4 measurable expected outcomes + an explicit statement of the enablement mission.
s1.tip: Lean on real cases from your own teams rather than an abstract "AI everywhere" — specifics convince leadership faster.

s2.title: Mandate and team composition
s2.why: A CoE works only with a clear mandate and a small team tied to real functions. An inflated headcount before demand appears is a classic mistake. A core team of 3-5 covers the key roles without becoming a bottleneck.
instructions: Describe the mandate: what the CoE owns (shared infrastructure, best practices, training, tooling, governance liaison) and what it does NOT do (building specific products).
Assemble a core team of 3-5 roles: Head of AI / Chief AI Officer, Senior ML/AI engineer, AI Product Manager, AI Ethics & Governance lead.
Establish reporting lines and an executive sponsor so the CoE carries weight in tooling and governance decisions.
Define the staffing model: some roles can be part-time at the start, with expansion driven by proven demand.
s2.validate: There's an approved CoE mandate (a one-paragraph "we do / we don't") and a list of 3-5 named roles with an executive sponsor.
s2.tip: Start with a minimum viable team: 3 people tied to real functions beats 8 staffed "for growth" with no demand.

s3.title: Centralize vs federate
s3.why: The CoE's key architectural decision: what to keep central and what to hand to teams. Centralizing everything makes the CoE a bottleneck; full federation brings back duplication. The line runs between the shared (infra, governance, tooling) and the domain-specific (building solutions).
instructions: List centralization candidates: vector DBs, LLM API contracts, monitoring, company-wide tool selection, coordination with security/legal.
List what gets federated: building specific features and products inside tactical teams for their domain.
Apply the test: "is this expensive to duplicate in every team?" — yes, then center; "is it domain-specific?" — yes, then team.
Capture the gray zone (e.g., templates and patterns) as "the center creates, teams use and extend".
s3.validate: There's a two-column table (centralize / federate) with concrete items and an explicit rule by which you split them.
s3.tip: When in doubt — federate the build and centralize only what's reused by 3+ teams.

s4.title: CoE services
s4.why: The mandate turns into value through concrete services. This is the CoE's operating core: shared infrastructure, a best-practices library, training, office hours, and lightweight review. These are what deliver the "5-10× faster" effect for subsequent teams.
instructions: Launch a best-practices library: CLAUDE.md templates, Skills, reusable patterns — with a clear entry point for teams.
Build a three-level training program: foundational, intermediate, advanced.
Introduce weekly office hours open to anyone, plus lightweight architecture review of AI initiatives (without turning into a gate-bottleneck).
Package shared infrastructure as a service: access to vector DBs, LLM API contracts, and monitoring.
Add a regular showcase (monthly AI demos) so knowledge spreads across the company.
s4.validate: At least 3 services are live: the template library, training (at least the foundational level), and office hours; each has a defined way teams use it.
s4.tip: Review should accelerate, not block: frame it as "advice and a template," not "mandatory approval at every step."

s5.title: Value metrics
s5.why: Without metrics there's no way to tell enablement from busywork. Metrics must measure how much the CoE accelerates other teams, not the volume the CoE builds itself — otherwise it drifts back toward execution.
instructions: Make the headline metric an enablement one: number of CoE-enabled launches per quarter.
Add time-to-launch for new AI initiatives (target: from 6 months to 2 months) as the key speed indicator.
Measure reuse: how many teams use the shared infrastructure and templates from the library.
Add supporting metrics: training reach and office-hours attendance.
Agree on a quarterly metrics review with the sponsor.
s5.validate: 3-5 metrics are defined with a headline one (CoE-enabled launches / quarter); each has a data source and a measurement cadence.
s5.tip: Avoid vanity metrics like "number of models the CoE built itself" — they push the team into the execution trap.

s6.title: Launch and checklist
s6.why: The launch turns the plan into a working CoE and sets the rules of the game for the whole company. The checklist ensures the mandate, team, centralization boundary, services, and metrics didn't stay on paper.
instructions: Run the readiness checklist: mandate approved, core team named, centralize/federate boundary described, 3+ services live, metrics defined.
Announce the CoE company-wide: communication channels, office hours, how to request help and templates.
Run the first cycle: take one real team initiative and run it through CoE services as a pilot.
Set the date for the first quarterly metrics review and showcase.
Lock in the improvement loop: what to add to the library/training based on pilot results.
s6.validate: The CoE is officially announced, at least one pilot support cycle has been run, and the first quarterly metrics review is on the calendar.
s6.tip: Pick a visible, achievable first pilot — a successful case sells the CoE to other teams better than any presentation.

en-roi-measurement.title: AI ROI Measurement
en-roi-measurement.subtitle: Turning "AI saves time" into "AI saved $X this quarter"
en-roi-measurement.whatItIs: A course on measuring the return on AI investments at enterprise scale: counting cost and value, separating the AI effect from other factors, choosing leading and lagging metrics, and estimating payback period. The goal is to replace vibes with numbers that survive the CFO's "show me the money?".
en-roi-measurement.approach: We move from goal to report. First we fix why we measure ROI and what outcome the business needs. Then we pick value metrics per initiative, capture a pre-AI baseline, build a benefits-and-costs model (including hidden and intangible parts), honestly settle attribution, and finally assemble leadership-grade reporting with a checklist. Each step produces an artifact reused in the next.
outcomes: You understand why ROI measurement matters and what it gives an AI program
You can pick value metrics for a specific initiative, not an averaged blur
You capture a correct baseline, without which any ROI number is unprovable
You build a benefits-and-costs model covering direct, indirect, hidden and intangible parts
You defend the numbers to finance and leadership through honest attribution

applyIn.title: Annual and quarterly budgeting
applyIn.description: Enter budget planning with documented ROI per initiative instead of promises — budget approval moves faster.

applyIn.title: Prioritizing AI initiatives
applyIn.description: Compare initiatives by return, kill the losers and double down on winners based on numbers, not intuition.

applyIn.title: C-level and finance conversations
applyIn.description: When executives ask about AI value, answer quantified: payback period, value vs cost, target > 3× cost.

pitfalls: Counting only cost savings and ignoring intangible value — capability gains, team morale, future optionality
Claiming ROI without a pre-AI baseline — no reference point, the number can't be defended
Attributing the entire effect to AI when other factors played a role (new process, seasonality, different team)
Hiding indirect and hidden costs (training, change management, governance, opportunity cost) — ROI is inflated and collapses under audit
Measuring too early: before 3-6 months in production the metrics are still noisy and misleading

exercises.question: You have an "AI support assistant" initiative that saves agents' time. Which 3-4 value categories will you put in the model besides time saved?
exercises.hint: Look at the value side from the node: quality (cost of errors avoided), revenue (new capabilities), risk reduction, customer satisfaction and its retention impact.

exercises.question: A team claims: "after rolling out AI, ticket handling time dropped 30%". What two attribution questions will you ask before recording this in ROI?
exercises.hint: Was there a control group or before/after under equal conditions? Did the process, team composition or ticket volume also change in that period — is it really AI and not an external factor?

exercises.question: The CFO wants a single health benchmark for an initiative. Which metric and threshold would you propose and why?
exercises.hint: The node's target is documented ROI per initiative > 3× cost. Explain why it must be documented, not estimated, return.

s1.title: Fix the measurement goal and the outcome needed
s1.why: Without ROI measurement AI initiatives ride on vibes, and the program can be cut at the first finance question. Before counting, agree on why we do this and what outcome serves the business.
instructions: State which business question the measurement answers: budget approval, prioritization, or defending value to C-level
Define the report audience (finance, leadership, initiative owners) — it sets the level of detail
Fix the initiative health benchmark: documented ROI > 3× cost
Sanity-check timing: measure after 3-6 months of AI in production, otherwise metrics are still noisy
s1.validate: You can state in one sentence why you measure ROI and who will read the result.
s1.tip: If measurement runs "because we should" rather than for a specific decision, it becomes a report for its own sake. Tie it to a decision: budget, kill/scale, priority.

s2.title: Pick value metrics per initiative
s2.why: AI value rarely collapses into one number. Different initiatives create different value, and an averaged metric hides both winners and failures.
instructions: For each initiative walk the value side: time saved, quality improvement, new revenue, risk reduction, customer satisfaction
Split metrics into leading (early signals — adoption, usage frequency) and lagging (outcomes — revenue, retention)
For each metric fix the unit and how it converts to money (e.g. time × hourly cost of the role)
Don't force every category onto every initiative — keep the relevant ones, drop the rest
s2.validate: Each initiative has a set of 2-4 value metrics with a clear money conversion.
s2.tip: Leading metrics show an initiative is alive long before lagging metrics confirm financial impact — watch them so you don't kill an initiative too early.

s3.title: Capture the pre-AI baseline
s3.why: ROI is always a comparison of "with AI" against "without AI". Without a fixed baseline any return number is unprovable and collapses at the first critical question.
instructions: For each chosen metric capture the pre-AI value over a representative period
Fix the baseline conditions: volume, team composition, process — so later you compare like for like
Where possible carve out a control group that keeps working without AI as a reference point
Record the baseline as a dated artifact — it can't be quietly adjusted later
s3.validate: Each metric has a pre-AI value with described conditions that can be referenced later.
s3.tip: Ideally capture the baseline before launching AI. If the moment is missed, reconstruct from historical data but honestly mark such numbers as reconstructed.

s4.title: Build the benefits-and-costs model
s4.why: Honest ROI needs both sides of the equation. Understated costs inflate return, and ignoring intangible value undervalues the program — both lead to wrong decisions.
instructions: Gather the cost side: direct (AI API, tools, infrastructure), indirect (training, change management, governance), hidden (opportunity cost of team time)
Gather the value side from step 2 metrics, converting them to money against the step 3 baseline
Separately note intangible value (capability gains, morale, future optionality) — even if it can't be precisely quantified
Compute ROI and payback period, compare against the > 3× cost benchmark
s4.validate: There is a model showing all cost and value categories, the resulting ROI and payback period.
s4.tip: AI cost management is its own discipline: if API and infrastructure numbers are fuzzy, fix that first, otherwise the cost side is fiction.

s5.title: Settle attribution and honesty
s5.why: Finance's main question is "how do you know AI caused this?". Without honest attribution the numbers look fudged and undermine trust in the whole program.
instructions: For each key claim choose an attribution method: before/after comparison, control group, or A/B test on features
For high-stakes claims apply counterfactual analysis: what would have happened without AI
Explicitly list alternative factors (new process, seasonality, team change) and estimate their contribution
Tag each number's confidence level — proven, estimated, reconstructed
s5.validate: Every significant ROI number carries an attribution method and an honest confidence tag.
s5.tip: Better a narrow but defensible number than a broad and disputable one. One debunked inflated claim zeroes out trust in the whole report.

s6.title: Assemble leadership reporting and a checklist
s6.why: Measurement is useless if it doesn't reach decisions. Reporting must hit the right audience at the right cadence, otherwise ROI stays in a spreadsheet instead of moving the budget.
instructions: Set the cadence: monthly per tactical direction, quarterly aggregate to leadership, annual full impact report
For leadership present the bottom line quantified: ROI vs cost, payback period, status against the 3× target
Include intangibles as a separate block so the program isn't judged on cost savings alone
Run the final checklist: goal clear, metrics picked, baseline exists, model complete, attribution honest, audience and cadence set
s6.validate: There is a report format per audience level and a completed six-point checklist.
s6.tip: Present the same dataset differently: details for tactical teams, three numbers and a takeaway for leadership. A detail-heavy exec report goes unread.

en-risk-management.title: AI Risk Management
en-risk-management.subtitle: Systematically identify, assess, and mitigate AI-specific risks — from hallucinations to regulation
en-risk-management.whatItIs: AI Risk Management is the systematic identification, assessment, and mitigation of risks unique to AI systems: hallucinations in production, model drift, data leaks, regulatory non-compliance, bias, and vendor dependencies. The goal is risk awareness, not risk avoidance. You don't abandon AI because of risk — you manage it with eyes open.
en-risk-management.approach: AI risks differ from traditional IT risks: they are probabilistic, evolving, and often invisible until late. Classic risk frameworks don't catch them. This course's approach: build a risk register by category, score each risk on a probability×impact matrix, define concrete mitigations, set up continuous monitoring, and embed the process from day 1 of every AI initiative — rather than reacting after an incident.
outcomes: Understand how AI risks fundamentally differ from ordinary IT risks
Know the 6 key categories of AI risk and concrete mitigations for each
Can score a risk on a probability×impact matrix and prioritize accordingly
Can build and maintain a living risk register with quarterly updates
Have a launch checklist to stand up a risk program before production

applyIn.title: Before shipping AI to production
applyIn.description: Run the use case through all 6 risk categories, score each, and get sign-off before the system touches real users.

applyIn.title: Regulatory readiness
applyIn.description: A documented risk program is the foundation for EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF compliance, and an argument for lower insurance cost.

applyIn.title: Operating existing AI systems
applyIn.description: Annual risk review plus continuous monitoring of model drift and quality, so degradation is caught before customers notice it.

pitfalls: Thinking risk management = a compliance checklist. Real management means analyzing edge cases, scenarios, and second-order effects. A checklist alone gives false security.
Starting risk work only after an incident instead of from day 1 of the initiative.
Scoring only probability and ignoring impact (or vice versa) — risk is prioritized by their product.
Building a risk register and forgetting it — without quarterly updates it goes stale, since AI risks evolve.
Relying on a single vendor with no abstraction layer or fallback — vendor lock is itself a risk.

exercises.question: Take one real AI feature at your company and run it through the 6 risk categories. Which 2 categories turned out sharpest, and what mitigations already exist (or are missing) for them?
exercises.hint: Categories: hallucinations, model drift, data leaks, bias, regulation, vendor lock. For the sharp ones, look at customer-facing output and handling of sensitive data.

exercises.question: For the risk 'hallucination in a customer-facing answer', score probability (low/medium/high) and impact, then place it on the matrix. Which quadrant does it fall in and what does that mean for priority?
exercises.hint: High probability × high impact = red zone, act now. Low×low = accept/monitor. Consider reputational and legal impact.

exercises.question: Design minimal monitoring for model drift: which 2-3 signals would you track and what threshold would trigger an alert or rollback?
exercises.hint: Think about golden test sets, a quality metric over time, and comparing behavior before/after a model update.

s1.title: Why manage AI risk, and the outcome
s1.why: AI risks are probabilistic, evolving, and often invisible until late — classic IT frameworks don't catch them. Without a systematic approach, the first serious incident (leak, discrimination, regulatory fine) hits without warning.
instructions: State the program's goal: risk awareness, not risk avoidance — you manage risk rather than abandon AI.
Fix the launch triggers: day 1 of every initiative, before production launch, annually for existing systems, after any notable industry incident.
Define target outcomes: zero high-severity incidents (ideal), regulatory readiness for EU AI Act and NIST, a documented program to lower insurance.
Assign a program owner and a review cadence (quarterly for the register).
s1.validate: You have stated the goal, launch triggers, and a measurable program outcome; an owner is assigned.
s1.tip: Don't confuse risk management with a compliance checklist — a checklist alone gives false security.

s2.title: AI risk categories
s2.why: Without a clear taxonomy, risks slip through the cracks. The 6 categories cover the main sources of AI failure and give a shared language for the team, legal, and leadership.
instructions: Privacy/data leaks: customer and sensitive data with model providers — mitigations: data classification, approved vendors, encryption, audit logs.
Accuracy/hallucinations: AI confidently returns wrong info — mitigations: RAG with citations, human review for customer-facing, quality monitoring.
Security/model drift: AI behavior changes without notice (model update, data shift) — mitigations: continuous quality monitoring, golden test sets, rollback ability.
Reputation/bias: AI discriminates (hiring, pricing, content) — mitigations: bias testing, diverse data, monitoring by demographic.

Regulation and vendor lock: GDPR / EU AI Act / sector-specific violations and total dependence on one provider — mitigations: compliance review per use case, legal sign-off, abstraction layer, multi-vendor strategy, internal fallback.
s2.validate: Each of your AI use cases is mapped to at least one of the 6 categories, and concrete mitigations are recorded for each.
s2.tip: Vendor lock is a risk in its own right: even a great model is dangerous if you have no fallback.

s3.title: Assessment: probability × impact
s3.why: Resources are limited — you can't mitigate every risk equally. Probability times impact gives an objective priority and filters out panic over unlikely trivia.
instructions: For each risk, score probability on a scale (low/medium/high) over a horizon, e.g. one year.
Score impact: account for financial, legal, reputational, and user-safety consequences.
Place the risk on a 3×3 matrix (probability × impact) and determine the quadrant.
Red zone (high×high) — act immediately; yellow — mitigation plan; green — accept and monitor.
Record the rationale for the score so changes are visible at the next review.
s3.validate: Each risk has a probability and impact score, is placed on the matrix, and has a priority (red/yellow/green).
s3.tip: Low probability × catastrophic impact (e.g. a data leak) still demands a mitigation — don't dump it in the green zone.

s4.title: Mitigations
s4.why: An identified risk with no mitigation is just an alarm. Concrete, category-tied mitigations turn the register from a list of fears into an action plan.
instructions: For each priority risk, pick a mitigation from step 2 and adapt it to your context.
Distinguish preventive mitigations (RAG with citations, data classification) from detective ones (quality monitoring, audit logs).
Assign an owner and a deadline to each mitigation — a mitigation without an owner doesn't ship.
For the red zone, add a response plan: kill switch, rollback, escalation.
Tie mitigations to existing Atlas practices where applicable (governance, model limitations).
s4.validate: Every red- and yellow-zone risk has a concrete mitigation with an owner and a deadline.
s4.tip: One mitigation can cover several risks (e.g. audit logs help against both leaks and drift) — those are the most valuable mitigations.

s5.title: Monitoring risks
s5.why: AI risks evolve: models update, data shifts, new regulations appear. Without continuous monitoring the register goes stale, and drift and degradation stay invisible until customers complain.
instructions: Build golden test sets and run them regularly to catch model drift and quality drops.
Track a catch-rate metric: identified vs occurred risks — target >90%.
Define signals and thresholds for alerts (quality drop, demographic anomalies, rising errors).
Set a register review cadence — quarterly, plus an off-cycle review after any notable industry incident.
Log every risk that materializes to improve scores and mitigations.
s5.validate: You have working monitoring with golden test sets, a catch-rate metric, and a defined register review cadence.
s5.tip: The identified vs occurred metric is the best maturity indicator: if risks keep 'happening' by surprise, your identification is weak.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A risk program only matters once it's embedded in real launch processes. A checklist makes it repeatable and independent of any one person's memory.
instructions: Embed risk review in the pre-production-launch gate: no AI use case ships without clearing the 6 categories.
Assemble a launch checklist: categories cleared, risks scored, mitigations assigned, legal sign-off obtained, monitoring set up.
Lock quarterly register updates and annual reviews of existing systems into the calendar.
Document everything for regulatory readiness (EU AI Act, NIST) and insurance.
Pilot on one real initiative and refine the process from what you learn.
s6.validate: Risk review is embedded in the pre-launch gate, a launch checklist and review calendar exist, and the process is proven on a pilot.
s6.tip: Start with one use case end-to-end, not all at once — a refined process scales more easily than a raw one rolled out company-wide.

en-talent-strategy.title: AI Talent Strategy: hiring and upskilling your team
en-talent-strategy.subtitle: How to build a durable AI talent strategy: skills map, upskilling, hiring, and champion roles
en-talent-strategy.whatItIs: An approach to building your company's AI capability: hiring AI roles, upskilling existing employees, retaining people in a scarce AI-talent market, and creating career paths for AI-augmented roles. AI tools are a commodity and easy to buy. AI talent is not: it is the hardest and longest-running part of AI success.
en-talent-strategy.approach: The strategy follows the principle of "broad upskilling + targeted hiring," not one instead of the other. First, fix why you need a talent strategy and which results you measure. Then build a skills map and find the gaps. Next, raise the level of existing teams through a three-tier learning program. Then for each gap decide: train your own people or hire externally. Appoint AI champions as the engine of change. Finally, lock in results with retention metrics and a recurring review checklist.
outcomes: A documented AI skills map of the team: clear who sits at which level (foundational / intermediate / advanced) and where the gaps are
A three-tier upskilling program with protected learning time (4-8 hours/month) and AI skills counted in performance reviews
A resolved "train vs hire" decision for each gap, with clear criteria and timelines
Appointed AI champions in every team, responsible for spreading practices
A retention metric and a recurring review cycle, rather than a one-time project

applyIn.title: Scaling the AI program
applyIn.description: When a pilot has proven value and AI is rolling out company-wide, without a talent strategy growth hits a wall of too few people able to build and support solutions.

applyIn.title: Rising attrition in AI roles
applyIn.description: When people with AI skills start leaving for Big Tech, a retention strategy built on career paths and career capital brings retention back to 90%+.

applyIn.title: Before launching a new tactical initiative
applyIn.description: Before every major AI direction, check whether you have people with the needed skills, or build hiring/training into the plan in advance.

pitfalls: Hiring ML engineers and thinking the talent strategy is done: they build, but do not cover skill needs in product, marketing, support
Betting only on hiring OR only on upskilling — a working strategy always combines both
Launching training without protected time: "learn in your spare time" means no one learns
Treating the strategy as a one-time project — the talent market and skills change, so continuous review is required
Ignoring retention: investing in training people who then leave because AI projects offer no career growth

exercises.question: Build a mini skills map for one of your teams: for each person note the level (foundational / intermediate / advanced) and one real AI task they already do. Where is the clearest gap?
exercises.hint: Don't rate "in general" — tie it to a concrete task. Foundational = uses ready-made AI tools confidently; intermediate = builds prompts/workflows; advanced = creates solutions for others.

exercises.question: Take one gap from the map and work through the "train vs hire" decision: how long would training your own person take, how long would external hiring take, and what matters more — speed or keeping team context?
exercises.hint: Training wins when the skill builds on domain context a newcomer lacks. Hiring wins when the skill is deeply specialized (ML eng) and training would take months.

s1.title: Fix the why and the target result
s1.why: A talent strategy without a measurable goal turns into a pile of disconnected trainings. First understand which business problem it solves (attrition, slow hiring, lack of builders) and which metrics will tell you it works.
instructions: State 2-3 concrete problems the strategy must solve (e.g., "losing AI-skilled people to Big Tech", "AI roles take 4+ months to fill")
Fix target metrics: AI talent retention (target 90%+), time-to-fill for AI roles, internal mobility into AI-augmented roles
Define the leading indicator metric: AI skills inventory — % of employees with a documented AI level
Lock in that the strategy is continuous, not one-off: assign an owner and a review cadence
s1.validate: You have a list of 2-3 problems and, for each, a measurable metric with a current and a target value.
s1.tip: If you can't state the current value of a metric, that is task one: measure the baseline before launching any programs.

s2.title: Build the skills map and find the gaps
s2.why: You can't plan upskilling or hiring blindly. A skills map shows who sits at which level and where the real gaps are — turning the gut feeling "we're short on people" into a concrete list of gaps.
instructions: Define 3 AI proficiency levels: foundational (everyone), intermediate (active users), advanced (builders)
For each role describe its AI-augmented version: what an AI-augmented PM, designer, analyst should be able to do
Run an inventory: mark each person's/team's current level and the needed level
Identify gaps — the distance between current and needed level — and prioritize them by impact on the goals from step 1
s2.validate: A table "role, current level, needed level, gap" is ready, and gaps are ranked by priority.
s2.tip: Tie levels to observable actions, not self-assessment: "builds multi-step workflows" is more precise than "knows AI well".

s3.title: Raise the level of existing teams (upskilling)
s3.why: Broad upskilling is the backbone of the strategy: most gaps are cheaper and faster to close by training your own people, who already have domain context. Without protected time and recognition, learning doesn't happen.
instructions: Build a program for each of the 3 levels: foundational for everyone, intermediate for active users, advanced for future builders
Allocate protected learning time: 4-8 hours/month that day-to-day work can't eat
Add AI skills to performance reviews — a signal that learning is not optional
Run cross-team AI showcases where teams present working cases and learn from each other
s3.validate: Each level has a program, protected time is blocked in calendars, AI skills are added to review criteria.
s3.tip: Celebrate failed AI experiments as learning — otherwise people stop trying and upskilling stalls.

s4.title: Decide for each gap: train or hire
s4.why: Some gaps can't be closed by training within a reasonable time — they need targeted hiring. The key mistake is picking only one path. A working strategy deliberately combines upskilling and targeted hiring per gap.
instructions: For each priority gap from step 2, weigh the time to train your own person against the time to hire externally
Train when the skill builds on domain context; hire when the skill is deeply specialized (ML engineers, AI ethicists)
For hiring, build a framework: roles needed, compensation benchmarks (AI talent premium), sourcing channels (universities, conferences, communities)
Record a "train / hire / hybrid" decision per gap, with a timeline
s4.validate: Each priority gap has a "train / hire / hybrid" decision with an owner and a timeline.
s4.tip: Hiring ML engineers doesn't replace upskilling product/marketing/support — these are different gaps closed by different paths.

s5.title: Appoint AI champion roles
s5.why: A strategy doesn't spread itself. AI champions inside teams are the people who push practices, help colleagues, and connect the central program with real work. Without them, upskilling stays on paper.
instructions: Pick an AI champion in each team from intermediate/advanced people who have credibility with colleagues
Describe the champion role: help with upskilling, collect cases, route feedback to the strategy owner
Make AI projects career capital: an AI assignment should feel like an opportunity, not a burden
Support champions' external brand: conference talks, posts, GitHub — this drives both retention and employer brand
s5.validate: Every key team has an appointed AI champion with a clear role, and AI work is framed as a career opportunity.
s5.tip: A champion is not an extra burden "from above" but a recognized role; otherwise your best people will decline it.

s6.title: Lock in results and start the review cycle
s6.why: The talent market and the set of needed skills change constantly. A talent strategy is a continuous process, not a one-time project. You need a checklist and a review rhythm so the skills map and hiring decisions don't go stale.
instructions: Build a closing checklist: step-1 metrics are measured, the skills map is current, train/hire decisions are being executed, champions are appointed
Track the AI skills inventory as the main health metric of the strategy
Schedule a recurring review of the skills map and gaps before each new AI direction
Link retention to career paths: verify AI-augmented roles deliver real growth, not burnout
s6.validate: The checklist is complete, metrics are tracked, and the next strategy review date is on the calendar.
s6.tip: The main signal of a working strategy is 90%+ retention and rising internal mobility into AI-augmented roles, not the number of trainings run.

ds-design-research.title: AI Design Research
ds-design-research.subtitle: Synthesizing usability research with AI: from raw sessions to a prioritized backlog in hours, not weeks
ds-design-research.whatItIs: A practice of AI-powered user research for designers: AI extracts patterns and pain points from usability tests, session recordings, and interviews, while the designer validates findings through a design lens. The goal is to shift the balance from "50% of time on synthesis / 50% on design" toward "20/80", cutting time-to-insight from days to hours.
ds-design-research.approach: The course walks through the full synthesis workflow: why it matters and what the outcome is, how to collect and prepare the material (transcripts, notes, survey data), the key synthesis of patterns (extracting pain points by frequency and severity, grouping by journey), designer validation against part of the source data, quality and risk control (emotional nuance, edge cases), and rollout into the working process with a checklist. The principle: AI extracts themes — the designer always stays eye-on-data.
outcomes: Cut time-to-insight from days to hours for a round of 5-15 sessions
Produce a structured research report with pain points ranked by frequency and severity
Build a prioritized backlog with quick wins separated from structural issues
Validate findings through a design lens rather than trusting AI blindly
Embed a repeatable synthesis workflow into every usability round

applyIn.title: Usability testing rounds
applyIn.description: 5-15 sessions with transcripts: AI extracts pain points and groups them by task/journey, the designer checks severity against the source recordings.

applyIn.title: Competitor design research
applyIn.description: Analyzing competitor patterns: AI surfaces recurring UI solutions and divergences, the designer assesses applicability to their own product.

applyIn.title: Card sorting and interview analysis
applyIn.description: Grouping responses and coding themes from interview notes and card sorting results for information architecture.

pitfalls: AI synthesis without designer eye-on-data: the model misses emotional nuance and frustration patterns
Trusting AI 100% — edge cases and rare but critical scenarios get lost in aggregation
Feeding raw, unstructured material: without clean transcripts and survey data, synthesis produces noise
Confusing frequency with severity: a frequent minor complaint isn't more important than a rare blocker
Stopping at a list of themes without prioritizing quick wins vs structural issues

exercises.question: You have 10 session transcripts. How do you organize the AI synthesis so you don't lose emotional nuance and edge cases?
exercises.hint: AI extracts themes, then the designer manually reviews ~20% with the original recordings, then carries that confidence to the rest.

exercises.question: AI returned 30 pain points sorted by frequency. Why is sorting by frequency alone insufficient, and what should you add?
exercises.hint: Add a severity axis: a rare blocker outweighs a frequent cosmetic complaint. Build a frequency × severity matrix.

exercises.question: How do you turn a list of themes into a prioritized backlog for the design team?
exercises.hint: Separate quick wins from structural issues, rank solutions by feasibility, frame them as hypotheses to test.

s1.title: Why AI research and what the outcome is
s1.why: Research is a critical but time-intensive part of design. Understanding the goal (shifting the synthesis/design balance toward 20/80) sets the right expectations: AI speeds up extraction but doesn't replace design judgment.
instructions: Record the current time-to-insight: how many days from finishing sessions to ready findings
Pick a concrete case: a usability round, competitor research, or card sorting analysis
State the expected outcome: a structured research report + a prioritized backlog
Lock in the principle: AI extracts themes, designer validates — AI doesn't work alone
s1.validate: You have one concrete research case with a measurable goal (e.g. "cut processing of 10 sessions from 3 days to 4 hours").
s1.tip: Don't start with "let's run everything through AI". Start with one round that has clean sources — it's easier to measure the effect.

s2.title: Collect and prepare the material
s2.why: Synthesis quality depends directly on input quality. Raw, scattered material produces noise; clean transcripts and structured data yield extractable patterns.
instructions: Gather session recording transcripts (5-15 sessions for one round)
Add user interview notes and pre/post task survey data
Normalize to a single format: remove noise, mark which session and task is which
Confirm the original recordings are accessible — you'll need them for validation in step 4
s2.validate: All material is in one place, in a readable format, with access to the original recordings preserved.
s2.tip: Keep the "theme to source session" link. Without traceability you can't verify an AI finding against the original.

s3.title: Key synthesis: extracting patterns
s3.why: This is the heart of the workflow. AI extracts pain points by frequency and severity and groups them by task/journey — what would take a designer days of manual coding.
instructions: Ask AI to extract pain points along two axes: frequency and severity
Group the findings by user task / journey stage
Separate quick wins from structural issues
Generate improvement hypotheses based on the grouped patterns
s3.validate: You have a structured list of pain points with frequency, severity, journey mapping, and draft improvement hypotheses.
s3.tip: Ask AI to cite which sessions each pain point comes from — it sharply simplifies validation in the next step.

s4.title: Key check: validating the findings
s4.why: AI misses emotional nuance, frustration patterns, and edge cases. Designer eye-on-data is a mandatory step that turns raw output into reliable insight.
instructions: Review ~20% of the findings against the original recordings
Rate the severity of each pain point through a design lens, not by frequency alone
Find edge cases and emotional nuance the AI may have missed
Carry confidence from the verified sample to the rest of the set
s4.validate: At least 20% of findings are checked against sources, severity is re-rated by the designer, and critical edge cases are added manually.
s4.tip: If checking 20% reveals many errors, don't trust the other 80% — widen the sample or rerun the synthesis.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: Without quality control, AI research breeds false confidence. Explicitly accounting for risks (lost nuance, frequency/severity confusion) protects decisions built on the research.
instructions: Check that frequency and severity are kept separate, not merged into one rating
Make sure rare but critical blockers haven't drowned in aggregation
Mark where AI has low confidence or thin data — flag it as needing more research
Document the report's limitations: what AI may have missed (emotion, context)
s5.validate: The report explicitly flags low-confidence areas, separates frequency and severity, and preserves critical edge cases.
s5.tip: Add a "limitations and risks" section to the report — it's honesty toward the team and a guard against overrating AI findings.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A one-off synthesis doesn't change the process. A repeatable workflow embedded in every usability round is the shift toward 20/80 that this was all about.
instructions: Finalize the output: a structured research report + a prioritized backlog (quick wins / structural)
Rank solutions by feasibility and tie them to improvement hypotheses
Capture the workflow as a template: inputs, then AI steps, then designer validation, then output
Measure the result: time-to-insight and the number of shipped design improvements
s6.validate: A repeatable synthesis-workflow template and a prioritized backlog are ready; time-to-insight is measured against step 1.
s6.tip: Per-round checklist: clean sources, then AI synthesis (frequency + severity), then validate 20%, then flag risks, then backlog. Five items keep the process intact.

ds-prototype-generation.title: AI Prototype Generation: From Mockup to Code
ds-prototype-generation.subtitle: Turn an idea or mockup into a working prototype in hours, not days: AI handles the technical part, the designer brings the taste
ds-prototype-generation.whatItIs: A course on using AI to generate prototypes: mockup to HTML/React code, sketch to Figma composition, one brief to 5-10 layout variants. AI handles the "technical" aspect — turning an idea into code or a mockup — while the designer focuses on concept and critique. The key principle: AI gives 70% of the path from idea to code; the last 30% (taste, brand fit, accessibility) stays with the human.
ds-prototype-generation.approach: We follow a real prototype workflow: first lock in the why and the target outcome, then turn a brief into a precise prompt, generate variants (key step 1), select and iterate (key step 2), check quality and risks, then embed it into your design process with a checklist. Every step is an action, not theory. AI is a starting point, not a final.
outcomes: Cut time-to-prototype from 2 days to ~4 hours on a typical concept
Get 5-10 layout variants instead of 1-2 for the same time budget
Write brief-prompts that specify brand color, font, mood and structure
Tell apart where AI output is a ready start and where manual refinement is needed
Embed prototype generation into your design cycle without losing quality

applyIn.title: Early-stage exploration
applyIn.description: When at the start of a concept you need to quickly see many layout variants so you don't get stuck on the first idea.

applyIn.title: Mockup to code
applyIn.description: When you have a finished mockup and need a working HTML/React prototype fast as a starting point for development.

applyIn.title: Variants for A/B and design system
applyIn.description: When you need several variants of a component or screen for testing and validating hypotheses.

pitfalls: Expecting pixel-perfect output from AI — it gives 70%, the designer does the last 30% by hand
Treating AI code as final — that yields mediocre results; final = start + 30-50% refinement
A vague brief without brand color, font, mood and structure leads to vague variants
Generating a single variant instead of several — you lose the main advantage of coverage speed
Ignoring accessibility and brand fit, assuming AI "handled it" — it almost never does

exercises.question: Write a brief-prompt for a 3-step onboarding flow prototype for a B2B SaaS so that AI produces predictable variants.
exercises.hint: Include 4 things: structure (3 steps), brand color (hex), font, and mood in 2-3 words.

exercises.question: AI produced 5 layout variants. By what criterion do you pick 2 to turn into code instead of refining all 5?
exercises.hint: Think about fit to the concept and brand fit, not the beauty of a single screen; refinement is costly, so selection saves time.

exercises.question: Estimate which 30% of the work on your last prototype AI would definitely not have done for you.
exercises.hint: Taste, brand fit, accessibility, edge states — that is usually what requires a human.

s1.title: Why this and what's the outcome
s1.why: Prototyping is a bottleneck in the design cycle. Without understanding exactly what you're speeding up and where AI's boundary is, you'll expect a final from it and be disappointed.
instructions: Capture your current time-to-prototype: how many hours/days from brief to a clickable result
Write down the target metric: time-to-prototype, number of variants per concept, iteration speed
Adopt the 70/30 frame: AI does the technical part (idea to code/Figma), you do concept and critique
Decide which of your tasks fall in scope: exploration, mockup-to-code, variants for A/B
s1.validate: You have current and target numbers (e.g. from 2 days to 4 hours) and the understanding that AI is a start, not a final.
s1.tip: Don't try to speed up everything. Start with early-stage exploration — that's where variant coverage speed pays off most.

s2.title: From idea to brief-prompt
s2.why: Variant quality depends directly on brief precision. A vague request leads to vague output. The brief is your contract with AI about structure and style.
instructions: Describe the structure: screen/flow type and number of steps (e.g. onboarding flow, 3 steps)
Set the brand color in hex (e.g. #2563eb) and the font (e.g. Inter)
State the mood in 2-3 words (e.g. friendly + confident)
Specify the target output format: HTML/React code or a Figma composition
Ask for several layout variants at once (e.g. 5), not just one
s2.validate: The brief contains structure, brand color, font, mood and output format — with no gaps.
s2.tip: Keep the brief as a reusable template with placeholders — it speeds up the next concepts.

s3.title: Key step 1 — generating variants
s3.why: AI's main advantage is coverage: 5-10 variants in the time that used to yield 1-2. This turns exploration from "expensive" into "cheap".
instructions: Hand over the brief from step 2 and request 5 layout variants in one pass
Don't refine variants at this stage — the goal is to build a field to choose from, not polish one
Review at the level of concept and structure, not pixels
If all 5 look alike — add an axis of difference to the brief (e.g. compact vs airy, text-led vs visual)
s3.validate: You have 5+ noticeably different layout variants covering different approaches to the concept.
s3.tip: Look-alike variants signal that the brief is too narrow. Give AI an explicit range of styles.

s4.title: Key step 2 — selection and iteration
s4.why: Refining every variant is expensive. The power of the process is in picking 1-2 promising ones and iterating on those: AI generates code, the designer refines.
instructions: Pick the 2 most promising variants by fit to the concept and brand fit
Ask AI to generate React/HTML code for each selected variant
Refine the result: via Figma or direct code edits, expecting 30-50% rework
Iterate in short cycles: tweak the brief/prompt, then regenerate the needed block, not the whole screen
s4.validate: You have 1-2 working code prototypes refined to a state fit to show or test.
s4.tip: Note which 30-50% you rework by hand each time — it hints at what to add to the brief next time.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: The main mistake is treating AI output as final. The last 30% (taste, brand fit, accessibility) AI barely covers, and without a check the prototype comes out mediocre.
instructions: Check brand fit: are the specified color, font and mood actually used
Check accessibility: contrast, touch-target sizes, focus states — AI often skips these
Check edge states (empty, error, loading) — generation usually gives only the "happy path"
Reality-check the code output: it's a starting point for development, not production-ready code
s5.validate: The prototype passed checks on brand fit, accessibility and edge states; you know what's still not done in it.
s5.tip: Keep a short quality checklist and run every AI prototype through it — that is your "30%".

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: For the speed gain to repeat, generation must become part of the design cycle, not a one-off experiment.
instructions: Lock steps 2-5 as a standard mini-process: brief, then 5 variants, then pick 2, then code, then quality check
Save the brief template with placeholders for reuse on new concepts
Agree with the team on the 70/30 frame so the prototype isn't mistaken for final markup
Measure actual time-to-prototype after rollout and compare with the number from step 1
s6.validate: The process is reproducible without your manual reminder, and the new time-to-prototype beats the original.
s6.tip: If the time gain isn't backed by numbers — go back to step 2: the weak spot is most often the brief.

ds-design-ops.title: AI Design Operations
ds-design-ops.subtitle: Roll out AI that continuously maintains design system documentation, audits, and QA
ds-design-ops.whatItIs: A course on putting design ops on autopilot with AI: automatic component documentation, change-logs, asset audits for divergence, pre-handoff QA, and Figma library health monitoring. The goal is to move from "we have everything but no one knows where" to a state where AI maintains documentation continuously and lives inside the same tools designers work in.
ds-design-ops.approach: We go from pain to rollout. First fix why it matters and which metric to measure, then pick automation candidates (component docs and asset audit), implement two key processes, guard against risks, and ship with a checklist. The recurring principle: AI must live in Figma, Slack, and CI/CD for design — not in a separate Notion no one reads.
outcomes: Component documentation is generated and updated by AI automatically, with no manual designer effort
Asset audit catches component divergence before it spreads across the product
Pre-handoff QA checks tokens, accessibility, and spacing before handing off to development
Designer time on ops drops by roughly half and new hire onboarding speeds up
A measurable design system health score and library visibility appear

applyIn.title: Mature but undocumented design system
applyIn.description: Components exist, but new hires keep asking "where is X?" and docs are stale. AI takes over documentation and change-logs.

applyIn.title: Multiple designers, diverging components
applyIn.description: Buttons and styles drift across screens. The AI asset audit regularly catches divergence and proposes unification.

applyIn.title: Weak quality control before handoff
applyIn.description: Pre-handoff QA is not done systematically. AI checks tokens, accessibility, and spacing and assembles a QA report for developer review.

pitfalls: Generating AI docs in a separate tool (Notion) detached from the workflow — no one reads them
Automating everything at once instead of two key processes with clear payoff
Trusting the AI audit blindly without human review of disputed divergences
Not setting a metric upfront — you cannot prove ops actually improved
Ignoring change-log freshness: a stale diff is worse than none

exercises.question: Which two design ops processes cause your team the most pain while still being measurable? Define a before/after metric for each.
exercises.hint: Look at recurring manual work: component documentation and asset divergence audit are typical fast-payoff candidates.

exercises.question: Where exactly must the AI live so designers actually use the output?
exercises.hint: Not a separate doc. Think Figma plugin, Slack notifications, and CI/CD for design — inside the workflow.

exercises.question: What set of checks belongs in pre-handoff QA to make the report useful to a developer?
exercises.hint: Token usage, accessibility (contrast, touch target sizes), spacing aligned to the grid.

s1.title: Fix the why and the target outcome
s1.why: Design ops are invisible until they break. Without an explicit goal and metric, automation becomes a toy whose payoff can't be proven.
instructions: Describe the current pain: asset chaos, outdated components, missing docs, new hires asking "where is X?"
Pick 1-2 target metrics: designer time on ops, onboarding duration, component reuse rate
Capture today's baseline — without it progress can't be measured
Align the expected effect with the team (benchmark: ops time -50%, onboarding from 2 weeks to 1)
s1.validate: There is a document with the pain, target metrics, and current baseline values.
s1.tip: One or two metrics max. Ten metrics = none.

s2.title: Pick automation candidates
s2.why: Not everything is worth automating at once. Component documentation and asset audit deliver the fastest, most visible payoff.
instructions: List routine ops tasks: documentation, change-log, divergence audit, handoff QA, library health
Score each on a "frequency × manual effort" pair
Pick two key processes: component documentation and asset audit
Define the data source (Figma file) and output format (MD docs, divergence flags)
s2.validate: Exactly two processes are chosen with a clear Figma input and result format.
s2.tip: Start with what designers already do by hand every week.

s3.title: Key step 1 — auto component documentation
s3.why: Documentation goes stale the fastest. AI reads Figma and maintains docs and change-logs continuously, taking the load off people.
instructions: Set up Figma file reading: AI generates an MD doc per component
Add a weekly diff: AI compares changes and appends a changelog
Place docs where designers work — a Figma plugin, not a separate Notion
Verify a new component lands in the documentation automatically
s3.validate: Component documentation is generated automatically and updated by a weekly changelog.
s3.tip: The diff matters more than the snapshot: value lies in the visible history of component changes.

s4.title: Key step 2 — asset audit and handoff QA
s4.why: Component divergence is invisible until it spreads across the product. AI catches it early and checks quality before handing off to development.
instructions: Set up a product scan: AI finds inconsistent components and flags them ("button styles diverge across 5 screens")
Add pre-handoff QA: checks for token usage, accessibility, spacing
Generate a QA report for developer review before handoff
Wire up Slack notifications so flags reach the team within the workflow
s4.validate: The asset audit emits divergence flags and a pre-handoff QA report is produced before dev handoff.
s4.tip: The QA report must be actionable: not "there are issues" but specific screens and tokens.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: AI without human control and without tool integration creates false confidence and dead artifacts.
instructions: Introduce human review for disputed divergence flags — AI proposes, a human decides
Check change-log freshness: delete or mark stale diffs
Ensure results live in Figma/Slack/CI, not in a detached document
Set up library health: weekly AI finds unused components and outdated tokens and suggests cleanup
s5.validate: Disputed cases go through review, artifacts live in working tools, and a weekly library health exists.
s5.tip: The main antipattern is docs in an isolated Notion. If they aren't visible in the flow, they don't exist.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Automation only pays off when it runs reliably in the team's real process and metrics are monitored regularly.
instructions: Roll out both processes to one team as a pilot and gather feedback
Compare metrics with the baseline from step 1 (ops time, onboarding, reuse)
Lock in cadence: weekly changelog, audit, and library health
Run the checklist: docs auto-generated, audit flags, QA report present, metrics improving, everything living in designers' tools
s6.validate: The pilot is done, metrics are compared with baseline and improved, and processes run on a regular cadence.
s6.tip: Expand to other teams only after the pilot metrics confirm the effect.

ds-accessibility.title: AI Accessibility Automation
ds-accessibility.subtitle: Embed AI accessibility checks at every design step — from a WCAG audit twice a year to accessibility-by-default
ds-accessibility.whatItIs: A system where AI checks accessibility (a11y) in real time during design: contrast, alt-text, focus states, keyboard navigation, semantics. Instead of a separate expensive audit at the end — continuous checking against WCAG criteria right inside the workflow.
ds-accessibility.approach: AI takes on the bulk mechanical checking — contrast, alt-text, focus, color as the sole indicator, running the WCAG checklist. This covers ~80% of issues and catches them at the design stage, where fixing is 10× cheaper. The remaining ~20% require manual testing on real assistive technologies and testing with real users with disabilities. AI accelerates but does not replace the human.
outcomes: A11y bug rate drops from ~30% to ~5%: issues are caught at the design stage, not after release
WCAG AA is reached confidently and repeatably, not by guesswork
Legal risk (accessibility lawsuits) is significantly reduced
Clear understanding of the boundary: what AI covers and what mandatorily requires manual checking and real users
A repeatable check pipeline: design phase, then pre-handoff, then post-launch

applyIn.title: Design system setup
applyIn.description: Bake contrast, focus states, and semantics into components at the design-system level so accessibility is inherited by default.

applyIn.title: Launching a new feature with UI
applyIn.description: Before handoff, run an AI audit against the WCAG checklist and get a report mapped to criteria before the code goes to engineering.

applyIn.title: Quarterly product audit
applyIn.description: Regularly check the live product via AI screen reader and keyboard navigation simulation to catch regressions and respond to complaints.

pitfalls: Treating AI as a full replacement for a11y testing. AI catches ~80%; the last ~20% require manual checking and real users
Skipping testing on real assistive technologies (real screen readers, real keyboard navigation) — simulation is not the same as the real experience
Using color as the sole indicator of state — AI flags this, but teams often ignore it
Checking accessibility only at the end, when reworking is expensive, instead of in real time during design
Chasing a 100% automated WCAG score and forgetting that some criteria inherently require human judgment

exercises.question: On your latest screen, AI flagged that an icon button has no alt-text and order status is shown by color only. Which two WCAG criteria are violated here, and what do you fix first?
exercises.hint: Think about non-text content (alt) and 'color as the sole carrier of meaning' (use of color). Fix first what completely blocks understanding for a blind user.

exercises.question: The AI audit passed WCAG AA 'green' on every automated item. Why does this still not mean the product is accessible? Name two classes of problems automated checks won't catch.
exercises.hint: Consider the meaningfulness of alt-text (not just its presence), the logic of focus order in a real scenario, and clarity for a screen reader user.

exercises.question: Design which three points in the process (design / pre-handoff / post-launch) you'll embed AI checks into, and exactly what you check at each.
exercises.hint: Contrast and focus earliest, in design. The full WCAG checklist before handoff. Screen reader and real-UX simulation after release.

s1.title: Why and the outcome: WCAG as the goal
s1.why: Without a clear goal, a11y becomes a formality. WCAG AA is a measurable standard: you can rely on it, track progress against it, and reduce legal risk. Early adoption is 10× cheaper.
instructions: Fix the target level: WCAG 2.x AA as the baseline reference for the product
State the business reason: fewer a11y bugs (from ~30% to ~5%), reduced legal risk, reaching more users
Define the metrics: % WCAG compliance and number of a11y issues per release
Shift checking left: agree that accessibility is checked during design, not at the end
s1.validate: The team has one fixed target level (WCAG AA) and 1-2 metrics to measure progress against.
s1.tip: Don't aim for AAA right away. AA is a realistic and legally sufficient target for most products.

s2.title: What to check: contrast, alt, focus, semantics
