s2.why: Most a11y problems boil down to a few recurring classes. Knowing them turns vague 'make it accessible' into a concrete checkable list.
instructions: Contrast: text/background color ratio against WCAG thresholds (4.5:1 for normal text)
Alt-text: every meaningful image has a text description; decorative ones are marked as empty
Focus: visible focus states on all interactive elements, no keyboard traps
Semantics and ARIA: correct roles/structure, color is not the sole indicator of meaning
s2.validate: There is a checklist of 4 check classes (contrast, alt, focus, semantics/ARIA) tied to specific WCAG criteria.
s2.tip: The 'color as the sole indicator' check is the most commonly forgotten: duplicate the meaning with an icon, text, or pattern.

s3.title: Key step 1: automated AI audit
s3.why: This is the heart of the system. AI runs mechanical checks on every screen in real time, catching ~80% of issues at the design stage, where fixing is cheapest.
instructions: In the design phase: AI checks contrast on every screen and suggests alt-text for images
AI flags missing focus states, keyboard traps, and color as the sole indicator
Pre-handoff: automatic run of the full WCAG checklist
AI produces a report: list of issues + recommendations + mapping to specific WCAG criteria
Post-launch: screen reader simulation — AI describes how a blind user would experience the UX
s3.validate: The AI audit runs at three points (design / pre-handoff / post-launch) and outputs a report mapping each issue to a WCAG criterion.
s3.tip: Require AI to provide not just a list of issues but a mapping to specific WCAG criteria — this makes the report actionable and auditable.

s4.title: Key step 2: fixes
s4.why: An audit without fixes is just a report. Value appears when issues are resolved and prioritized by user impact.
instructions: Prioritize by impact: first what fully blocks access (no alt, keyboard trap), then what degrades the experience
Fix contrast by tuning colors within the brand palette, not by patching a single screen
Add meaningful alt-text (not 'image123'), visible focus states, and duplicate color with an icon/text
Fix systemically: edit the component in the design system, not each occurrence separately
Re-run the AI audit to confirm the issue is closed and no new ones appeared
s4.validate: Each found issue is either fixed or consciously deferred with a priority; a re-run shows a lower number of issues.
s4.tip: Fix at the design-system component level — one fix closes dozens of screens at once.

s5.title: Quality and risks: AI doesn't replace people
s5.why: The main mistake is treating AI as a full replacement for a11y testing. AI catches ~80%, but the last ~20% require real assistive technologies and real users with disabilities. Without this, a 'green' report is misleading.
instructions: Fix the boundary: AI = ~80% coverage, the remaining ~20% is manual checking
Run manual testing on real assistive tech: real screen readers, real keyboard navigation
Involve real users with disabilities in testing — their experience cannot be simulated
Check meaningfulness, not presence: alt-text must be useful, focus order logical
Treat the automated WCAG score as a necessary but not sufficient condition
s5.validate: The process explicitly includes manual checks on real assistive technologies and testing with users with disabilities — these are not skipped for speed.
s5.tip: If your team has no users with disabilities, reach them through dedicated communities or vendors; simulation won't replace this.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A one-off audit doesn't change the product. A lasting result comes from a built-in pipeline that repeats on every release and doesn't depend on one person's enthusiasm.
instructions: Embed three points into the process: design phase, pre-handoff, post-launch
Make the AI audit a mandatory gate before feature handoff
Set up a release checklist: contrast / alt / focus / semantics / ARIA / manual check on assistive tech
Track metrics on every release: % WCAG compliance and number of a11y issues
Schedule a quarterly audit of the live product and a process for responding to user complaints
s6.validate: There is a repeatable checklist and a gate built into the process; every release records WCAG-compliance metrics and the number of a11y issues.
s6.tip: Make the a11y gate part of the regular definition of done — then accessibility stops being a separate 'project' and becomes the norm.

ds-design-system.title: AI Design System Evolution
ds-design-system.subtitle: Turn a static design system into a living one: tokens, variants, migration via AI
ds-design-system.whatItIs: A course on using AI to evolve a design system: generating token sets, creating component variants (sizes/states/themes), maintaining documentation, and migrating usage on breaking changes. The goal is to remove the operational burden and keep the system fresh — without making AI the decision-maker for architecture.
ds-design-system.approach: We move from inventorying the current system to tokens, then to generating variants and docs, then to migrating breaking changes, and finish with consistency control and rollout. AI is the executor: it generates and migrates, while brand strategy and UX principles stay human-owned. Each step produces a verifiable artifact (token set, variant matrix, migration PR).
outcomes: A single source of truth for design tokens (color/spacing/typography scales) generated with AI
A full component variant matrix: sizes, states, themes — generated and reviewed
Always-current documentation that updates when components change
A repeatable breaking-change migration process: from weeks to days
A clear split: what the human decides (architecture) vs what AI executes (generation/migration)

applyIn.title: Refreshing a stagnating system
applyIn.description: The design system exists but maintenance burden is high and breaking changes are postponed — AI removes the upkeep routine.

applyIn.title: Migrating to new tokens
applyIn.description: Moving to a new token system (e.g., changing the spacing scale): AI scans code and Figma, generates a migration PR and a change list.

applyIn.title: Scaling component variants
applyIn.description: You need to quickly create sizes/states/themes for base components and consolidate scattered documentation in one place.

pitfalls: Relying entirely on AI for design system decisions — brand strategy and UX principles stay human decisions; AI is only the executor
Generating variants without reviewing tokens: AI will replicate the mistake across all sizes/states/themes
Running a breaking-change migration without a full code + Figma scan — some usage will stay on old tokens
Documentation detached from components: docs go stale if not tied to the source of change
Accepting 100% of AI token output without manual adjustment — usually ~30% manual tuning for the brand is needed

exercises.question: A designer says "warm palette, modern feel". AI generated a full set of color/spacing/typography scales. What should you do before generating component variants on top of them?
exercises.hint: AI token output is ~70% of the answer. A mistake in a base token replicates across every variant, so review and manual adjustment come before variant generation.

exercises.question: The team changes token spacing from 4px to 8px. Which two usage sources must AI scan for the migration to be complete, and what artifact should it produce?
exercises.hint: Usage lives in both code and design. The artifact is a reviewable change, not a silent edit.

exercises.question: Where is the line between AI's role and the human's role in evolving a design system? Give one example for each side.
exercises.hint: AI = executor (token generation, variant fan-out, migration PR). Human = decision-maker (system architecture, brand strategy, UX principles).

s1.title: Why AI in the design system and the target outcome
s1.why: Design systems stagnate due to lack of maintenance resources: breaking changes get postponed and docs scatter. A clear goal up front keeps AI in the executor role and sets a measurable outcome.
instructions: Pin down the problem: where the maintenance burden lives now — tokens, variants, migrations, or documentation
Define target metrics from the node: update velocity (3-5× faster), migration speed (from weeks to days), documentation freshness (always current)
Separate roles: AI executes (generation, migration), the human decides (system architecture, brand strategy, UX)
Pick one component or one token scale as a pilot — not the whole system at once
s1.validate: 1-2 pain points, target metrics, and an explicit "AI executor / human decision-maker" boundary are written down.
s1.tip: If you can't name a metric for a step, it's a human decision task, not an AI task.

s2.title: Tokens and system inventory
s2.why: Tokens are the foundation: variants, migrations, and docs all build on them. Without inventorying current usage, AI generates in a vacuum and creates duplicates instead of a single source of truth.
instructions: Collect current design tokens and their usage in code and Figma — the baseline inventory
Give AI brand context in words ("warm palette, modern feel") and ask it to generate color/spacing/typography scales
Review the output: ~70% taken as-is, ~30% manual adjustment for the brand
Fix the final token set as the single source of truth
s2.validate: There is an agreed token set (color/spacing/typography) tied to real usage, with clear traces of manual tuning.
s2.tip: Vet tokens before generating variants — a base-token mistake replicates across every size/state/theme.

s3.title: Generating variants and documentation
s3.why: The key acceleration step: on top of tokens, AI fans out component variants and maintains docs. This is what delivers 3-5× update velocity and keeps documentation always-current.
instructions: Create a base component (e.g., button) on top of the approved tokens
Ask AI to generate the matrix: sizes (sm/md/lg), states (default/hover/focus/disabled), themes (light/dark)
Get the artifacts: a Figma file + code stubs for each variant
Set AI to maintain MDX documentation per component with auto-updates on changes
Review the matrix for consistency with the tokens
s3.validate: A full variant matrix (sizes × states × themes) + documentation tied to the source of change.
s3.tip: Documentation detached from a component goes stale — tie docs to the component itself so they update automatically.

s4.title: Migrating breaking changes
s4.why: Breaking changes are the main cause of stagnation: they get postponed because of the manual workload. AI turns migration into a repeatable process (from weeks to days) by scanning all usage.
instructions: State the change explicitly (e.g., "token spacing from 4px to 8px")
Run an AI scan across both usage sources: codebase + Figma files
Get reviewable artifacts: a migration PR for code and a list of Figma changes
Check coverage — make sure no usage stays on old tokens
Run the PR through human review before merge
s4.validate: A migration PR + Figma change list is generated; the scan covered both code and design, and no old-token usage remains.
s4.tip: Never let AI silently edit usage — a migration must be a reviewable change, not an invisible one.

s5.title: Quality and risks: consistency
s5.why: AI scales not only the good but also the mistakes. Consistency control after generation and migration protects the system from replicated defects and preserves brand/UX integrity.
instructions: Verify all variants use the approved tokens, not hardcoded values
Check brand strategy and UX principles against the AI output — this is the human-review zone
Run a visual/structural check of the variant matrix for deviations
Log discovered risks (replicated token errors, unclosed usage) and roll back if needed
s5.validate: All variants are consistent with the token set, brand/UX are human-reviewed, and no replicated errors are found.
s5.tip: One wrong base token = an error in every variant; check the source, not each copy individually.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: For a lasting effect, the process must be locked in as repeatable, not one-off. A checklist moves the system from "a live experiment" to a stable practice with predictable artifacts.
instructions: Lock in the pipeline: tokens, then variants, then docs, then migration, then consistency review
Cement the roles: what AI generates/migrates, what the human decides
Set up the metrics from step 1 (update velocity, migration speed, doc freshness) to track impact
Roll the process out from the pilot to the rest of the system's components
Run the final checklist before declaring the system "living"
s6.validate: The pipeline is documented, roles are fixed, metrics are tracked, and the process is repeatable on new components.
s6.tip: A "living" system is not a one-off generation but a repeatable update process; without a checklist it stagnates again.

ds-content-design.title: AI Content Design: UX Copy Without the Bottleneck
ds-content-design.subtitle: Set up a process where AI generates contextual microcopy and the designer curates brand voice and quality
ds-content-design.whatItIs: AI help with UX writing: microcopy for buttons, forms, errors, onboarding flows, empty states, and helper text. A shift from "designer writes copy in free time" to "AI generates contextual copy, designer curates the voice".
ds-content-design.approach: The course moves from rationale and metrics to a working process: you document brand voice and microcopy guidelines, set up UX-text generation by slot, build i18n with an AI draft and human review, address tone and accuracy risks, then roll out the process with a coverage checklist. The goal is 100% of UI elements with intentional copy and a consistent brand voice, without compromising legal/compliance text.
outcomes: Documented brand voice and microcopy guidelines that AI uses as context
Working UX-text generation by slot (title, description, CTA, errors, success) with 5 variants per slot
An i18n process: AI does the first-pass translation, a local copywriter refines it
Quality metrics: copy coverage %, brand-voice consistency score, tone and accuracy control
A rollout checklist that separates ordinary copy from critical copy (privacy, ToS, regulatory)

applyIn.title: New feature launch
applyIn.description: Generate intentional copy for every UI element of a feature instead of "TBD" placeholders by the deadline.

applyIn.title: Error and onboarding standardization
applyIn.description: Bring error messages and onboarding flows to a single brand voice and a clear tone.

applyIn.title: International product
applyIn.description: Scale UI text across multiple languages via an AI draft and human review.

pitfalls: Using AI for legal/compliance copy without human review — "AI wrote it" does not release you from accountability
Generating copy without a fixed brand voice — variants come out disconnected and inconsistent
Shipping AI translation to production without a local copywriter — naturalness and language nuance are lost
Accepting the first variant without curation — the core value of the designer's role is lost
Not measuring coverage and consistency — without metrics the process degrades back to "TBD"

exercises.question: Take one screen of your product and list every microcopy slot on it (title, description, CTA, error states, success, empty state). How many are intentionally written, and how many are placeholders or random text?
exercises.hint: Count any point where the user reads interface text as a slot. Coverage = intentional slots / all slots.

exercises.question: Define your product's brand voice in 3-5 attributes (e.g., friendly, direct, jargon-free) and give one "we write like this" / "we don't write like this" example for each.
exercises.hint: Attributes should be verifiable: "friendly" works better with an example phrase than as an abstraction.

exercises.question: Pick one type of copy in your product and decide: can it be trusted to AI generation, or is it critical human copy? Justify it.
exercises.hint: Privacy notices, ToS, regulatory text are always human-written, with AI only for review.

s1.title: Why and what outcome
s1.why: UX copy is critical to the experience, but designer time for it is always insufficient. Without an explicit goal and metrics, the process won't stick and rolls back to "TBD" placeholders.
instructions: Fix the problem: where copy is currently written last or left as a placeholder
Define target metrics: copy coverage % (share of UI elements with intentional text) and a brand-voice consistency score
Set a benchmark: copy generation time -70%, 100% UI-element coverage
Split the zones: ordinary copy (AI allowed) and critical copy — privacy, ToS, regulatory (human only)
s1.validate: You have a written problem statement, 2-3 metrics, and a clear boundary between the AI zone and critical copy.
s1.tip: The coverage metric matters more than the beauty of a single phrase: 100% intentional copy beats a perfect button with ten "TBD"s.

s2.title: Brand voice and microcopy guidelines
s2.why: AI generates coherent copy only with given context. Brand voice is the context the designer sets once and reuses across all generations.
instructions: Describe brand voice in 3-5 verifiable attributes with "we write like this" / "we don't" examples
Set microcopy rules: CTA length, error tone, how to address the user, jargon ban
Compile a content style guide as the single source of truth for copy
Prepare this document in a form you can paste into a prompt as context
s2.validate: There is a content style guide with voice attributes and microcopy rules, ready to serve as AI context.
s2.tip: The more concrete your "not like this" examples, the less the AI drifts off tone — negative examples work harder than abstractions.

s3.title: Key step 1: generating UX text by slot
s3.why: This is the heart of the process: the designer gives surface context, AI produces variants for each slot, the designer picks and refines. This is how copy stops being a bottleneck.
instructions: For each UI surface, give context: "password reset flow, friendly tone"
Ask AI to generate 5 variants for each microcopy slot: title, description (1 sentence), primary CTA, error states (3-5 likely), success state
Pick the best variant and refine manually if needed
Ask AI to suggest improvements based on brand voice
Document the final copy in the content style guide
s3.validate: For the target surface, all slots are filled with intentional copy that passed designer curation.
s3.tip: Always generate several variants per slot: choosing from 5 yields a better result, and faster, than editing a single draft.

s4.title: Key step 2: i18n and localization
s4.why: For an international product, copy must scale across languages. AI speeds up the first pass, but naturalness and nuance still require a human.
instructions: Use AI for the first-pass translation of already-approved source copy
Hand the translation to a local copywriter for review and adaptation
Check that brand voice and tone are preserved in each language, not just literal meaning
Store the translated strings in the same system as the source copy
s4.validate: Each target locale has an AI draft reviewed by a local copywriter, with brand voice preserved.
s4.tip: Don't ship AI translation to production without a human: literal correctness is not the same as naturalness in the user's language.

s5.title: Quality and risks: tone and accuracy
s5.why: AI speeds things up but does not remove accountability. Tone errors and factual inaccuracy in copy damage trust, and in legal/compliance they carry legal risk.
instructions: Check each final copy against brand voice (consistency score)
Check factual accuracy: copy must not promise what the product doesn't do
Flag critical copy (privacy, ToS, regulatory) — it is human-written, AI only for review
Fix the rule: "AI wrote it" does not release you from accountability for published text
s5.validate: Each text passed tone and accuracy checks; critical copy is human-written; accountability for publishing is assigned.
s5.tip: For critical copy, invert the roles: the human writes, AI reviews — not the other way around.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Without a checklist and metrics built into the process, the team reverts to "copy in free time". Rollout cements the habit and a measurable result.
instructions: Build copy generation into the feature design process as a mandatory step, not a final touch-up
Create a per-surface checklist: all slots filled, brand voice respected, accuracy checked
Track metrics: copy coverage % and brand-voice consistency score
For an international product, add i18n status per locale to the checklist
Regularly update the content style guide as new patterns emerge
s6.validate: The process is built into feature work, the checklist is in use, and coverage and consistency metrics are tracked.
s6.tip: Make the checklist part of the feature's definition of done — then copy stops being the thing finished at the last moment.

ds-team-workflow.title: AI Design Team Workflow
ds-team-workflow.subtitle: How to turn scattered, per-designer AI usage into a shared team process
ds-team-workflow.whatItIs: An operating model for a design team with AI: a shared Claude Project with brand voice and design system, shared Figma plugins and skills, weekly "AI office hours" and critique sessions where AI runs accessibility and brand checks beforehand. The goal is to move from "every designer with their own Claude" to a team augmented by AI as a whole.
ds-team-workflow.approach: First, define why the team needs a shared process and what outcome it should produce. Then separate what you hand to AI (routine, checks, synthesis) from what stays with the designer (taste, concept, decisions). Next, build two key mechanisms: a shared knowledge base and shared skills/rituals. Then set up quality, roles, and risks. Finally, roll it out through value rather than coercion, with a readiness checklist.
outcomes: A unified brand voice and consistent components instead of diverging per-designer versions
Team velocity +25-35% by automating routine work and checks
A new designer becomes productive in 3-5 days instead of weeks
Critique sessions focus on craft and concept rather than bug-hunting
An "AI-augmented designer" career track emerges as a senior path

applyIn.title: Team of 3+ designers
applyIn.description: When several designers already use AI inconsistently and it starts fragmenting the brand.

applyIn.title: Design-driven product
applyIn.description: Consumer apps and brand-heavy products where voice and visual consistency are critical to perception.

applyIn.title: Onboarding and scaling
applyIn.description: When the team grows and you need to bring new designers into shared standards and tools quickly.

pitfalls: Equating "AI in design" with "designers must use AI" — forced adoption kills creative ownership
Leaving AI at the individual level: voice diverges, components duplicate, lessons are not retained
Loading AI without an up-to-date knowledge base — it generates off-brand and off-system output
Making AI the judge of taste and concept — that is the designer's zone; AI takes routine and checks
Running rituals for show without reviewing the team's real wins and failures

exercises.question: List three tasks in your design team that everyone currently does their own way, and decide which can be handed to AI without losing quality.
exercises.hint: Look for routine and checks: microcopy, component documentation, accessibility and brand checks, research synthesis.

exercises.question: Define what should live in your team's shared Claude Project "Design Workspace" so AI replies in the brand voice.
exercises.hint: At minimum: brand voice guide, design system docs, accessibility rules, component library reference, synthesis of past research.

exercises.question: Design a weekly "AI office hours" format for your team: 30 minutes — what you discuss, who leads, what you capture.
exercises.hint: Share both wins and failures; capture findings back into the shared base so lessons stick instead of getting lost.

s1.title: Why the team needs a shared process and what outcome
s1.why: Individual AI usage does not scale: brand voice diverges, components duplicate, and one person's lessons never reach others. Without an explicit goal, the team won't understand why to change habits.
instructions: Capture the symptoms: where brand voice diverges, where components duplicate, where lessons get lost
State the target in one sentence: "a team augmented by AI" instead of "everyone with their own Claude"
Define a measurable outcome: team velocity, brand consistency, new-designer onboarding speed
Check the threshold: the process makes sense with 3+ designers actively using AI
s1.validate: You have a short list of concrete pains and 2-3 measurable goals for the process.
s1.tip: Don't launch the process "because it's trendy" — without real pain, the team will see it as overhead.

s2.title: What to hand to AI and what stays with the designer
s2.why: The responsibility boundary is the basis of trust in the process. Without it, AI will either touch the creative zone or be underused on routine work.
instructions: List team tasks and split them into "routine/checks" and "taste/concept/decisions"
Hand to AI: microcopy, component documentation, accessibility and brand checks, research synthesis
Keep with the designer: concept, artistic decisions, final taste, and accountability
Record the AI task list as candidates for future skills
s2.validate: There is a clear "AI does / human does" table, and only routine and checks are in the AI zone.
s2.tip: If a task requires taste or a strategic choice, it stays with a human — AI only prepares the material.

s3.title: Key step 1 — a shared knowledge base
s3.why: AI is useful to the team only when it replies in the brand voice and knows the design system. A shared Claude Project turns scattered answers into consistent ones.
instructions: Create a shared Claude Project "Design Workspace" for the whole team
Load the brand voice guide, design system docs, synthesis of past research, and a component library reference
Describe design principles, brand voice, and accessibility rules in a shared principles file (see [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]])
Give all designers access and assign an owner for keeping the base current
s3.validate: Any designer on the team gets an AI answer in the brand voice that references your design system.
s3.tip: A stale base is worse than none — build in regular updates from the start, not "someday".

s4.title: Key step 2 — shared skills and rituals
s4.why: The knowledge base gives context; skills and rituals turn it into repeatable actions and shared learning. Without them, value will pool with individuals again.
instructions: Build shared skills as Figma plugins + Claude: microcopy-generator, component-doc-writer, accessibility-checker, research-synthesizer
Introduce weekly "AI office hours" (30 min): designers share wins and failures
Set up a quarterly "AI in design" retrospective to revisit the process
Capture office-hours findings back into the shared knowledge base
s4.validate: Skills are available to everyone, rituals are on the calendar, and team lessons reach the shared base.
s4.tip: Office hours are about exchange, not reporting; failures are as valuable here as wins.

s5.title: Quality, roles, and risks
s5.why: The process must raise the quality bar, not blur it. Clear roles and built-in checks protect both the brand and creative ownership.
instructions: Embed AI checks before critique: AI runs accessibility and brand checks beforehand
Redirect critique toward craft and concept rather than bug-hunting
Assign roles: knowledge-base owner, skills owner, office-hours host
Track the risk of forced adoption — AI is chosen through value, not mandate
s5.validate: Critique sessions discuss the substance of the work, routine checks are done before the meeting, roles are assigned.
s5.tip: If a designer doesn't want to use AI but quality and speed are fine — that's not a problem, it's a signal the value isn't obvious yet.

s6.title: Rollout and readiness checklist
s6.why: The process takes root through value and gradual adoption, not by decree. The checklist confirms the team has actually moved to the new state.
instructions: Roll out through value: start with 1-2 skills that give obvious benefit and expand on demand
Give designers the right to choose — adoption grows where AI makes the work better, faster, happier
Measure the outcome: team velocity, brand consistency, onboarding speed
Run the checklist: live shared base, skills available, rituals running, roles assigned, new designer productive in 3-5 days
s6.validate: All checklist items are met, and at least one measurable metric (velocity or onboarding) has improved.
s6.tip: A sign of a mature process (Stage 3): a new designer becomes productive in 3-5 days without manual hand-holding.

ec-pdp-gen.title: AI PDP Generation
ec-pdp-gen.subtitle: A pipeline that turns a raw CSV into CMS-ready product cards in 3 languages within minutes
ec-pdp-gen.whatItIs: An automated pipeline that takes raw product data (name, attributes, photos, category) and generates a full Product Detail Page: SEO title, meta description, marketing body in brand voice, and an attribute table — in multiple languages and in a format ready to load into the CMS.
ec-pdp-gen.approach: First fix the why and the metric you measure, then prepare clean data and a brand guide, then build the generation step and the SEO + fact-check layer, set a quality gate against fabricated specs, and only then scale in batches with an acceptance checklist. Never launch on the whole catalog at once — grow volume from a 50-100 SKU pilot.
outcomes: You understand which metrics (catalog size, team size, number of languages) make PDP generation pay off, and which numbers you'll track
You can prepare the input: a clean attribute CSV and a brand guide, without which the output is generic
You assemble a working generation pipeline: title, then meta, then body, then attribute table
You embed an SEO layer and a fact-check that catches fabricated specs before publishing
You run scaling in batches with a quality gate and an acceptance checklist

applyIn.title: Launching new assortment
applyIn.description: 50+ new SKUs arrive monthly — cards publish on delivery day instead of weeks of manual copywriting.

applyIn.title: Localizing to new markets
applyIn.description: One catalog rolls out in 3+ languages in brand voice, without hiring a copywriter per language.

applyIn.title: Closing SEO gaps
applyIn.description: Thousands of cards lacking descriptions and meta get full copy, lifting organic traffic on the long tail of the catalog.

pitfalls: Launching on the whole catalog at once — quality degrades on the long tail; start with 50-100 SKUs and brand voice tuning
No quality gate — the catalog gets cluttered with generic text that buyers immediately spot
Fabricated specs — the model invents material, size, or compatibility that aren't in the data; without a fact-check this ships to production and damages trust and returns
Unlocalized voice — generic UK English in the Finnish or another market puts buyers off
No measurable outcome — without baseline metrics for time-to-publish, coverage, and SEO traffic you can't prove the pipeline paid off

exercises.question: Take 5 real SKUs from your catalog and check: does the source data have enough attributes to write an honest body without inventing? Which fields will you have to fill manually?
exercises.hint: If the copy needs material, size, compatibility, or composition that aren't in the CSV — that's a source of future hallucinations. Fix the data first, then generate.

exercises.question: State your store's brand voice in 5 rules (tone, sentence length, what's forbidden, how you address the buyer, signature phrasings). Generate one card with the guide and one without — compare.
exercises.hint: The gap between generic text and brand-voice text shows up exactly in the contrast. That's the argument for a quality gate.

exercises.question: Design a 6-8 point acceptance checklist that lets an editor decide publish / send back in under a minute.
exercises.hint: Include: facts match the data, title/meta within length limits, brand voice, no fabricated specs, correct localization, attribute table filled.

s1.title: Why, and what outcome you measure
s1.why: Without a fixed goal and baseline metrics the pipeline can be neither justified nor evaluated. First decide which pain you close and which numbers prove success.
instructions: Fix the adoption trigger: catalog >500 SKUs, content team ≤5, localization needed in 3+ languages, or SEO worse than competitors
Capture baseline metrics BEFORE launch: current time-to-publish per SKU, coverage (% of cards with full copy), organic traffic to cards
Set targets: time-to-publish from 4 hours to 5 minutes, coverage up to 100%, SEO traffic +25-40% over 3 months, localization cost −70%
Define that AI covers 80% of the work while copywriters shift to strategy (brand guides, longreads, CRO copy)
s1.validate: You have a one-pager: the pain, current numbers, target numbers, and who signs off on card acceptance.
s1.tip: Count coverage honestly: a card with a single sentence is not "full copy." Otherwise the 100% target is fictional.

s2.title: Product data and brand voice
s2.why: Output quality is determined by input quality. A dirty CSV and a missing brand guide are the main cause of generic text and fabricated specs.
instructions: Assemble the input in one format: name, attributes, image_url, category — one SKU per row
Check attribute completeness: an honest body needs material, size, composition, compatibility — things that must not be invented
Describe the brand voice as a guide: tone, sentence length, prohibitions, how you address the buyer, signature phrasings
Prepare a localized version of the voice per market — don't translate UK English word for word
Select a pilot batch of 50-100 SKUs from a single category for the first tuning
s2.validate: You have a clean CSV for the pilot batch and a brand guide (general + localized) that lets you tell "your" text from generic.
s2.tip: Explicitly mark fields missing from the data as "no data" — it's a signal for the model not to invent but to skip the spec.

s3.title: Key step 1 — card generation
s3.why: This is the pipeline core: a card draft is born from a raw CSV row. A clear sequence of steps yields a predictable, verifiable result.
instructions: Extraction step: determine the product type and key attributes from the CSV row
Generate a 300-500 word marketing body strictly in brand voice and based only on the passed attributes
Generate an attribute table in HTML for insertion into the CMS
Run it on the pilot 50-100 SKUs and collect the output as CMS drafts, not straight to publish
s3.validate: On the pilot batch you get coherent drafts in brand voice where the body relies only on real attributes.
s3.tip: One SKU = one pipeline run with the same step structure. A stable structure beats "creativity" — it's easier to verify and scale.

s4.title: Key step 2 — SEO and fact-check
s4.why: A card must sell, be findable in search, and not lie. The SEO layer and fact-check turn a draft into publishable material.
instructions: Generate an SEO title within ~60 characters and a meta description within ~160 characters
Verify that title and meta contain the product type and key attributes, not filler
Cross-check every spec in the text against the source CSV — anything not in the data counts as fabricated and is removed
Establish the fact-check as a separate mandatory stage before the quality gate
s4.validate: Title and meta fit the limits and are meaningful, and every claim in the text is backed by data from the CSV.
s4.tip: Make the fact-check an automated "claim ↔ CSV field" match, not a manual read — across 500 cards manual fact proofing is unrealistic.

s5.title: Quality and risks — a gate against fabricated specs
s5.why: Without a quality gate the catalog fills with generic text and false specs that hurt trust, conversion, and returns. This is the critical step between generation and scale.
instructions: Introduce a quality gate: human review or auto-publish only above a threshold (e.g. score 0.85)
On the pilot, the editor reviews 50 random cards, logs error types, and refines the brand voice and the fact-check
Specifically catch hallucinations: material, size, compatibility not present in the data
Check localization: the voice must sound natural in each market, not like machine translation
Iterate the prompt until the next batch ships without edits
s5.validate: After refinement the new batch passes the quality gate with almost no manual edits, and fabricated specs never reach publication.
s5.tip: Track not only pass/fail but also the share of cards rejected for hallucinations — a rising share signals the input data has degraded.

s6.title: Scaling and the acceptance checklist
s6.why: The pilot proved quality — now you must safely grow volume without losing control. Scaling without a gate and a checklist brings back all the long-tail risks.
instructions: Grow volume in batches (50-100, then 500, then whole catalog), not all at once
Keep the quality gate and sampling on every batch, lowering the sample share as trust grows
Lock in the acceptance checklist: facts match the data, title/meta limits, brand voice, no fabricated specs, correct localization, attribute table filled
Compare actual metrics against the targets from step 1 and publish the result to the team
Schedule a regular run for new SKUs so the pipeline keeps up with incoming product
s6.validate: The catalog is covered batch by batch, metrics approach the targets, and every card passes the checklist before publishing.
s6.tip: Don't fully drop the quality gate even on a mature pipeline — keep a sampling audit, otherwise input data degradation slips through unnoticed.

ec-search-opt.title: AI Search Optimization for E-commerce
ec-search-opt.subtitle: Hybrid search: keyword + semantic embeddings + Claude reranking
ec-search-opt.whatItIs: Semantic search on embeddings layered on top of classic keyword search. A user types "warm jacket for minus 20" — the system finds a down jacket even when the title contains neither "warm" nor "winter". A hybrid stack: keyword gives exact matches on SKUs and brands, semantic captures meaning and synonyms, and Claude reranks the candidates at the final stage and explains why these specific products.
ec-search-opt.approach: We don't replace keyword search — we extend it. A four-stage architecture: embed the query, then vector search over the product index (top-50 candidates), then keyword filter (category, price, availability), then rerank with Claude (top-10 with reasoning). The course moves from rationale and metrics through preparing catalog data to the two key steps (semantics and ranking), then to controlling result quality and a controlled production rollout with a checklist.
outcomes: Understand where classic search loses 20-40% of queries and how hybrid closes that gap
Can prepare product context for embeddings — not just title, but attributes, description, reviews
Configure vector search with a keyword filter on category, price, and availability
Implement Claude reranking with "why these products" reasoning
Control irrelevant results and stale data through metrics and re-indexing

applyIn.title: Catalog with diverse categories
applyIn.description: 5k+ SKUs where buyer wording systematically diverges from product names: long queries show low CTR, and semantic captures intent.

applyIn.title: High "no results" rate
applyIn.description: More than 20% of search sessions end in "no results" — each one is lost conversion, and hybrid drops the rate down to 5%.

applyIn.title: Multilingual store
applyIn.description: Embeddings carry meaning across languages, so a query in one language finds products described in another without manual synonym lists.

pitfalls: Replacing keyword search with semantic entirely — you lose exact matches on SKUs and brands. Hybrid only.
Building embeddings from title only — you skip attributes, descriptions, and reviews; index the full product context.
Ignoring stale data: without re-indexing when the catalog changes, search shows out-of-stock products.
Serving raw vector results to users without reranking — the top-50 by vector proximity often contains irrelevant noise.
Launching without an offline relevance measurement on real queries — you can't catch result regressions by eye.

exercises.question: The query "jacket for minus 20" returns the top-50 by vector proximity, but the top positions are summer windbreakers. What's the cause, and which architecture stage fixes it?
exercises.hint: Vector proximity ≠ relevance to a specific query. Think about what the fourth stage does and which signal (a temperature range in attributes) must be in the product context.

exercises.question: After adding new models to the catalog, search stopped finding them even though they're in the database. What's missing in the pipeline?
exercises.hint: Embeddings and the vector DB don't update on their own. Recall the rule about stale data and re-indexing when the catalog changes.

exercises.question: Marketing wants to disable the keyword branch since semantic is "smarter". Which class of queries breaks, and how do you argue against it?
exercises.hint: SKUs, article numbers, exact brand names. Semantics blurs exact matches — give an example of a query by SKU.

s1.title: Why search needs AI and what outcome we target
s1.why: Without a clear goal and baseline metrics the project becomes technology for its own sake. Classic keyword search loses 20-40% of queries to synonyms, typos, and the buyer's wording not matching product names — every "no results" is lost conversion.
instructions: State the problem in money: how many search sessions end in "no results" and what lost conversion that represents
Capture baseline metrics: no-results rate, search conversion, CTR on long queries (>3 words), bounce on the search-result page
Set target values as a reference: no-results from 25% to 5%, search conversion +20-40%, time to click −30%
Describe the target hybrid architecture in one paragraph: keyword + semantic + reranking, an extension, not a replacement
s1.validate: You have a document with current and target metrics and one sentence explaining why hybrid specifically, not pure semantic.
s1.tip: Compute lost conversion from real search logs over the last month — it beats any generic argument about AI.

s2.title: Catalog and query data: the index foundation
s2.why: Search quality is determined not by the model but by what goes into the index. Embeddings from title only skip attributes, description, and reviews — that's exactly where the signals the buyer searches by live ("for minus 20", "for running", "stain-resistant").
instructions: Assemble the full product context for each SKU: title, attributes, category, description, key reviews
Export logs of real search queries and label those that returned "no results" — this is your offline test set
Normalize structural fields for the keyword filter: category, price, availability, brand, SKU
Define a freshness policy: which catalog changes (availability, price, new SKUs) trigger re-indexing
s2.validate: For a sample of SKUs the full product context is assembled, not a single title; a labeled set of real queries exists for later evaluation.
s2.tip: Keep out-of-stock and discontinued products as a separate flag in the keyword layer rather than purging them from the index — it's easier to manage results without re-indexing.

s3.title: Key step 1 — semantics and synonyms via embeddings
s3.why: This is the stage that closes the gap of classic search: meaning, synonyms, typos, and buyer phrasing. Embeddings map the query and products into a shared vector space where proximity means semantic similarity, not word overlap.
instructions: Build embeddings from the full product context from step 2 and load them into a vector DB
Embed the query with the same model and run vector search — top-50 candidates
Check multilingual and synonym behavior on the labeled set: "warm jacket" should find a down jacket
Confirm the keyword branch runs in parallel and collects exact matches on SKUs and brands
s3.validate: On the test queries from step 2 the top-50 contains relevant candidates classic search missed, while exact SKUs are still found by the keyword branch.
s3.tip: The query and products must be encoded with the same embeddings model — otherwise the vector spaces are incomparable and proximity means nothing.

s4.title: Key step 2 — ranking and reranking with Claude
s4.why: Vector proximity yields candidates but not order: the top-50 by proximity contains noise and irrelevant items. Final ranking decides what the buyer sees. Claude is strong precisely at this stage — it scores the match to the query and returns reasoning.
instructions: Apply the keyword filter to the top-50: category, price, availability — cut off the clearly irrelevant
Hand the remaining candidates to Claude with the query: score how well each fits, return the top-10
Request brief reasoning per product — the basis for the UI explanation "why these"
Fix the response format (a structured list with score and reason) for stable parsing
s4.validate: On the test queries the post-rerank top-10 is noticeably more relevant than the raw top-50, and each product has a clear reason for inclusion.
s4.tip: Pass Claude not just the candidate's title but the key attributes from product context — without them reranking guesses just like vector search.

s5.title: Quality and risks: controlling irrelevant results
s5.why: The main risk of semantic search is confidently shown irrelevant or stale results. You can't catch regression by eye, and a stale vector DB serves out-of-stock products. You need measurable checks before and after release.
instructions: Run the labeled query set from step 2 and measure top-10 relevance — this is your offline benchmark
Check edge cases: SKUs and brands (keyword precision), long queries, multilingual, nonsense input
Set up re-indexing per the policy from step 2 so availability and new SKUs are reflected in search
Build a fallback: if rerank or the vector DB is unavailable — degrade to keyword search, not empty results
Define the relevance drop on the benchmark at which a release is blocked
s5.validate: A reproducible offline relevance measurement exists, edge cases pass, re-indexing is configured, and keyword fallback works on failure.
s5.tip: Schedule a regular benchmark run after every catalog or prompt change — relevance degrades quietly and cumulatively.

s6.title: Rollout and launch checklist
s6.why: A sharp full switch is risky: new results can drop conversion unnoticed. A controlled rollout with measurement on real traffic turns the "+20-40%" forecast into a confirmed result.
instructions: Launch on a share of traffic and compare with the baseline from step 1: no-results rate, search conversion, CTR, bounce
Surface the "why these" explanation in the UI based on the reasoning from step 4 — it raises trust in the results
Set up monitoring of no-results, fallback share, and reranking response time in production
Pass the final checklist: hybrid (not a replacement) ✓, full product context ✓, re-indexing ✓, fallback ✓, offline benchmark ✓
Once the metrics are confirmed, expand the traffic share to 100%
s6.validate: On live traffic search conversion and no-results rate move toward the step-1 targets, the checklist is fully passed, and production monitoring is active.
s6.tip: Compare search traffic only with search traffic — site-wide conversion is noisy with factors outside search and will hide the real effect.

ec-personalization.title: Store AI Personalization
ec-personalization.subtitle: How to adapt your storefront to the individual shopper with Claude
ec-personalization.whatItIs: Personalization is a layer that changes the home page, recommendations, and copy based on a shopper's browsing history, purchases, and segment. Claude here isn't a standalone recommender system — it's an agent that interprets user behavior and decides "show X or Y". One agent with access to profile and behavior replaces expensive ML infrastructure (data team, ML engineers, MLOps).
ec-personalization.approach: Start from value, not from technology. First fix which metric you're moving and which control group you measure against. Then collect user data legally and transparently. Design segment and decision logic, embed the result into one or two high-value surfaces, check quality and risks (privacy, filter bubble, cold start), and roll out via an A/B test with a checklist. Do not personalize everything at once.
outcomes: You know which metric (conversion, AOV, retention, CTR) and which control group measures the personalization effect
You can collect user context legally and transparently: profile, recent views, purchases, segment
You designed the logic: segments + a Claude prompt returning a structured decision (collection, categories, copy tone)
You embedded personalization into one or two high-value surfaces (home, search) with a cold-start fallback
You launched the rollout via an A/B test and closed privacy and filter-bubble risks with a checklist

applyIn.title: Marketplace with distinct segments
applyIn.description: B2C and B2B on one site: Claude swaps the hero collection and copy tone by segment, leveling retention across groups.

applyIn.title: Catalog over 1k SKUs
applyIn.description: A large assortment where a generic home loses returning users: personalized recommendations lift CTR by 40-60%.

applyIn.title: SaaS-eCommerce with no ML team
applyIn.description: A startup without data engineers launches basic personalization on a single Claude agent and raises retention by ~22% in a quarter.

pitfalls: Personalizing everything at once. Start with 1-2 high-value surfaces (home, search results); expand only after a confirmed effect.
Ignoring cold start. A new buyer has no data — you need a fallback to segment or generic. Never "hi, we don't know you".
Not measuring. Personalization without an A/B test and control group is faith, not science.
Collecting data non-transparently. Gathering data without consent and a clear privacy policy is a legal risk and erodes trust.
Trapping users in a filter bubble. Showing only similar items stops discovery — add a share of fresh items to the output.

exercises.question: You're launching home page personalization. Which single metric do you pick as primary, and how do you set up measurement so the result is provable?
exercises.hint: Think about returning users and what to compare the personalized experience against.

exercises.question: A new user lands for the first time with no history. What does your logic return instead of a personal decision?
exercises.hint: Cold start: no data about the person, but segment or a generic variant is available.

exercises.question: Define the structured response Claude should return for a home-page personalization request so the frontend can render it.
exercises.hint: Recall the node example: hero_collection, recommended_categories, voice_attributes.

s1.title: Why and what outcome
s1.why: Generic UX gives generic conversion, but personalization for its own sake is wasted money. First fix which metric you're moving and what lift you expect, or you'll have nothing to prove value with.
instructions: Pick 1 primary metric: returning-user conversion (+30-50%), AOV (+10-25%), 30-day retention (+15-30%), or recommendation CTR (+40-60%)
State the hypothesis in one sentence: "personalizing surface X lifts metric Y by Z%"
Decide what counts as the control group (users without personalization) for a fair comparison
Fix the success threshold and observation window (e.g., effect over a quarter)
s1.validate: You have one primary metric, a hypothesis, and a defined control group — before writing any code.
s1.tip: Don't grab 5 metrics at once: one primary plus 1-2 guardrails (so you don't sink the rest).

s2.title: User data: legal and transparent
s2.why: Personalization only works on user context, but you must collect it with consent and a transparent policy. Otherwise you get legal risk and lost trust instead of metric growth.
instructions: Define the minimal context: profile, last ~10 views, last ~3 purchases, segment
Verify the collection is covered by user consent and a privacy policy (GDPR / local rules)
Assemble the context into a single object loaded at session start
Don't pull extra personal data into Claude — only what actually drives the decision
s2.validate: A user-context object is available at session start, and data collection is legally and transparently justified.
s2.tip: Data minimization isn't just law — it's quality: less noise in the prompt means a sharper decision.

s3.title: Key step 1: segments and decision logic
s3.why: This is the core of personalization. Here Claude interprets behavior and decides what to show. Clear segments and structured output make the decision predictable and testable.
instructions: Describe 3-5 segments (e.g., new, returning B2C, B2B, premium) and the rule for assigning a user to one
Write the Claude prompt: input is user context, output is strict JSON
Fix the output schema: { hero_collection, recommended_categories[5], voice_attributes[3] }
Add a cold-start branch: no data, then decide by segment or generic
Build in a discovery share in recommendations so the output doesn't collapse into a filter bubble
s3.validate: On a test context Claude returns valid structured JSON, and the fallback fires for an empty context.
s3.tip: Ask Claude to return only schema JSON — the frontend renders without guessing and you validate easily.

s4.title: Key step 2: embed into the storefront
s4.why: Claude's decision is useless until it changes a real page. Embed it into one or two high-value surfaces, not everything at once — that's cheaper, safer, and more measurable.
instructions: Pick 1-2 highest-value surfaces: home page and/or search results
Wire Claude's output to rendering: hero_collection to banner, recommended_categories to blocks, voice_attributes to copy tone
Ensure a fast runtime fallback: if Claude doesn't answer in time, show the generic variant
Leave other surfaces untouched at this stage
s4.validate: On the chosen surface you see personalized content for a user with history and a correct generic for a new one.
s4.tip: Personalization must not block rendering: treat it as an enhancement, not a required loading step.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: Personalization touches privacy and can harm the experience (filter bubble, weird recommendations, cold start). Check this before rolling out to everyone, or metric growth turns into complaints.
instructions: Check privacy: the user understands which data is used and can opt out
Check the filter bubble: the output includes a share of fresh/unexpected items, not only similar ones
Check cold start on a real new account — no "hi, we don't know you"
Test edge cases: empty history, contradictory behavior, a failed Claude response
Verify guardrail metrics: personalization doesn't drag down other indicators
s5.validate: All four risks (privacy, filter bubble, cold start, Claude failure) have a working answer and are manually verified.
s5.tip: Keep a blocklist of topics/categories you must never recommend — cheap insurance against awkward output.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Rolling out without an experiment is faith, not science. An A/B test against a control group proves the effect and justifies expanding personalization further.
instructions: Run an A/B test: personalized group vs. a control group without personalization
Track the primary metric from step 1 and the guardrail metrics across the observation window
Run the pre-rollout checklist: data consent — yes; cold-start fallback — works; primary metric — logged; control group — carved out; discovery in output — present
If the effect is confirmed, expand to the next surface; if not, iterate on segments/prompt
Record the result and the "expand / roll back" decision
s6.validate: The test ran its window, the primary metric is compared against the control group, and an expand-or-iterate decision is made.
s6.tip: Expand one surface at a time so each lift stays attributable to a specific change.

ec-merchandising.title: AI Merchandising for an Online Store
ec-merchandising.subtitle: Product collections are assembled automatically from catalog, sales and trends — a human only validates
ec-merchandising.whatItIs: An AI curator for collections: instead of a merchandiser hand-building collections like "summer for women 25-35", Claude reads sales data, catalog metadata and seasonal signals and proposes 10-20 ready-made collections with rationale. The human stays in the loop as a validator, not as an assembler.
ec-merchandising.approach: Not an autopilot but a conveyor: "AI assembles, then human reviews, then CMS publishes". AI removes the routine of "find 20 relevant products on a theme", but business rules (minimum margin, exclusions, stock availability) and the final decision stay with the human. Every AI collection is compared to a manually curated one so you see the real uplift instead of taking it on faith.
outcomes: Time-to-collection drops from ~4 hours to ~20 minutes per collection
50+ collections active at once instead of 15, refreshed weekly instead of monthly
Sales from curated collections grow 30-50% with a proper baseline
Reaction to trends shrinks from weeks to days
The merchandiser shifts from manual assembly to strategy and quality control

applyIn.title: Large catalog, small team
applyIn.description: Catalog of 2k+ SKUs and 1-3 merchandisers: manual assembly cannot keep up with the assortment, AI closes the gap.

applyIn.title: Seasonal and trend collections
applyIn.description: Seasonal goods need a refresh every season and trends live for days — AI rebuilds collections to match current demand faster than a human.

applyIn.title: Stale collections on the site
applyIn.description: If storefront collections are older than 2 weeks and new products don't make it into collections for weeks — AI keeps the storefront fresh daily.

pitfalls: Auto-publish without a human gate: AI may assemble a collection from out-of-stock or low-margin products
Ignoring business rules (minimum margin, exclusion lists) — AI optimizes "by relevance" while the business loses money
No baseline: without comparison to manual collections you cannot prove the real uplift
Stale sales and stock data fed in — AI recommends what is out of stock or no longer sells
Too many collections at once: 50 collections without prioritization dilute the storefront and cannibalize each other

exercises.question: You have 8k SKUs and 2 merchandisers. Which first collection do you hand to AI for a pilot, and why?
exercises.hint: Pick a segment with clear demand and fast staleness — e.g. a seasonal or trend category where manual refresh obviously lags.

exercises.question: AI proposed a 20-product collection. By which 3 rules do you reject it before publishing?
exercises.hint: Check stock availability, minimum margin and exclusion lists — that's the human-gate baseline.

exercises.question: After a month, sales from AI collections are up 25%. How do you tell it's AI's doing and not the season?
exercises.hint: Compare against the baseline — manual-collection sales for the same period and/or last year for the same category.

s1.title: Why do this and what outcome we target
s1.why: Without a clear goal and metric the project turns into "playing with AI". You must fix what AI removes (assembly routine) and how you measure success.
instructions: State the bottleneck plainly: how many SKUs, merchandisers, and how fast collections go stale
Fix target metrics: time-to-collection, number of active collections, sales from curated collections
Explicitly outline the loop: AI assembles and justifies, human validates, CMS publishes — no autopilot
Write down the constraint: 1 pilot collection at the start, not the whole storefront
s1.validate: You have on paper: one bottleneck, 2-3 measurable metrics, and the human's role in the loop.
s1.tip: The "sales from curated collections" metric is meaningless without a baseline — plan to collect it right away.

s2.title: Data prep: sales, stock, catalog
s2.why: AI is only as good as the freshness of its inputs. Stale stock and sales lead to recommending what isn't in stock.
instructions: Gather three inputs: a catalog snapshot with metadata, last 30 days of sales, demand signals (trending searches, season)
Make sure the catalog has fields for filtering: category, gender/segment, margin, stock
Set up data refresh cadence — at minimum before each merchandising review
Clean obvious junk: duplicate SKUs, discontinued products, zero stock
s2.validate: AI receives a current catalog + 30 days of sales + demand signals, with no stale stock.
s2.tip: The "stock" and "margin" fields in metadata are not optional: business rules later act exactly on them.

s3.title: Key step 1 — generating collections (the layout)
s3.why: This is the heart of AI merchandising: Claude turns data into ready collections with a name, description and rationale for each choice.
instructions: Give Claude the input (catalog + sales + signals) and the task: "propose 10 collections for next week"
For each collection require: a name, a description, 15-25 products, a rationale for each one
Ask for the rationale explicitly — without it you cannot validate fast or catch AI errors
Generate the first batch on one segment (e.g. seasonal), not the whole catalog
s3.validate: The output is 10 collections, each with 15-25 products plus a name, description and rationale.
s3.tip: The selection rationale is the key artifact: it makes a 10-minute validation possible.

s4.title: Key step 2 — business rules and automation
s4.why: Without rules AI optimizes "by relevance" and drags out-of-stock and low-margin products into collections. Rules + a schedule turn a one-off experiment into a conveyor.
instructions: Describe the business rules: minimum margin, exclusion lists, mandatory stock availability
Embed rules as an input filter and an output check on AI
Set a trigger for a regular run — e.g. a weekly merchandising review
Keep a mandatory human gate before publishing to the CMS — no auto-publish
s4.validate: Collections are generated automatically on schedule, pass the business-rule filter, and wait for human review.
s4.tip: An exclusion list is cheaper than any ML tuning: an explicit ban on products/brands removes 80% of weird collections.

s5.title: Quality and risks: baseline and control
s5.why: Without comparison to manual collections you cannot prove value, and without stock and margin control it's easy to lose money on pretty but unprofitable collections.
instructions: Fix the baseline: sales of manual collections over a comparable period
Compare AI collections to the baseline by conversion and revenue, not by a "feeling of relevance"
Check every collection before publishing for out-of-stock and low-margin items
Log rejected collections and reasons — this is feedback for the rules and the prompt
s5.validate: A baseline exists, uplift is computed, and no collection goes live without a stock and margin check.
s5.tip: If an AI collection doesn't beat the baseline, that's not a failure but a signal to fix data or rules, not to switch AI off.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A pilot must become a stable process: schedule, owners, metrics, and scaling from one collection to dozens.
instructions: Lock in the process: trigger, then generation, then business rules, then human review, then publish
Assign an owner for validation and for the uplift metrics
Scale gradually: from 1 pilot collection to 10, then to 50+
Plan a regular review of the prompt and rules based on rejection logs
Checklist before each release: fresh data, rules applied, baseline computed, human gate passed
s6.validate: The process runs weekly without manual assembly, metrics grow, and the checklist is passed before each publish.
s6.tip: Scale by proven uplift: add new collections only where AI already beats the baseline.

ec-cro.title: AI Conversion Rate Optimization for E-commerce
ec-cro.subtitle: Claude as a conversion analyst: hypothesis generation and A/B-test analysis in minutes instead of days
ec-cro.whatItIs: A practical course on embedding Claude into an online store's CRO process. Claude works as a conversion analyst: from funnel data, reviews, and competitors it generates hypotheses, proposes copy and UI variants for A/B tests, and after the test explains why a variant won or lost. This is not a replacement for the CRO specialist, but a 5-10× acceleration of the ideation and synthesis phases.
ec-cro.approach: The main CRO bottleneck isn't running tests — it's hypothesis generation and result analysis. The course is built around these two phases: first you teach Claude to find funnel bottlenecks and formulate justified hypotheses, then to generate test variants and run post-mortems. Prioritization discipline (one variable per test) and statistical significance rank above speed: AI produces plenty of ideas, but a valid test remains exactly one variable over two weeks.
outcomes: Embed Claude into the store's CRO cycle without replacing the specialist: AI accelerates ideation and synthesis, humans validate and decide
Find funnel bottlenecks from data and formulate justified hypotheses — 10-15 per week instead of 2-3
Generate copy variants and UI briefs for A/B tests and run post-mortems in 2 hours instead of 2 days
Verify statistical significance of results and avoid shipping variants based on noise
Build a repeatable rollout checklist: one variable per test, human review, control of factual errors

applyIn.title: Product page conversion
applyIn.description: From funnel data, reviews, and competitor pages, Claude produces 5 hypotheses to improve the product page with rationale; the CRO picks 1-2 and formulates the test.

applyIn.title: CTA and hero copy
applyIn.description: For the chosen hypothesis, Claude generates 3 CTA copy variants and 3 hero-image briefs, ready for an A/B test after human review.

applyIn.title: Test post-mortem
applyIn.description: After a 2-week test, Claude analyzes the result (variant B won on conversion, lost on AOV), names the likely cause, and proposes the next hypothesis.

pitfalls: Testing AI-generated variants without human review — they may contain factual errors about the product
Testing everything: AI generates many ideas, but a valid CRO test is one variable over two weeks
Running on traffic below 10k visitors/month — statistical significance is unattainable and conclusions are noise
Stopping a test early at the first 'winner' — without reaching significance the result is random
Treating Claude as a replacement for the CRO specialist: AI = acceleration, not a substitute for a domain expert

exercises.question: You have a store with 25k visitors/month and conversion plateaued for 4 months. Where do you start embedding Claude into CRO?
exercises.hint: First gather funnel data (where users drop off), reviews, and competitor pages — this is the input for hypothesis generation, not copy variants right away.

exercises.question: Claude produced 12 hypotheses from one prompt. How many will you launch as tests this week, and why?
exercises.hint: A valid test = one variable over two weeks. Prioritize 1-2 hypotheses with the highest expected impact; the rest goes to the backlog.

exercises.question: Variant B shows +8% conversion on day 4 of the test. Can you ship it?
exercises.hint: No, not until statistical significance is reached and a full cycle (at least two weeks) is complete. Early leads often disappear.

s1.title: Why AI in CRO and what outcome
s1.why: Without understanding exactly where Claude accelerates the process, the team will start generating copy variants while bypassing data analysis — producing many ideas with no rationale. The main CRO bottleneck is hypothesis generation and result analysis, not running tests.
instructions: Record current cycle metrics: how many hypotheses per week, how long a single test post-mortem takes
Identify the two phases Claude accelerates: ideation (hypotheses) and synthesis (result analysis)
Set a numeric goal: hypothesis throughput from 2-3 to 10-15/week, time-to-postmortem from 2 days to 2 hours
Anchor the principle: Claude accelerates the phases, humans validate and make strategic decisions
s1.validate: You can name the two phases Claude accelerates and the current throughput and analysis-time figures.
s1.tip: The quarterly goal is a cumulative conversion uplift of +15-25% from more fast iterations, not one 'magic' test.

s2.title: Funnel bottlenecks
s2.why: Hypotheses untethered from funnel data are guesswork. For Claude to produce justified ideas, it needs correct input: exactly where users drop off, what reviews say, what competitors do.
instructions: Collect funnel data: conversion by step (view, then cart, then checkout, then payment) and drop-off points
Add qualitative context: customer reviews and pages of 2-3 competitors
Pass it all to Claude and ask it to surface the top-3 bottlenecks tied to the data
Confirm traffic is sufficient (>10k visitors/month), otherwise tests won't reach significance
s2.validate: You have a list of the top-3 funnel bottlenecks, each backed by a number from the funnel data.
s2.tip: Qualitative data (reviews, competitors) often explains 'why' the drop-off happens — this sharply improves hypothesis quality.

s3.title: Key step 1 — hypotheses with Claude
s3.why: This is the first of the two phases AI is adopted for. An hour of discussion per hypothesis turns into minutes — but only if Claude has the data from the previous step and a requirement for rationale.
instructions: Give Claude the collected input and ask for 5 hypotheses on the chosen bottleneck, each with rationale
Require the format: what changes, which metric it moves, why you expect the effect
Run a human review: check for factual errors about the product
Prioritize: pick 1-2 hypotheses with the highest expected impact; send the rest to the backlog
s3.validate: From 5+ hypotheses, 1-2 are selected, each with rationale and one clearly named variable to test.
s3.tip: Prioritization discipline beats speed: AI generates many ideas, but you must launch one variable per test.

s4.title: Key step 2 — A/B test and analysis
s4.why: The second phase AI is needed for: generating test variants and the post-mortem. Without structured analysis the team spends a day dissecting one test and never learns what to test next.
instructions: Ask Claude to generate variants for the hypothesis: e.g. 3 CTA copy variants + 3 hero-image briefs
Run a human review of the variants and launch the A/B test for at least 2 weeks
After the test, give Claude the results and ask for analysis: who won on conversion and on AOV, the likely cause
Get the next hypothesis from Claude for the iteration (what to test next)
s4.validate: The test runs on one variable, and afterward there is a post-mortem with the cause of the result and a proposed next test.
s4.tip: Analyze not only conversion but also AOV: a variant can win on conversion and lose on average order value.

s5.title: Quality and risks — statistical significance
s5.why: Generation speed is useless if conclusions rest on noise. An early 'winner' often disappears, and factual errors in AI variants harm the brand. This step is the filter between generation and rollout.
instructions: Check statistical significance before declaring a winner — don't stop the test early
Confirm the test ran a full cycle (at least 2 weeks) and gathered enough data
Mandate a human review of all AI variants for factual errors about the product
Reject results on traffic below 10k/month as statistically unreliable
s5.validate: For every test a significance check is recorded and a human review of variants is completed before rollout.
s5.tip: Better to cancel an immature test than to ship a variant on a random lead — a rollback costs more than a pause.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A one-off success doesn't scale without a repeatable process. To move from 1 test per month to 1 per week at the same headcount, you need a fixed cycle and checklist, not ad-hoc prompts.
instructions: Formalize a repeatable cycle: funnel data, then hypotheses with Claude, then prioritization, then variants, then A/B test, then post-mortem
Build a pre-test checklist: one variable, human review, traffic >10k, a 2-week plan
Assign roles: Claude — ideation and synthesis; CRO specialist — validation and decisions
Log test results and accumulated uplift to track the cumulative effect over the quarter
s6.validate: The team has a documented cycle and checklist by which every test passes the same control stages.
s6.tip: The rollout goal is a steady pace of 1 test/week at the existing headcount, not a record in a single sprint.

ec-experimentation.title: AI experimentation in e-commerce: from hypotheses to rollout
ec-experimentation.subtitle: How to run experimentation at scale with AI without losing statistical rigor
ec-experimentation.whatItIs: A practical course on embedding AI into the experiment loop: hypothesis generation, test design, result analysis, and building a knowledge base. AI closes two bottlenecks — ideation and synthesis — but replaces neither A/B tools (Optimizely, VWO, GrowthBook) nor statistics.
ec-experimentation.approach: We follow a real experiment cycle: first fix the why and the target outcome, then build a hypothesis flow and prioritize, design a correct test, analyze the result, separately handle quality and risks (peeking, significance), and finally roll out with a checklist. Each step shows what to do by hand and exactly where AI helps.
outcomes: Run 50-100% more tests with the same headcount without losing quality
Every test yields a structured insight, not "variant B kinda seems better"
Prioritize hypotheses by an impact × confidence matrix, not intuition
Hold an archive of past tests that AI reuses for new hypotheses
Stop neither too early nor confuse an early signal with a result

applyIn.title: CRO and funnel optimization
applyIn.description: AI generates a hypothesis backlog for the product page, cart, and checkout, prioritizes it, and helps interpret a series of test results.

applyIn.title: Quarterly experimentation review
applyIn.description: Feed AI 20-30 completed tests and get a retrospective: which hypothesis categories drove uplift, where you burned cycles, plus a roadmap for the quarter.

applyIn.title: Unblock without a dedicated analyst
applyIn.description: A team with no data analyst uses AI for test design and basic interpretation while keeping significance and decisions in human hands.

pitfalls: Trusting AI early signals: on a 50% sample it "sees" a confident pattern and tempts you to stop before stat-sig
Not documenting tests: without a structured archive every new experiment starts from scratch and AI is useless
Ignoring confidence intervals: AI gives a narrow answer to a broad question — always look at uncertainty
Peeking — checking results and stopping the test at a "random" lead: inflates false positives
Treating AI as a replacement for the A/B tool or statistics — it boosts ideation and synthesis, not the test itself

exercises.question: You have 12 raw test ideas for the product page. How do you turn them into a prioritized backlog with AI?
exercises.hint: Ask AI to score each by impact and confidence, plot a matrix, and explain its reasoning — keep the decision yourself.

exercises.question: A test has run 5 days; AI notes variant B leads confidently on half the sample. Stop it?
exercises.hint: No. That's an early signal, not a result. Check the pre-set sample size and horizon; stopping before stat-sig is peeking.

exercises.question: You ran 25 tests this quarter. How do you extract recurring insights, not just a win/loss list?
exercises.hint: Give AI the full archive with hypothesis metadata and ask it to group by category, find uplift patterns, and propose a roadmap.

s1.title: Why and the target outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal experimentation becomes "test whatever comes to mind": many tests, little learning. First fix the business outcome you move.
instructions: State the North Star funnel metric you move (conversion rate, AOV, retention)
Check readiness: the team runs ≥4 tests per month, otherwise the process is premature
Pinpoint the current bottleneck — ideation (too few hypotheses) or synthesis (unclear what results mean)
Decide what AI owns and what stays human (significance, rollout decisions)
s1.validate: You have one measurable metric and clarity on which loop bottleneck AI should close.
s1.tip: If you run fewer than 4 tests/month, build the flow first — AI won't fix a missing experimentation culture.

s2.title: Hypotheses and priority
s2.why: Ideation is the first bottleneck. AI widens the hypothesis flow, but priority still rests on an impact × confidence matrix, not intuition.
instructions: Give AI context: the metric, the page/funnel stage, user behavior data, and the archive of past tests
Ask it to generate a hypothesis backlog as "if we change X, metric Y rises because Z"
Ask it to score each hypothesis by impact and confidence and build a matrix
Pick the top hypotheses by hand — AI proposes, the team decides
s2.validate: You have a prioritized backlog with an explicit statement and rationale for each hypothesis.
s2.tip: The richer the archive of past tests in context, the more relevant AI's hypotheses — feed it history.

s3.title: Experiment design
s3.why: Correct design before launch prevents peeking and unreliable results. AI helps with design, but the test is configured in your existing A/B tool.
instructions: Fix the primary metric and guardrail metrics (so uplift doesn't break something else)
Compute the required sample size and test horizon BEFORE start — this guards against early stopping
Ask AI to check the design for common errors: mixed changes, wrong randomization unit
Configure the test itself in Optimizely / VWO / GrowthBook — AI doesn't replace the tool
Pre-write what counts as success, failure, and inconclusive
s3.validate: Sample size, horizon, and success criteria are written down before launch.
s3.tip: One test = one change. Change several things at once and you won't know what worked.

s4.title: Result analysis
s4.why: Synthesis is the second bottleneck. AI turns raw numbers into a structured insight, but a human verifies that significance was reached.
instructions: Wait for the planned horizon and stat-sig, only then analyze
Give AI the results with hypothesis metadata and ask for a structured insight: what held, what didn't, why
Request not just a point estimate but confidence intervals — look at uncertainty
Record the conclusion as a learning, not "variant B kinda better"
s4.validate: You have a structured conclusion with effect size, confidence interval, and an explicit learning.
s4.tip: If AI gives a confident narrow answer, ask back about uncertainty; a broad question has no narrow answer.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: The main traps of AI experimentation are peeking, trusting early signals, and ignoring significance. A dedicated control step guards against false conclusions.
instructions: Confirm the test was not stopped before the planned horizon (no peeking)
Separate early signals from the result: a confident pattern on a 50% sample is not a conclusion
Ensure statistical significance was reached, not just "looks better"
