Check guardrail metrics: did anything suffer for the sake of the primary metric's uplift
Record the confidence level of the conclusion honestly, including "inconclusive"
s5.validate: The test reached stat-sig with no peeking, and false-conclusion risks are checked and documented.
s5.tip: The costliest mistake is rolling out a variant that won by chance. Significance beats speed.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: A test matters only if the result is rolled out and feeds the knowledge base. The archive makes each next cycle denser — AI is only good with history.
instructions: Roll out the winning variant or, on a negative result, record the hypothesis as rejected
Log the test in the structured archive: hypothesis, design, result, confidence interval, learning
Run the checklist: goal, then hypothesis prioritized, then design before start, then stat-sig, then no peeking, then learning recorded
Feed the archive to AI for the next hypothesis round — the learning loop closes
Quarterly, review all tests: which categories drove uplift, where you burned cycles
s6.validate: The result is rolled out, the test is archived, the checklist passed, and the archive is available to AI for a new cycle.
s6.tip: The archive is an asset. A team without one starts from scratch every time, even with the smartest AI.

ec-checkout-opt.title: AI Checkout Optimization
ec-checkout-opt.subtitle: Find checkout drop-off from data and lower the risk of changes
ec-checkout-opt.whatItIs: An approach where AI reads checkout funnel data, finds the steps with the highest drop-off, proposes hypotheses for the cause, and generates variants to test. Checkout is special: every step is critical and expensive to redesign, so AI is used not for mass edits but for prioritization — what exactly to change first.
ec-checkout-opt.approach: We don't rewrite checkout wholesale. First we see where people actually leave (funnel data, heatmaps, support tickets), then we form a hypothesis backed by evidence, change exactly one element, test it, and measure. AI cuts the time to find friction from days to hours, but any decision touching payments always goes through manual review.
outcomes: See the top-3 checkout drop-off points with evidence instead of guesses
Change only where drop-off is largest and the hypothesis is strong — minimal risk
Completion rate rises by 5-15 percentage points per quarter
The gap between mobile and desktop checkout narrows by roughly half
Time from "where is the friction" to an answer drops from days to hours

applyIn.title: Low completion rate
applyIn.description: Completion below 70% — AI finds the steps where most people are lost.

applyIn.title: Mobile clearly worse than desktop
applyIn.description: Segment the funnel by device and see what exactly breaks mobile checkout.

applyIn.title: Multi-step checkout
applyIn.description: More than 3 pages — AI flags which step is redundant or confusing.

pitfalls: Changing many steps at once — impossible to tell what produced the effect. One change per test only.
Ignoring payment provider errors: AI reads funnel analytics but doesn't see payment failures — that data must be brought in separately.
No segmentation: mobile/desktop, new/returning, paid/organic traffic behave differently, so an averaged picture is useless.
Dark patterns for the numbers: hidden checkboxes, forced add-ons and concealed cost lift completion in a test but destroy trust and drive returns.
Drawing conclusions from a small sample: a couple dozen orders is noise — you need enough data volume and test duration.

exercises.question: Your completion rate is 62%, and 48% on mobile. Where do you start the analysis without breaking payments?
exercises.hint: Start with device segmentation and collecting funnel data plus tickets; don't touch payments yet, find the step with the largest drop-off.

exercises.question: AI proposed 5 changes to the payment form. How many do you ship in the first test, and why?
exercises.hint: Exactly one — otherwise you can't attribute the effect. Take the hypothesis with the biggest drop-off and the strongest evidence.

exercises.question: How do you tell honest checkout simplification from a dark pattern?
exercises.hint: Honest reduces user effort without deception; a dark pattern lifts the number by hiding info or forcing add-ons — check returns and trust, not just completion.

s1.title: Why this and what outcome
s1.why: Checkout is the most expensive part of the funnel to optimize: you risk breaking payments, so teams fear touching it. AI lowers the risk through data-driven prioritization.
instructions: Record the current completion rate and its month-over-month drop
Pin down the pain: low completion, poor mobile, or too many steps
State the goal in percentage points (e.g., +5-15 pp per quarter)
Agree: AI prioritizes, a human decides on anything touching payments
s1.validate: You have one measurable goal and a clear sense of which checkout symptom you're treating.
s1.tip: Don't set the goal as "rewrite checkout" — set it as "raise completion by N pp".

s2.title: Abandoned-cart analysis
s2.why: Without data, any edits are guesses. You need to see at which step and which segment leaves, and cross-check it against what support is asked.
instructions: Collect step-by-step funnel data, heatmaps, and payment-related support tickets
Segment: mobile/desktop, new/returning, paid/organic traffic
Give AI this data and ask for the top-3 drop-off points, each with evidence
Bring payment provider errors separately — AI doesn't see them in analytics
s2.validate: You have a list of 3 drop-off points, each with where people leave and what backs the cause.
s2.tip: If the data isn't segmented, the averaged picture is useless — start with segmentation.

s3.title: Key step 1: simplification and hints
s3.why: Drop-off is most often caused by extra fields, unclear microcopy, and missing hints at the right moment. This is the cheapest and safest class of changes.
instructions: Take drop-off point #1 from the analysis and write the hypothesis: what blocks and why
Ask AI for variants: remove a field, rewrite a label, add a hint
Remove anything not required for payment on the critical step
Verify the simplification is honest — it doesn't hide cost or force add-ons
s3.validate: One concrete change variant is ready, justified by the data.
s3.tip: Microcopy and field order often beat a full-page redesign.

s4.title: Key step 2: testing
s4.why: A change without measurement is faith, not optimization. One test per change gives clean attribution of the effect.
instructions: Ship exactly one change per test — otherwise you can't tell what worked
Set a sufficient sample size and duration to avoid conclusions from noise
Compare completion in the relevant segment (e.g., mobile separately)
After 30 days, repeat the funnel analysis on the same data
s4.validate: The test runs on a single change, with the metric and segment defined in advance.
s4.tip: A small sample lies: a couple dozen orders is noise, not a result.

s5.title: Quality and risks: trust, not dark patterns
s5.why: You can lift completion through deception — hidden checkboxes, concealed price, forced add-ons. The number rises in the test, but trust and repeat purchases fall.
instructions: Check each change: does it lift the number through clarity or through concealment
Look beyond completion — at returns, complaints, and repeat purchases
Make sure cost and terms are visible before payment confirmation
Reject variants AI proposed if they are manipulative
s5.validate: Accepted changes pass the check: the gain is honest, with no hidden terms.
s5.tip: If a change would be embarrassing to show the customer openly, it's a dark pattern — reject it.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: To make optimization a regular practice rather than one-off heroics of "rewrite checkout once a year", you need a repeatable cycle.
instructions: Set up a monthly checkout review: data, then top-3 frictions, then one test
Keep a prioritized backlog with an estimated impact for each point
After each test, repeat the analysis and take the next drop-off point
Record that payment errors are brought into the analysis separately from analytics
s6.validate: There's a repeatable cycle and a backlog; the team fixes 3-5 friction points per quarter.
s6.tip: One working cycle of "analyze, then one test, then measure" beats ten ideas in your head.

ec-recommendations.title: AI Recommendations for Your Store
ec-recommendations.subtitle: Embeddings + Claude reranking: personal "similar", "bought together", "next purchase" picks without a data scientist
ec-recommendations.whatItIs: A recommendation system is the "you might like", "bought together", and "next purchase" blocks that pick products personally for each user. The classic approach (collaborative filtering, market-basket) needs a data scientist and heavy infrastructure. Here you build a lightweight version on embeddings + Claude: embeddings produce a top-50 set of similar candidates, Claude does the reranking (picks the best 6 for the specific user) and the explanation ("why this is recommended to you"). This delivers roughly 80% of the quality of classic systems at 20% of the complexity.
ec-recommendations.approach: Work from the business result back to the tech. First, fix what uplift you measure and where the recommendation blocks live. Then gather two data sources — the catalog (products, price, availability, margin) and user behavior (views, purchases). The core logic sits in two steps: first embedding similarity selects candidates and market-basket gives "bought together", then Claude reranks and explains. Next, embed the blocks into the storefront, check quality and risks (privacy, repeats, out-of-stock), and roll out via A/B against a baseline to measure real lift.
outcomes: Understand the architecture: embedding similarity, then history filter, then Claude rerank, then render with explanation
Select candidates via embeddings and "similar / bought together" logic
Embed recommendations into the product page, cart, and emails so they stay relevant
Filter out-of-stock, already-purchased, and low-margin before display instead of blindly optimizing for clicks
Run A/B against random recommendations and read uplift in CTR, AOV, and cross-sell

applyIn.title: Product page
applyIn.description: "Similar products" and "bought with this" blocks: embedding similarity supplies candidates, Claude picks 6 relevant to the user's history and adds a short explanation.

applyIn.title: Cart and checkout
applyIn.description: Cross-sell "add to your order": market-basket "bought together" logic plus a filter for already-added and out-of-stock items, to raise AOV without annoyance.

applyIn.title: Email and retention
applyIn.description: "Next purchase" email based on history: a personal set with an explanation of why these items, to bring the user back.

pitfalls: Only collaborative filtering on small data — a "cold start" problem: new products and users have nothing to recommend. Content embeddings fix this.
Not filtering out-of-stock and low-margin before reranking — AI optimizes for clicks while the business loses money and shows unavailable items.
Not measuring against random: without an A/B baseline you don't know how much better AI is than random, and can't prove ROI.
Not removing already-purchased and viewed items — recommendations look pointless and lose trust.
Ignoring privacy: using behavioral data without consent and anonymization is a legal and reputational risk.

exercises.question: You have a catalog of 800 SKUs and 2k active users per month. Should you launch personal recommendations right now?
exercises.hint: Check the applicability thresholds: catalog >1k SKUs, active users >5k/month, repeat purchase >10%. Consider whether you have enough data to personalize and whether cold start will block you.

exercises.question: Embedding similarity returned a top-50 candidate set. Which filters, and in what order, must you apply before Claude reranks?
exercises.hint: Recall the chain: remove already bought/viewed (history filter), remove out-of-stock and low-margin. Claude should rank only what the business actually wants and is able to sell.

exercises.question: How do you prove AI recommendations beat the old "random products" block?
exercises.hint: You need an A/B test against a baseline. Which metrics to measure — CTR on the block, AOV, cross-sell rate. Without a control group the numbers mean nothing.

s1.title: Why, and what result you measure
s1.why: Recommendations are one of the highest-ROI AI cases: 20-35% of large-store revenue runs through them. But without a metric fixed up front, the project becomes a "pretty block with no effect". First agree on what counts as success.
instructions: Fix the current baseline: what share of revenue currently comes through recommendations (often 0%), plus AOV and cross-sell rate.
Pick target metrics: revenue from recommendations (goal 15-25% of total), AOV (+10-20%), cross-sell (+30-50%), CTR on the block (3-8% vs 0.5-1.5% for random).
Check applicability: catalog >1k SKUs, active users >5k/month, repeat purchase rate >10%.
Decide the display points (product page, cart, email) and priority — start with one.
s1.validate: You have a document with baseline numbers, target metrics, and one chosen display point for the pilot.
s1.tip: Don't launch recommendations "because everyone has them". Without a measurable baseline and data thresholds, you'll have nothing to prove uplift with.

s2.title: Data: catalog and behavior
s2.why: Recommendation quality is 80% data quality. You need two sources: the catalog (what we can sell) and behavior (what the user likes). Without them neither embeddings nor Claude will be relevant.
instructions: Collect the catalog: for each SKU — title, description, category, price, availability (in/out of stock), margin.
Collect behavioral data: views, add-to-carts, purchases per user and per session.
Build product embeddings from text (title + description + category) — this is the basis of similarity and solves cold start.
Prepare user history in a form you can pass to Claude: recent views and purchases, categories.
Check privacy: data is anonymized and there is consent to use behavior.
s2.validate: For a test user you can get their history in seconds, and for any product the top similar items by embedding.
s2.tip: Content embeddings (not just behavior-based) are critical: they give recommendations even for new products and new users, where collaborative filtering is helpless.

s3.title: Key step 1 — "similar / bought together" logic
s3.why: This is the core of the system: select candidates. Embedding similarity handles "similar products", market-basket handles "bought together". This step yields the top-50 candidates that Claude will choose from.
instructions: For the current product X, compute embedding similarity and take the top-50 similar SKUs.
In parallel, compute market-basket "bought together" pairs (what is most often bought with X) — these are cross-sell candidates.
Apply the history filter: remove from candidates anything the user already bought or recently viewed.
Remove out-of-stock and, if needed, low-margin — the business shouldn't show unavailable or loss-making items.
Assemble the final candidate pool (similar + bought together) to pass into reranking.
s3.validate: Input is product X — output is a clean list of ≤50 available, not-yet-bought candidates with metadata (price, availability).
s3.tip: Apply filters BEFORE Claude, not after. Feeding Claude a dirty pool with out-of-stock items wastes ranking on products you can't sell.

s4.title: Key step 2 — Claude rerank and embed into the storefront
s4.why: Embeddings give similarity but don't understand user context. Claude reranking picks the best 6 of the 50 candidates for the specific person and explains the choice — and explainability gives +15% CTR over unexplained recommendations.
instructions: Build the reranking prompt: give Claude the list of 50 candidates + user history + the rule "pick the 6 most relevant, accounting for history, price, and availability".
Ask it to return a short explanation per product ("you viewed similar items in category Y").
Parse the response and render the block: 6 products + an explanation for each.
Embed the block into the chosen point (product page / cart / email) with a clear heading ("bought with this", "you might like").
Cache the result for a reasonable time so you don't call Claude on every render.
s4.validate: A real product page shows 6 personal recommendations, each with a relevant explanation, all available to buy.
s4.tip: Ask Claude to account for price and availability right in the prompt — so reranking won't suggest an item 10x pricier than what was viewed, or one nearly sold out.

s5.title: Quality and risks: privacy, repeats, balance
s5.why: Recommendations easily slip into anti-patterns: repeating already-bought items, leaking private data, optimizing only for clicks at the cost of margin. This step protects user trust and business money.
instructions: Check there are no repeats: already-bought and recently-viewed items must not appear in the output.
Balance clicks and margin: don't let AI optimize for CTR alone — watch the share of low-margin items shown.
Privacy: use only anonymized data with consent, and don't surface sensitive inferences about the user in explanations.
Add a cold-start fallback: for new users — category bestsellers or content embeddings instead of personalization.
Check diversity: the block shouldn't be 6 near-identical products.
s5.validate: Across test scenarios (new user, returning user, cart with a pricey item) recommendations are relevant, with no repeats or out-of-stock items.
s5.tip: If AI optimizes for clicks unconstrained, the business loses money. Margin and availability must be hard filters, not wishes.

s6.title: Rollout + checklist and A/B measurement
s6.why: Without an A/B against a baseline you don't know how much better AI is than random recommendations — and can't prove ROI. The final step turns the pilot into a measurable, manageable product.
instructions: Launch the A/B: control group — old block / random, test group — AI recommendations.
Track the target metrics from step 1: CTR on the block, AOV, cross-sell rate, share of revenue from recommendations.
Run the checklist: filters (out-of-stock, bought, low-margin) work; explanations show; privacy respected; cache and fallback in place.
Record the uplift and, if positive, roll out to the other display points.
Set up monitoring: alerts on CTR drops and on showing unavailable items.
s6.validate: The A/B test shows a statistically significant uplift of the test group over baseline on key metrics, and the checklist passes fully.
s6.tip: Roll out one display point at a time (product page first, then cart, then email) — so you isolate each block's effect and don't confuse the causes of changes.

ec-support.title: AI Support in E-commerce
ec-support.subtitle: Claude as a tier-1 support agent: instant answers on orders, shipping and returns — escalating the hard cases to a human
ec-support.whatItIs: Claude acting as a tier-1 support agent for an online store. It answers routine queries (order status, shipping, returns) using order management data and an up-to-date knowledge base, and escalates hard cases (disputed returns, payment issues, B2B specifics) to a human with full context. A concrete application of [[node:cs-tier1|tier-1 automation]] in the commerce domain.
ec-support.approach: The course shows how to roll out AI support step by step: from understanding which 70-80% of queries are routine, to configuring answers from the knowledge base and order status, escalation rules, quality control and a final launch checklist. Grounded in a real architecture: intent recognition, then tool call to the order API, then answer or escalation.
outcomes: Understand which support queries are routine and automatable, and which require a human
Configure Claude's answers from the knowledge base and real order status via tool calls
Define clear escalation rules so hard cases reach an agent with context
Control answer quality: tone, policy freshness, deflection rate
Launch a pilot with measurable metrics (deflection, response time, CSAT)

applyIn.title: Online store with high ticket volume
applyIn.description: Support drowns in "where is my order" and "how do I return" queries. AI closes 60-80% instantly, agents switch to hard cases.

applyIn.title: Marketplace or D2C brand
applyIn.description: Status, shipping and return queries come in around the clock. Claude answers instantly at any time, escalating only what needs a human.

applyIn.title: Seasonal sales peaks
applyIn.description: On Black Friday or sales events ticket volume multiplies. The AI layer keeps response time without hiring temporary agents.

pitfalls: Auto-escalating everything — no deflection, the support team is not unloaded. Clear escalation rules are needed upfront.
Not syncing the knowledge base — AI answers from old return policies, the policy changed, complaints follow.
Ignoring tone — generic AI tone in support drives customers away. Brand voice tuning is mandatory.
Letting AI answer where a human is needed (disputes, defects, payment) — growing dissatisfaction instead of relief.
Launching without metrics — you can't prove deflection rate or CSAT improvement, nothing to justify scaling.

exercises.question: Take your store's last 50 tickets. What percentage falls into three categories: order status, shipping, returns?
exercises.hint: These routine categories account for 70-80% of volume and are closed by AI instantly. The rest are escalation candidates.

exercises.question: Define 3-4 escalation rules: under what conditions must a query go to a human rather than AI?
exercises.hint: Example triggers: product defect, return dispute, payment issue, B2B customer. Defect = human.

exercises.question: What tool calls does Claude need to answer "where is my order #12345"?
exercises.hint: At minimum — a call to the order management API (GET /orders/{id}) for status, ship date and tracking number.

s1.title: Why AI support and what's the outcome
s1.why: Without a clear goal the project becomes a "chatbot for the sake of a chatbot". You need to grasp that the value of AI support is freeing agents from routine workload that brings no upsell or relationship.
instructions: Capture the problem: response time on simple questions, share of order-status queries, CSAT drop.
Define target metrics: tier-1 deflection rate (goal 60-80%), response time (from 2 hours to instant), agent capacity on hard cases (+200%).
Describe who wins and how: customer — instant answer, agent — only hard cases, business — CSAT up by 0.3-0.7.
s1.validate: You have a 1-page doc with the problem and 3-4 measurable goals.
s1.tip: Capture baseline metrics BEFORE launch — otherwise there's nothing to prove the effect against.

s2.title: Map of routine queries: order, shipping, return
s2.why: 70-80% of e-commerce queries are routine. For AI to close them you need to break the flow into intents and understand what data each answer requires.
instructions: Export 100-200 real tickets and group them by intent: order_status, shipping, return, other.
For each intent describe where the answer comes from: knowledge base (policies) or order API (status, tracking).
Mark intents AI must NOT close — they go into escalation rules in step 4.
Estimate the share of each intent — this is your potential deflection.
s2.validate: You have an intent table with answer source and share of flow.
s2.tip: Order_status is usually the most frequent intent (>20% of queries) — start automation there.

s3.title: Key step 1 — answers from the base and order status
s3.why: This is the core of deflection. Claude recognizes intent, makes a tool call to the order API or pulls an answer from the knowledge base — and replies to the customer instantly with fresh data.
instructions: Connect Claude to order management via a tool call: GET /orders/{id} returns status, ship date, ETA, tracking number.
Connect the knowledge base (return/shipping policies) as the source for intents that don't touch an order.
Set up intent recognition: query, then intent detection, then tool selection, then answer.
Build answer templates: "Your order shipped on May 23, delivery May 25, tracking X" — specifics, not generic phrases.
Tune brand voice: the store's tone, not generic AI.
s3.validate: On "where is my order #12345" Claude makes the correct tool call and answers with real data in the right tone.
s3.tip: The knowledge base must be the single source of policies — never hardcode the return policy into the prompt.

s4.title: Key step 2 — escalating hard cases to a human
s4.why: Deflection doesn't mean "AI answers everything". Hard cases (defect, dispute, payment, B2B) must go to a human — but with full context so the agent doesn't start from scratch.
instructions: Define escalation rules: defect = human, disputed return = human, payment issue = human, B2B = human.
Set up context handoff on escalation: order details + customer history + (if needed) a photo upload prompt.
Add a fallback: if Claude is unsure of the intent or answer — escalate, don't guess.
Describe the agent handoff: where the ticket lands, in what form, with which priority tag.
s4.validate: "I want to return it, the item is broken" is recognized as return_with_defect and escalated to an agent with order context.
s4.tip: Better to over-escalate a borderline case than give a wrong answer on returns — that's costlier for the brand.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: AI support without quality control quickly accumulates risks: stale policies, wrong tone, incorrect order answers. They must be caught systematically.
instructions: Set up regular knowledge base sync — when a return/shipping policy changes, the source updates, not the prompt.
Introduce sampled review: check a sample of AI answers for correctness and tone.
Track metrics: deflection rate, share of wrong answers, share of false escalations.
Build a feedback loop: the customer can request a human at any moment.
s5.validate: There's a base-sync process and a regular review with quality metrics.
s5.tip: The most common complaint source is policy desync. Make base updates part of the policy-change process.

s6.title: Rollout and launch checklist
s6.why: A pilot on one intent with measurable metrics reduces risk and justifies scaling. A hard "everything at once" launch hurts CSAT.
instructions: Launch a pilot on one intent (usually order_status) on part of the traffic.
Compare metrics with the baseline from step 1: deflection, response time, CSAT.
Run the checklist: intents mapped, tool calls work, escalation rules defined, knowledge base synced, brand voice tuned, metrics captured.
Expand to shipping and return after confirming metrics on the first intent.
s6.validate: The pilot shows deflection in the target range without a CSAT drop, the checklist is fully passed.
s6.tip: The pilot goal is a 65% cut in tier-1 ticket volume in ~60 days. Scale only after proven numbers.

ec-loyalty.title: AI Loyalty Systems
ec-loyalty.subtitle: From a flat discount to an adaptive program tied to the customer lifecycle
ec-loyalty.whatItIs: A personal AI-driven loyalty program: the system analyses buyer behavior, identifies the segment (VIP, Active, Cooling, At-Risk, Churned) and picks a relevant offer — cashback, exclusive products, early access or a win-back offer. Not "one program for everyone" but an adaptive structure that shifts with the customer's lifecycle stage.
ec-loyalty.approach: The course moves from rationale (why leave the flat discount) through gathering purchase and churn data to the two key steps — segmentation with offer matching and retention triggers. It closes with quality control (privacy, spam, unit economics) and a rollout checklist. The backbone is the quarterly loyalty review: Claude segments the base, proposes a structure, the team validates and launches, and after 30 days the cycle repeats.
outcomes: You understand why a generic program (buy 10 times = 10%) gives flat results and where AI lifts ROI at the same spend
You have gathered purchase, frequency and churn data — the foundation for segmentation
You split the base into 5 segments and matched the optimal offer to each one's motivation while respecting margin
You set up retention triggers: win-back for cooling, onboarding for new, save-campaigns on churn signals
You rolled out the program with privacy controls, anti-spam limits and uplift measured against a control group

applyIn.title: Segmented loyalty instead of a flat discount
applyIn.description: Moving the base from a single 10% discount to 5 segments with different offers — targeting +25% retention in 90 days.

applyIn.title: Save-campaigns on churn signals
applyIn.description: AI spots churn signs (growing interval between purchases, falling basket) and fires a win-back before the customer is gone.

applyIn.title: Onboarding bonus for new buyers
applyIn.description: A new buyer gets not a generic discount but a bonus that drives the second purchase and locks in the habit.

pitfalls: Ignoring unit economics: generous VIP offers eat the margin — AI must respect business constraints
Not measuring: without A/B segments vs a control group you cannot prove uplift or separate program effect from seasonality
Forgetting exit: AI is great at finding churn signals, yet they get used only for acquisition, not for save-campaigns
Spamming segments: too-frequent messages cut engagement and trigger unsubscribes — frequency must be capped
Breaking privacy: using behavioral data without consent and transparency is a legal and reputational risk

exercises.question: The current program gives 4% redemption on a base of 8k active buyers with an 18% repeat rate. Should you adopt AI loyalty, and why?
exercises.hint: Check the thresholds in the 'when to apply' section: base >5k, repeat >15%, redemption <5%. All three hold — there is room to grow and the current program clearly isn't working.

exercises.question: Claude proposed 15% cashback for the VIP segment. What question must you ask before launch?
exercises.hint: Check margin: does the offer fit unit economics? VIP generosity can eat the profit. Request the margin impact and a comparison against the control group.

exercises.question: How do you prove the retention gain came from the program, not seasonal demand?
exercises.hint: You need a control group — part of the base without the new program. Comparing segment retention vs control isolates the program effect from external factors.

s1.title: Why leave the flat discount, and what result
s1.why: Generic loyalty (buy 10 times = 10%) gives everyone the same offer and a flat result. AI-driven loyalty matches the offer to individual motivation, lifting ROI at the same program spend.
instructions: Capture current metrics: program engagement, repeat purchase rate, CLV, churn rate
State the goal in numbers — target band: engagement from 5% to 30-40%, repeat +15-25%, CLV +20-35%, churn −10-20%
Describe how VIP motivation differs from cooling and new customers — the basis for different offers
Lock in the principle: the program is adaptive to the lifecycle, not static
s1.validate: You have a 'current to target' table across 4 metrics and understand why a flat discount doesn't move them.
s1.tip: Frame the goal as uplift against a control group, not an absolute number — that keeps the result provable.

s2.title: Gather purchase and churn data
s2.why: Segmentation and triggers only work on clean behavioral data. Without purchase history, frequency and churn signals, AI can't tell a VIP from a leaving customer.
instructions: Collect per customer: purchase history, frequency, average basket, date of last purchase
Add current program participation and redemption history
Compute derived signals: growing interval between purchases, falling basket — early churn signs
Check completeness and quality: gaps and duplicates distort segments
s2.validate: There is one dataset that lets you compute recency, frequency and monetary value per customer.
s2.tip: Recency, frequency, monetary is the minimal set that already supports a working segmentation.

s3.title: Key step 1 — segments and offers
s3.why: This is the program core: split the base into lifecycle segments and match each one its optimal offer with rationale and margin awareness.
instructions: Give Claude the data and ask it to segment the base into 5 groups: VIP, Active, Cooling, At-Risk, Churned
For each segment request the optimal offer with rationale: VIP — exclusive access, new — onboarding bonus
Require unit economics: the offer must not eat the segment's margin
Get the program structure + messaging + impact estimate per segment
Hand the result to the loyalty/marketing team to validate before launch
s3.validate: 5 segments defined, each with an offer that has a rationale and a margin check.
s3.tip: Ask Claude for a rationale per offer — it both checks the logic and arms the team to defend the budget.

s4.title: Key step 2 — retention triggers
s4.why: Segments are static without triggers. Retention rests on timely reaction: win-back before exit, onboarding to lock in the habit, save-campaigns on churn signals.
instructions: Define the trigger for At-Risk/Cooling: a win-back offer when the interval between purchases grows
Set the onboarding trigger for new customers — a bonus driving the second purchase
Use churn signals for save-campaigns, not only for acquisition
Set firing frequency and thresholds so one segment isn't spammed
s4.validate: Each segment has an assigned trigger with a firing condition and a frequency cap.
s4.tip: A churn signal is most valuable before the actual exit — catch Cooling, not just Churned, where winning back costs more.

s5.title: Quality and risks — privacy and spam
s5.why: A strong program breaks on risks: over-spamming kills engagement, a privacy breach is a legal and reputational hit, and ungrounded generosity eats profit.
instructions: Verify behavioral data is used with consent and transparency for the customer
Cap message frequency per segment — an anti-spam rule against unsubscribes
Run every offer through unit economics: does the margin go negative
Build in a control group to measure uplift and separate program effect from seasonality
s5.validate: There are privacy rules, frequency caps, a margin check and a dedicated control group.
s5.tip: A control group looks like lost reach, but without it any retention gain is disputable — it's your proof insurance.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Loyalty is a cycle, not a one-off launch. A quarterly review revisiting segmentation after 30 days turns the program into a self-learning system.
instructions: Launch the program on segments with the control group enabled
After 30 days give Claude the results — it analyses and refines the segmentation
Check the checklist: data, then 5 segments, then offers with margin, then triggers, then privacy/anti-spam, then measurement
Lock in a quarterly review rhythm to adapt to shifts in base behavior
s6.validate: The program is launched, the review cycle is scheduled, and the checklist passes with no gaps.
s6.tip: The first cycle is a hypothesis, not the end. The real value of AI loyalty is iterative segment correction on actual results.

ec-analytics.title: AI Commerce Analytics
ec-analytics.subtitle: Claude as a commerce analyst: from data to daily insights and actions
ec-analytics.whatItIs: A course on turning Claude into a first-pass commerce analyst for e-commerce. Instead of "here's a dashboard, figure it out", the team gets "here's what happened today and what to do about it": Claude reads sales, traffic (GA4) and ad spend data, spots anomalies, forms hypotheses and proposes concrete action items. The human analyst is not replaced — they validate and dig deeper, while the routine first-pass review goes to AI.
ec-analytics.approach: We move from value to rollout. First we lock in why this matters and what result to expect. Then we connect data sources (sales, traffic, margin) and check their quality. The two key steps are teaching Claude to find anomalies and to turn findings into insights with action items. Then we cover risks separately — the main one being confusing correlation with causation — and finish by embedding it into the work cycle with a checklist. The throughline: AI provides narrative and hypotheses, not exact attribution; humans make the decisions.
outcomes: You understand where AI analytics truly speeds up decisions and where it's dangerous, and which business result to measure (time-to-insight, anomaly detection lag).
You can assemble the minimal set of sources — sales, traffic, ad spend, margin, inventory — and check they reconcile before analysis.
You've set up a prompt that surfaces deviations from the norm and top movers by category, rather than just restating numbers.
You get a structured daily/weekly briefing as output: what happened, hypotheses, 3 prioritized action items.
You've embedded a process with guards against common mistakes: data checks, separating correlation from causation, an archive of past insights.

applyIn.title: Daily commerce briefing
applyIn.description: By 9:00 Claude posts a summary of yesterday to Slack: revenue vs average, top movers by category, anomalies with hypotheses and 3 actions for today. The team comments and executes.

applyIn.title: Weekly review prep
applyIn.description: Instead of raw table dumps, the analyst gets a structured read of the week: what rose/fell, likely candidate causes, what to verify. The meeting runs on insights, not on reading numbers.

applyIn.title: Early anomaly detection
applyIn.description: AI compares metrics against history daily and flags sharp deviations (conversion drop, CAC spike, category dip) on the day they appear, not a week later.

pitfalls: Using AI as an attribution engine. Claude does not know your real multi-touch attribution model — use it for narrative and hypotheses, not for pinpointing exact causation.
Ignoring data quality. On broken data AI will produce confident but false insights. Reconcile GA4 with actual sales before automating.
Keeping no archive. Without a history of past insights every day starts from scratch — AI is strong when it sees the context of prior findings and decisions.
Treating hypotheses as facts. A phrasing like "the likely cause is X" needs human verification, not immediate action on every point.
Automating too early. Until the prompt reliably produces useful output on manual runs, putting it on a schedule just scales the noise.

exercises.question: Your daily briefing reports: "Revenue dropped 18%, likely cause is rising CAC in Meta." What must you do before changing the ad budget?
exercises.hint: Think about the difference between correlation and causation and about data quality. A coincidence in time isn't a cause; first check whether the data pull broke and whether other simultaneous factors exist (seasonality, inventory, promos).

exercises.question: What is the minimal set of sources needed for insights to be meaningful, and why is revenue alone not enough?
exercises.hint: Revenue without traffic, spend and margin doesn't explain "why". You need at least sales, traffic (GA4), ad spend and margin/inventory to tell a demand drop apart from a traffic drop or rising costs.

exercises.question: The briefing starts "from a blank slate" every day and doesn't remember yesterday's hypotheses. How do you fix this?
exercises.hint: This is about documenting and history. Feed Claude an archive of past insights and their verification status so it can track whether yesterday's hypothesis held up.

s1.title: Why this matters and what result to measure
s1.why: Without a clear goal, AI analytics turns into nice text nobody uses. First we lock in the problem (low action item rate, slow review) and the result metrics, so later we can tell whether it worked.
instructions: Describe the current process: how often the team looks at metrics and how long it takes from data to decision (typically 3-5 days).
Check the applicability threshold: sales >$100k/month, metrics reviewed regularly, but action item rate is low and anomalies are spotted late.
Lock in 2-3 result metrics: time-to-insight (from days to 1 day), anomaly detection lag (from weeks to 24 hours), share of reviews with concrete actions.
State the AI's role explicitly: first-pass analysis and hypotheses, while validation and depth stay with a human.
s1.validate: You have written down the current time-to-insight, the target, and 2-3 metrics that will make it clear in a month whether AI had an effect.
s1.tip: If the team doesn't look at metrics regularly or sales are small, AI analytics is premature. The data habit comes first.

s2.title: Data sources: sales, traffic, margin
s2.why: An insight is only meaningful if there's enough data to explain "why". Revenue without traffic, spend and margin can't tell a demand drop apart from a traffic drop or rising costs.
instructions: Assemble the minimal set: sales (revenue, orders, AOV), traffic (GA4: sessions, conversion, sources), ad spend (CAC by channel), margin and inventory.
For each source, fix the export format and period (day/week) — Claude works with whatever you feed in.
Add a benchmark: averages for prior weeks, so there's something to compare deviations against.
Describe the business context: active promos, seasonality, launches — without it AI will mistake a normal event for an anomaly.
s2.validate: One input data package for a representative day/week is ready, including sales, traffic, spend, margin and averages for comparison.
s2.tip: Start with a manual export into a single document. Leave connection automation for later — first confirm the data is enough for a useful conclusion.

s3.title: Key step 1 — analysis and anomaly detection
s3.why: The core value is telling normal noise apart from a meaningful deviation. If Claude just restates numbers, it isn't analytics. We teach it to compare against the norm and surface top movers.
instructions: Give Claude the input data plus averages/benchmark and ask it to compare current metrics against the norm in percentages.
Ask it to surface top movers by category and channel — what rose and dropped the most.
Ask it to flag anomalies (sharp deviations from history) separately from expected fluctuations.
Fix the output format: metric, then deviation vs average, then anomaly flag, so the result is structured.
Run it on 2-3 different days and verify the AI doesn't flag ordinary noise as an anomaly.
s3.validate: On test data Claude reliably surfaces real deviations and top movers without raising false alarms on normal fluctuations.
s3.tip: Give the significance threshold explicitly (e.g., deviation >10% from average), otherwise the AI will react to any noise.

s4.title: Key step 2 — from insights to actions
s4.why: A deviation with no explanation or action is useless. This step turns "what happened" into "what we do": hypotheses per anomaly and prioritized action items.
instructions: Ask Claude to form 1-2 candidate cause hypotheses for each anomaly found, labeled as assumptions.
Ask for 3 prioritized action items for today — concrete and verifiable, not "improve conversion".
For each action, specify which data would confirm or refute the hypothesis.
Assemble it into a briefing format: summary, then anomalies with hypotheses, then 3 actions — ready to post to Slack.
Feed Claude an archive of past insights so it notes whether yesterday's hypothesis held up.
s4.validate: The output is a structured briefing with hypotheses (labeled as assumptions) and 3 concrete actions that can be executed and verified.
s4.tip: Require each action to be tied to a hypothesis and a way to verify it — this cuts out abstract advice.

s5.title: Data quality and causation risks
s5.why: The most expensive mistakes here come from acting on false insights. AI confidently interprets both broken data and coincidences in time, so explicit guards are needed before automation.
instructions: Before each analysis, reconcile GA4 with actual sales: a data mismatch makes any insight unreliable.
Separate correlation from causation: "likely cause" phrasings are hypotheses requiring human verification, not a command to act.
Don't use Claude as an attribution engine — it doesn't know your multi-touch model; use it for narrative, not exact attribution.
Check for simultaneous factors: seasonality, promos, inventory may explain a deviation better than the AI's first hypothesis.
Set a rule: a critical decision (budget, price) only after checking data and at least one alternative hypothesis.
s5.validate: You have a pre-action checklist: data reconciled, hypothesis separated from fact, alternative causes considered.
s5.tip: Add a prompt instruction to label confidence: "hypothesis / needs verification / confirmed by data" — it disciplines both the AI and the team.

s6.title: Embedding into the cycle and a checklist
s6.why: Value appears only when the briefing becomes part of the team's daily rhythm and accumulates history. This step turns manual runs into a sustainable process.
instructions: Lock in the rhythm: a daily briefing by morning and/or a structured weekly review, with a place to publish (e.g., Slack #commerce-daily).
Set up an insight archive: every briefing is saved, hypothesis status updated — so AI works with history, not a blank slate.
Automate the data feed only after manual runs are reliably useful.
Assign an owner who validates insights and closes action items — without one the process fades.
Once a week, check the step 1 metrics: did time-to-insight speed up, did the share of reviews with actions grow?
s6.validate: The briefing ships on schedule, insights have an archive and an owner, and the step 1 result metrics are measured regularly.
s6.tip: Start with one channel and one cadence. Expand only after the team actually uses the first briefings.

ec-pricing.title: AI Pricing Optimization
ec-pricing.subtitle: Deploy AI as decision support for pricing: data, then recommendations, then human decision
ec-pricing.whatItIs: A course on using Claude to support pricing decisions in e-commerce: AI analyses demand signals, competitor prices, cost structure and margin targets, then recommends optimal prices and promotional triggers. This is not automatic pricing (risk of catastrophic mistakes), but decision support for the merchandiser or pricing manager. The final pricing decision always belongs to a human.
ec-pricing.approach: We move from goal to deployment: first we fix why AI pricing support is needed and what result we expect; then we collect three data streams (demand, competitors, margin); then we build two key steps — price analysis and recommendations, then controlled tests with a human decision; next we close quality and risks (antitrust, price wars, data trust); and finally we roll out the process with a checklist. The throughline: AI recommends — a human decides. The course gives no financial advice; it describes a working process.
outcomes: Understand where pricing delivers high ROI and why a 1% price improvement = 8-12% to profit
Collect three data streams for recommendations: demand, competitor prices, margin
Build a prompt where Claude returns ranked price recommendations with rationale
Run controlled price tests where AI proposes and a human approves
Close legal and reputational risks: antitrust, price wars, data trust

applyIn.title: Weekly pricing review
applyIn.description: Once a week you run SKU-level sales, competitor prices and inventory through Claude and get 3-5 pricing opportunities instead of the usual 1-2 a quarter.

applyIn.title: Promotion decisions
applyIn.description: For SKUs with inventory build-up, AI estimates the impact of a promotion, and the pricing manager approves or rejects it in hours rather than days.

applyIn.title: Reacting to competitors
applyIn.description: When competitors drop a price by 15%+, AI suggests match or differentiate with margin in mind, and a human picks the strategy.

pitfalls: Auto-apply: applying price changes automatically with no human — AI may miss a supplier contract (minimum price) or promo commitments
Ignoring elasticity: recommending +5% on an elastic product loses more in volume than it gains in margin
Unvalidated competitor data: scraping breaks, and AI on bad data produces bad recommendations
Price coordination: using competitor data to coordinate prices is an antitrust violation, not optimization
Price war: blindly matching competitor prices triggers a downward spiral that kills margin for everyone

exercises.question: You have 800 SKUs, margins ranging from 8% to 45% across categories, 6 main competitors, prices reviewed quarterly by hand. Does this case fit AI pricing support?
exercises.hint: Check the thresholds from the deployment step: catalog >500 SKUs, margin spread >20%, competitors >5, decisions manual and rare.

exercises.question: Claude recommends a +5% price hike on a SKU with high demand elasticity. Why might this be a mistake and what should you check?
exercises.hint: An elastic product loses a lot of sales volume when the price rises — calculate whether the margin gain offsets the volume drop.

exercises.question: Explain why the pricing decision cannot be fully handed to AI, using two specific risks from the course.
exercises.hint: Recall supplier contracts (minimum price), promo commitments and antitrust constraints.

s1.title: Why AI in pricing and what result
s1.why: Pricing is a high-ROI lever: a 1% price improvement yields 8-12% to profit for a typical e-commerce business. Classical pricing tools are expensive and need a data science team. Claude + structured data covers 60-70% of that value at 20% of the cost, especially for teams without a dedicated pricing analyst. Without a clear goal, deployment becomes a toy rather than a tool with measurable impact.
instructions: Fix that AI here is decision support, not auto-pricing: the final decision stays with a human
Define target metrics: gross margin (+1-3 pts), pricing review frequency (from quarter to week), time-to-promotion-decision (from days to hours)
Assign a responsible human (merchandiser / pricing manager) who approves decisions
Agree that the course and process give no financial advice — it is an analysis working tool
s1.validate: You have 2-3 measurable goals written down and a named human who approves pricing decisions.
s1.tip: Start with one high-margin, high-competition category — the effect shows up there fastest.

s2.title: Collect data: demand, competitors, margin
s2.why: Recommendation quality equals input data quality. Without structured data on demand, competitor prices and margin, AI produces guesses. Three streams are the minimum that makes a recommendation grounded rather than random.
instructions: Demand: SKU-level sales for the last 30 days + inventory levels
Competitors: current competitor prices (scraped or from a feed) for the main categories
Margin: cost structure and margin targets per SKU or category
Record constraints: supplier contracts (minimum prices), promo commitments, MAP policies
Check freshness and correctness of competitor data — scraping breaks
s2.validate: You have three data streams for one period plus a list of pricing constraints (contracts, commitments).
s2.tip: Flag SKUs with contractual minimum prices immediately — AI must not recommend going below them.

s3.title: Key step 1: price analysis and recommendations
s3.why: This is the heart of the process: Claude turns three data streams into a ranked list of pricing opportunities with rationale. Without structure on output, the manager drowns in data instead of deciding faster.
instructions: Feed Claude the bundle: SKU-level sales + competitor prices + inventory + margin targets
Ask it to surface groups: where elasticity allows a price hike; where competitors are 15%+ lower (match or differentiate); where inventory build-up needs a promo
Require a rationale and estimated impact on margin/volume for each recommendation
Ask AI to explicitly account for elasticity differences, not a flat percent across all SKUs
Pass the list of pricing constraints so AI does not break contractual minimums
s3.validate: Claude returned a ranked list of several pricing opportunities with rationale and an impact estimate for each.
s3.tip: Ask AI to split recommendations into 'raise', 'lower/match' and 'promo' — easier to route into work.

s4.title: Key step 2: tests, the human decides
s4.why: A recommendation is not a decision. Auto-applying price changes is the main mistake: AI may miss a supplier contract or promo commitments and misjudge elasticity. Human in the loop is mandatory, and a controlled test separates real impact from noise.
instructions: The pricing manager validates each recommendation against contracts and promo commitments
Roll out changes on a limited set of SKUs as a controlled test, not the whole catalog at once
Compare actual impact on margin and volume with the estimated impact from the recommendation
Document accepted and rejected recommendations — this trains the process
Never give AI the right to change prices in the system automatically
s4.validate: Every price change passed manual approval, and the test effect is measured against the forecast.
s4.tip: Rejected recommendations with a reason are as valuable as accepted ones — they reveal AI blind spots.

s5.title: Quality and risks
s5.why: AI pricing carries not only business but also legal and reputational risks. Antitrust law, price wars and data trust can erase all the upside or lead to fines. Risk control is not optional — it is part of the process.
instructions: Antitrust: use competitor data only for your own decisions, never to coordinate/align prices
Price war: do not blindly match — consider that cuts trigger a spiral; sometimes differentiate is better
Data trust: validate competitor data before use, flag stale or suspicious values
Elasticity: review recommendations on elastic products separately to avoid losing volume
Log data sources and rationale — for audit and review of disputed decisions
s5.validate: You have a risk checklist (antitrust, price war, data quality, elasticity) that every recommendation passes through.
s5.tip: If you doubt the legality of using competitor data, that is a signal to stop, not to optimize.

s6.title: Deployment and checklist
s6.why: A one-off experiment delivers nothing — value is in a regular process. The shift from quarterly manual review to weekly AI-assisted review is the result. A checklist keeps discipline and the 'AI recommends — a human decides' principle.
instructions: Check fit criteria: catalog >500 SKUs, margin spread >20%, competitors >5, decisions manual and rare
Set the weekly pricing review as a recurring ritual with a fixed owner
Per-cycle checklist: data fresh, then competitor data validated, then constraints accounted, then recommendations received, then human approved, then risks checked, then impact measured
Expand category coverage only after a stable result on the first one
Revise the prompt and thresholds as you accumulate data on rejected recommendations
s6.validate: The weekly process runs, the checklist applies to every cycle, and the team finds 3-5 pricing opportunities a month.
s6.tip: Maturity benchmark: teams find and use 3-5 pricing opportunities a month instead of the usual 1-2 a quarter.

ec-inventory.title: AI Inventory Management
ec-inventory.subtitle: Demand forecasting, reorder points and over/understock control with AI
ec-inventory.whatItIs: An approach where AI supports inventory decisions: forecasting demand, generating replenishment triggers, detecting slow-movers and recommending dead stock clearance. Analysis is built on historical sales + seasonality + current signals (search queries, traffic to categories). It is not a replacement for an ERP, but structured analytics on top of existing data without heavy integration.
ec-inventory.approach: We move from value to control: first fix the why (the dual risk of overstock and stockout) and the outcome you need, then prepare sales and seasonality data, then two key steps — demand forecast and reorder points with alerts, then set up forecast quality control and risk management, and finally embed it into the buying team's weekly cycle with a checklist. The forecast always passes through human override — AI prepares the decision, a human places the PO.
outcomes: Stockouts on bestsellers cut by 50-70% via early replenishment alerts
Dead stock reduced by 30-50% through early slow-mover detection and clearance
Inventory turn ratio up 20-40% and 15-25% of cash freed from trapped inventory
A regular weekly inventory briefing instead of a rare monthly manual review
Measurable forecast accuracy with a feedback loop — the forecast improves every month

applyIn.title: Catalog >1k SKUs with frequent stockouts
applyIn.description: When bestsellers regularly hit zero and revenue is lost — AI flags SKUs at risk of stockout in the next 14 days in advance.

applyIn.title: Dead stock buildup
applyIn.description: If cash is trapped in slow-movers >90 days — AI finds them and recommends a clearance promo with an estimated lift, freeing cash.

applyIn.title: Seasonal business
applyIn.description: When demand swings by season — AI catches early signals (season approaching, category traffic rising) and suggests raising stock ahead of time.

pitfalls: Trusting the forecast without human override: AI is strong at pattern detection but blind to unprecedented events (viral post, competitor shutdown).
Ignoring supplier constraints: AI optimizes for demand, but lead times and MOQ are hard real-world limits.
Not measuring forecast accuracy: without a feedback loop the forecast does not improve and errors repeat.
Forecasting on dirty data: duplicate SKUs, returns mixed into sales, and gaps over out-of-stock periods distort the model.
Optimizing for demand only: forgetting cash limits and warehouse capacity, creating new overstock in other categories.

exercises.question: You have 1,500 SKUs, bestsellers regularly stock out, and manual review happens monthly. Where do you start adopting AI inventory management?
exercises.hint: First the why and outcome, then the data. Gather sales velocity, current stock, lead times and seasonal patterns — without them the forecast is meaningless.

exercises.question: AI suggests raising stock of category X by 40% before the season. What do you check before placing the PO?
exercises.hint: Human override + supplier constraints: are lead times and MOQ realistic, does the signal contradict known events, is there cash for the purchase.

exercises.question: A month after launch the forecast was off by 35% on several SKUs. How do you use this?
exercises.hint: This is the feedback loop: analyze where and why AI was wrong (unprecedented event? dirty data?) and adjust the input signals.

s1.title: Why and what outcome
s1.why: Inventory is a dual risk: overstock traps cash and leads to writedowns, stockout kills revenue and loyalty. Without a clear goal, AI becomes a pretty report no one uses.
instructions: Fix which pain is sharper now: stockouts on bestsellers or dead stock buildup.
Define a measurable goal: e.g. stockout rate -50% in a quarter or dead stock -30%.
Assign an owner — the buying team that will validate the forecast and place POs.
Agree that AI prepares the decision and a human makes it (human override as the rule).
s1.validate: One target metric with a number and deadline is defined, and there is an owner for decisions.
s1.tip: Do not try to solve overstock and stockout at once in the first cycle — pick one focus.

s2.title: Sales and seasonality data
s2.why: A forecast is only as good as the input data. AI combines sales history, seasonality and current signals — gaps and duplicates distort everything.
instructions: Gather per SKU: sales velocity, current stock, supplier lead times.
Add seasonal patterns and current signals — search queries, traffic to categories.
Clean the data: remove duplicate SKUs, exclude returns from sales, mark out-of-stock periods (otherwise demand is understated).
Capture supplier constraints — MOQ and lead times as separate fields.
s2.validate: There is a per-SKU table with velocity, stock, lead times and seasonal tags, free of obvious duplicates and gaps.
s2.tip: Out-of-stock periods are a common trap: zero sales there means demand was impossible, not absent.

s3.title: Key step 1 — demand forecast
s3.why: Demand forecasting is the core of the approach. AI finds patterns in history and seasonality and estimates expected demand per SKU, giving a basis for all purchasing decisions.
instructions: Pass the prepared data to AI and ask for a per-SKU demand forecast over a horizon (e.g. 14-30 days).
Ask it to factor in seasonal signals: season approaching, category traffic rising.
Request not just numbers but an explanation — why AI expects growth/decline on specific SKUs.
Flag SKUs with high forecast uncertainty separately — they need extra human override.
s3.validate: A demand forecast for top SKUs is produced with reasoning and a confidence-level note.
s3.tip: Ask AI to separate stable patterns from guesses — it instantly shows where to trust and where to verify.

s4.title: Key step 2 — reorder points and alerts
s4.why: A forecast without action is useless. Replenishment triggers and alerts turn demand into concrete signals to reorder now and clear now.
instructions: From the forecast and lead times, compute the reorder point: at what stock level to place a PO to avoid stockout.
Set an alert for top SKUs at risk of stockout in the next 14 days.
Add detection of slow-movers >90 days with a clearance promo recommendation and estimated lift.
Check that recommendations respect supplier MOQ and lead times, not just demand.
s4.validate: A list of restock alerts and slow-movers with concrete recommendations is produced, aligned with supplier constraints.
s4.tip: Compute the reorder point from lead time + buffer: the longer the supply, the earlier the alert.

s5.title: Forecast quality and over/understock risks
s5.why: Without accuracy control AI does not improve, and blind trust leads to new overstock or understock. The feedback loop is mandatory, not optional.
instructions: Every month compare forecast to actuals and compute forecast accuracy per SKU.
Analyze big errors: unprecedented event, dirty data, or ignored supplier constraints.
Watch both risks: overstock (cash trapped) and stockout (lost revenue) — do not optimize for just one.
Adjust input signals and rules based on the analysis — that is how the system learns.
s5.validate: There is a monthly accuracy review with conclusions, and the forecast visibly improves cycle over cycle.
s5.tip: Log every major error with its cause — in 2-3 months it becomes a library of patterns where AI is blind.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: The approach works only as a regular rhythm. A weekly inventory briefing embeds AI into the purchasing cycle, and a checklist guards against common errors.
instructions: Launch a weekly inventory briefing: input — per-SKU data, output — restock alerts, slow-movers, seasonal signals.
Fix the route: AI prepares the briefing, then buying team validates, then places the PO (human override).
Add a pre-PO checklist: lead times and MOQ checked, no known events against the signal, cash available.
Run a monthly accuracy review (step 5) and update the input signals.
s6.validate: The briefing ships weekly, decisions pass the checklist and human override, accuracy is reviewed monthly.
s6.tip: Start with one weekly briefing for the top category — expand coverage after the first quarter with a measurable result.

ec-segmentation.title: AI Customer Segmentation
ec-segmentation.subtitle: From demographics to behavioral segments in an hour, not a month-long ML project
ec-segmentation.whatItIs: An approach where AI finds natural behavioral groups in your customer base — not "men 25-35" but "buy every 2 weeks, discount-sensitive, open email in the evening". The segments become input for personalization, loyalty, and marketing campaigns.
ec-segmentation.approach: You collect behavioral signals (RFM plus categories, channels, time-of-day), turn customers into feature vectors, and cluster them with embeddings. Claude interprets the clusters into business-readable segments with characteristics and strategy. The goal is 4-8 actionable groups the team can truly operate, not statistical noise.
outcomes: Email engagement 50-100% higher than a blast send
Campaign ROI 30-60% higher thanks to precise targeting
The same revenue with a 20-30% smaller marketing budget
4-8 clear segments described as "who they are and what to offer them"
Ready-made targeting recipes for marketing, loyalty, and CRM

applyIn.title: Marketing campaigns
applyIn.description: Instead of identical emails for everyone, distinct offers and timing per segment, lifting open rate and conversion.

applyIn.title: Loyalty program
applyIn.description: Different retention mechanics for champions, dormant, and new customers — each gets a reason to return or buy more often.

applyIn.title: Storefront and recommendation personalization
applyIn.description: The segment determines which categories and price range to surface first, raising relevance.

pitfalls: Too many segments: more than 10 and the team can't operate them. Sweet spot is 4-8 actionable groups.
Not refreshing: customer behavior shifts, so refresh at least quarterly.
Ignoring business meaning: if you can't put a cluster into words, it's noise, not signal.
Segmenting on a small base: fewer than 5k active customers gives too few signals for stable groups.
Building segments on stereotypes and sensitive traits (gender, age, ethnicity) instead of real behavior — inaccurate and a privacy risk.

exercises.question: You have 8k active customers and one blast email for all. Which 5-6 behavioral signals will you collect into a feature vector to find segments?
exercises.hint: Think RFM plus behavior: frequency, recency of last purchase, average order value (AOV), favourite categories, preferred channel, time-of-day activity.

exercises.question: The algorithm returned a cluster of 1,200 customers. How do you tell whether it's a real segment or noise?
exercises.hint: Check: can you describe in words "who they are and what to offer them", is their behavior distinct from other groups, is the size large enough to run a campaign.

exercises.question: Segmentation was done six months ago and engagement is starting to drop. What's the likely cause and what do you do?
exercises.hint: Customer behavior has shifted and the segments are stale. You need a quarterly refresh — rebuild the vectors and re-cluster on fresh data.

s1.title: Why segment and what outcome
s1.why: Without understanding differences between cohorts, all marketing goes out as one message — that depresses engagement and burns budget. This step pins down the exact metric you're improving.
instructions: State the problem: identical emails for everyone, conversion varies sharply between groups, and it's unclear why.
Pick the target metric: email engagement, campaign ROI, or budget efficiency.
Record the expected effect as a reference: engagement +50-100%, ROI +30-60%.
Confirm the base is sufficient: more than 5k active customers for stable signals.
s1.validate: You have one measurable goal and confirmation that active customers exceed 5k.
s1.tip: Don't start for the sake of pretty segments — start for a concrete metric you'll show a quarter later.

s2.title: Collect data: RFM and behavior
s2.why: Segment quality equals signal quality. Demographics barely predict behavior, so the feature vector is built on customer actions.
instructions: Collect RFM signals: purchase frequency, recency of last purchase, average order value (AOV).
Add behavioral features: favourite categories, preferred channel, time-of-day activity (when they open emails / buy).
Normalize the data into a single feature vector per customer.
Exclude sensitive demographic fields (gender, age, ethnicity) from the clustering basis.
Check completeness: no customers with empty key signals.
s2.validate: Every active customer has a normalized vector of RFM plus 2-3 behavioral features, without sensitive demographics.
s2.tip: Time-of-day activity and preferred channel often separate segments more sharply than total spend.

s3.title: Key step 1 — derive the segments
s3.why: This is where groups are born. Embedding clustering finds natural patterns, and Claude translates them into business language — that's the leap from an ML month to an hour of work.
instructions: Run the feature vectors through embedding clustering, aiming for 6-8 natural groups.
Pass the clusters to Claude with the request: for each group give characteristics, size, value, and a recommended engagement strategy.
Give each segment a human-readable name (e.g. champions, dormant, discount hunters).
Trim to 4-8 actionable segments by merging small or indistinguishable groups.
s3.validate: You have 4-8 named segments, each with a description of characteristics, size, and value.
s3.tip: If two clusters lead to identical marketing actions, merge them: operational simplicity beats statistical purity.

s4.title: Key step 2 — actions per segment
s4.why: A segment without an action is useless. Value appears when each group maps to a concrete offer, channel, and timing.
instructions: For each segment write a targeting recipe: which offer, which channel, at what time.
Match the mechanic to motivation: a discount for price-sensitive, exclusivity for champions, reactivation for dormant.
State a hypothesis: what exactly will grow in this segment from this action.
Prepare the recipes in a format ready for marketing, loyalty, and CRM.
s4.validate: Each segment has a concrete targeting recipe (offer + channel + timing) and a testable hypothesis.
s4.tip: Dormant customers don't need another discount — they need a reason to return; champions need no discount at all.

s5.title: Quality and risk: privacy and stereotypes
s5.why: Segmentation works with personal data and can quietly slip into discrimination or noise. This step protects both accuracy and customers.
instructions: Check each segment for business meaning: can you explain "who they are and what to offer them".
Confirm the groups are built on behavior, not on sensitive traits and stereotypes.
Review privacy: what data is used, is there consent, do the segments reveal too much.
Drop clusters you can't interpret — that's noise, not signal.
Record that the targeting doesn't create unfair exclusions for groups of customers.
s5.validate: All segments are explainable in words, based on behavior, privacy-checked, and free of discriminatory logic.
s5.tip: A sanity test: if you'd be embarrassed to show a segment's description to the customer themselves, redo it.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Segmentation only delivers in production and with regular refresh — otherwise it goes stale along with customer behavior.
instructions: Load the segment definitions and targeting recipes into marketing/loyalty/CRM.
Launch campaigns by segment and compare metrics with the old blast send.
Schedule a quarterly refresh: rebuild vectors and re-cluster once a quarter.
Run the checklist: 4-8 segments, each named and explainable, an action exists, privacy checked, an owner and next refresh date assigned.
s6.validate: Segments run in live campaigns, metrics are compared against the baseline, and a next refresh date is set.
s6.tip: Set the refresh reminder the moment you launch — without a date on the calendar, segmentation quietly decays within a couple of quarters.

ec-team-workflow.title: Commerce Team AI Workflow
ec-team-workflow.subtitle: How to move AI to the team level in e-commerce instead of relying on individual heroes
ec-team-workflow.whatItIs: A course on how an e-commerce team (merchant, content, CRO, support, analyst) moves from individual AI usage to a single team process: a shared Project with brand voice and catalog taxonomy, reusable templates and Skills, a shared prompt library, and a steady knowledge-sharing rhythm. This is a meta skill that ties all role-based AI tasks into one workflow.
ec-team-workflow.approach: We start from the goal and a measurable outcome, then define exactly what to hand to AI (product cards, search/re-ranking, analytics), roll out the shared infrastructure, build two key team rituals (the shared library and weekly office hours), lock in quality through owners and metrics, and finish with a rollout plan and checklist. Every step is a concrete action, no abstractions.
outcomes: A single team standard for working with AI instead of fragmented individual approaches
A shared Project with brand voice, catalog taxonomy and templates, available to all roles
Reusable Skills and a shared prompt library with clear naming
Onboarding for a new team member drops from 2 weeks to 3-5 days
Measurable ROI: time saved, quality uplift and velocity on specific workflows

applyIn.title: A team of 4+ people on AI
applyIn.description: When several e-commerce roles already use AI but each in their own way — the course provides a single standard and shared infrastructure.

applyIn.title: Brand voice drift
applyIn.description: When product cards, newsletters and support all sound different because everyone has their own prompt — shared voice and templates align the tone.

applyIn.title: Lost knowledge and duplication
applyIn.description: When insights get stuck in the head of the most productive AI user and functions duplicate effort — the shared library and office hours solve it.

pitfalls: A team with no ownership: "everyone uses AI" = nobody owns the workflow. Every part (voice, templates, skills) must have an owner.
Individual heroes: knowledge piles up in one person's head and leaves with them. Shared infrastructure is needed from day one.
Ignoring measurement: without metrics "AI usage" stays abstract. Track time saved, quality uplift and ROI on specific workflows.
Copying someone else's stack without adaptation: foreign Skills and templates with no tie to your catalog and voice deliver weak results.
Launching everything at once: trying to roll out voice, templates, Skills and rituals in one go breaks adoption. Deploy in stages.

exercises.question: Name 3 parts of the team AI infrastructure that must have an owner, and suggest who on your team could be it.
exercises.hint: Look at brand voice, card/content templates, and reusable Skills — each part is a separate area of responsibility.

exercises.question: Which 3 metrics will you track to prove the ROI of the team AI workflow over a quarter?
exercises.hint: Think about time saved on a typical task, quality uplift (voice consistency, % of edits), and velocity / onboarding time.

exercises.question: Design the agenda for the first 30-minute weekly AI office hours for a team of 5 roles.
exercises.hint: Allocate time for 1-2 wins, 1 fail, a shared-library update, and one cross-functional case.

s1.title: Why a team AI workflow and what outcome
s1.why: Individual AI usage in commerce does not scale: roles work their own way, brand voice drifts, insights are lost across functions. A team that puts AI at the process level pulls 6-12 months ahead of competitors. Without a clear goal and metric, the rollout turns into an abstract "everyone uses AI".
instructions: State the problem concretely: where you have inconsistent results between roles (merchant, content, CRO, support, analyst).
Set a measurable quarterly goal: e.g. +30-50% team velocity and onboarding in 3-5 days instead of 2 weeks.
Pick 2-3 baseline metrics: time saved on a typical task, quality uplift (voice consistency), velocity.
Write the expected outcome in one paragraph so the team understands why the process is changing.
s1.validate: You have a written goal with concrete numbers and a set of 2-3 metrics to check the effect after a quarter.
s1.tip: Frame the goal from the team's pain, not the technology: "cards sound different" lands harder than "we must use AI".

s2.title: What to hand to AI: cards, search, analytics
s2.why: Before building infrastructure, you need to know which team tasks AI does well and consistently. In e-commerce there are three cores: generating and refining product cards (PDP), search and re-ranking results, analytics and segmentation. A clear task list keeps the workflow from sprawling into "everything".
instructions: Collect tasks by role and mark the recurring ones: PDP writing, search/re-ranking, weekly analytics, customer segmentation, support replies.
For each task define what goes to AI and what stays with a human (final decision, fact-check, brand sign-off).
Identify candidates for reusable Skills: pdp-writer, search-rerank, weekly-briefing, customer-segment-analyzer.
Sort tasks by frequency and ROI — start the rollout with the most frequent ones.
s2.validate: There is a table of team tasks marked "AI / human" and a list of 3-4 candidates for shared Skills.
s2.tip: If a task runs less than once a week, don't turn it into a Skill yet — start with a prompt template.

s3.title: Key step 1: shared Project and brand voice
s3.why: The foundation of a team workflow is a single workspace where brand voice, catalog taxonomy and templates live. Without a shared Project each role keeps its own context, and voice inevitably drifts. A shared Project + CLAUDE.md with rules make results predictable for the whole team.
instructions: Create a shared Claude Project "Commerce Workspace" with access for all roles.
Upload the base files: brand voice guide, product taxonomy, content templates, brand do/don't.
Add a CLAUDE.md with usage rules and naming conventions for prompts and Skills.
Assign an owner for brand voice and an owner for templates — they keep the files current.
s3.validate: Any team member opens the Project, sees current voice files and templates, and understands the naming conventions from CLAUDE.md.
s3.tip: A brand do/don't with "bad vs good" pairs works better than a long tone description — AI aligns to examples.

s4.title: Key step 2: shared library and office hours
s4.why: Infrastructure is dead without a knowledge-sharing rhythm. Two mechanisms keep it alive: a shared library of reusable Skills and prompts, and weekly AI office hours where the team shares wins and fails. This turns individual finds into a team asset and kills "individual heroes".
instructions: Turn the 3-4 most frequent workflows from step 2 into reusable Skills and put them in the shared Project.
Set up a shared prompt library with clear naming — anyone can take another's prompt without editing the source.
Launch 30-minute weekly AI office hours: 1-2 wins, 1 fail, library updates, one cross-functional case.
Assign someone responsible for maintaining the library and moderating office hours.
s4.validate: The first office hours have happened, and the library holds working Skills and prompts already used by at least one other role.
s4.tip: Fails at office hours are worth more than wins: they update brand do/don't and CLAUDE.md rules the fastest.

s5.title: Quality, roles and risks
s5.why: A team workflow without ownership and metrics degrades: voice drifts, knowledge leaves with people, the effect stays abstract. This step locks in who is responsible for what, how quality is measured, and which risks need to be kept under control.
instructions: Assign owners to each part of the infrastructure: brand voice, templates, Skills, prompt library.
Introduce a brand sign-off: a human checks AI output for voice consistency and facts before publishing.
Set up tracking for the step 1 metrics and make them visible to the team (time saved, quality uplift, velocity).
Document the risks: voice drift, individual heroes, lack of measurement — and a countermeasure for each.
s5.validate: Every part of the infrastructure has an owner, the brand sign-off works, metrics are collected and visible to the team.
s5.tip: Make the metrics dashboard part of office hours — what is shown regularly is what the team actually maintains.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: Rolling out everything at once breaks adoption. A staged launch with a checklist and a quarterly review turns a one-off setup into a sustainable process the team maintains itself. A maturity sign (Stage 3): a new team member is productive in 5 days, cross-functional projects run on shared infrastructure.
instructions: Deploy in stages: shared Project and voice, then templates, then Skills and library, then office hours and metrics.
Run the readiness checklist: owners assigned, CLAUDE.md filled, library alive, metrics collected, office hours on the calendar.
Run a new or hypothetical team member through onboarding on the infrastructure and measure how many days until they are productive.
Set up a quarterly review: which AI workflows delivered ROI and which did not — drop the weak ones, scale the strong ones.
s6.validate: The checklist is complete, the first quarterly review has happened, and onboarding on the infrastructure fits within 3-5 days.
s6.tip: Don't scale a workflow without confirmed ROI: better 3 working Skills than 10 abandoned ones.
